rows.title: Eurozone inflation jumps to highest level in three years
rows.content:
Olaf Storbeck in Frankfurt

Published October 2 2026

Eurozone inflation shot up to a three-year high of 3.8 per cent in September, after the escalating conflict in the Middle East triggered a resurgence in oil and gas prices.

The reading published by Eurostat on Friday was up from 3.2 per cent in August and higher than economists’ forecast of 3.6 per cent in a Reuters poll. In all four of the Eurozone’s largest economies, inflation rose at a faster pace than expected, with Spain reporting an annual rate of 5 per cent.

Rising inflation and concerns over the sustainability of public finances in more indebted countries such as France have triggered a surge in Eurozone borrowing costs.

That has pushed yields of French 10-year government bonds up as much as 0.1 percentage points to 4.96 per cent on Thursday, their highest level since 2002. They have since come back slightly to 4.92 per cent.

September marked the seventh month in a row that inflation in the 21-country bloc was above the ECB’s medium-term 2 per cent target.

The ECB was the first central bank in the G7 to respond to the Middle East energy shock, increasing borrowing costs by a quarter point in June and again in September.

Traders are betting that policymakers will respond by raising interest rates by another quarter point to 2.75 per cent by the end of the year.

Top ECB official Isabel Schnabel said this week that rate-setters must act pre-emptively to stop high energy prices from feeding into broader prices and wages.

rows.title: Volvo Cars issues profit warning as China sales fall
rows.content:
Kana Inagaki in London

Published October 2 2026

Volvo Cars has issued a profit warning and pulled its annual guidance, becoming the latest European carmaker to warn investors of a further decline in sales in China.

The Swedish group said the market downturn in China and a slower than expected recovery in the US would have “a significant negative impact” on quarterly core earnings and cash flow. Third-quarter vehicle deliveries fell by 11 per cent year on year.

The profit warning comes as European manufacturers have been hit by intense competition from Chinese rivals, higher US tariffs and rising raw-material costs caused by the conflict in the Middle East.

In China, which has long been one of the biggest sales drivers for the industry, the market has come under pressure from cut-throat price competition between domestic carmakers while higher fuel prices have led to a dramatic decline in demand for internal-combustion-engine vehicles.

A string of other European carmakers including BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Volkswagen have issued profit warnings in recent months, citing worsening conditions in the world’s largest car market as the collapse in petrol vehicle sales has been compounded by slower EV sales.

Volvo , which is owned by China’s Geely, had previously forecast full-year growth in sales volume and cash flow. Shares in the carmaker fell more than 4 per cent in morning trading on Friday.

“The market downturn in China showed no signs of easing, and the recovery in the US premium segment remained below our earlier expectations,” said Erik Severinson, chief commercial officer.

Klaus Zellmer, the former boss of Škoda, is set to take over as chief executive by October next year, replacing current head Håkan Samuelsson , who came out of retirement in 2025. Under Zellmer’s tenure, Škoda replaced Porsche as the biggest contributor to parent company Volkswagen’s profits.

Volvo said it would take “further decisive actions” to improve its performance following a recent freeze on the hiring of new white-collar jobs globally.

It said the European market remained “resilient”. But auto industry analyst Matthias Schmidt noted that only 39 of its new EX60 electric SUVs had been delivered in Sweden in September.

“If they do have an issue, it could be huge, given consumers are likely looking to transition to battery EVs at a faster rate given the pump price anxiety and their peers that have had a better ramp-up, particularly BMW,” Schmidt said.

Volvo said sales of EVs grew 29 per cent year on year during the third quarter, accounting for nearly one-third of all cars sold. It added that “allocations for the EX60s produced have so far mainly gone to countries other than Sweden”.

“In Europe, we continue to see strong demand for our new cars,” Severinson said, adding that the company was focused on increasing production of the EX60.

rows.title: Goldman Sachs bought Shein shares worth $220mn after dismal IPO
rows.content:
Arjun Neil Alim in Hong Kong

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Goldman Sachs bought shares worth about $220mn in Shein after stepping in following the online fast-fashion retailer’s rocky stock market debut last month.

The Wall Street bank purchased 42mn shares, or 13 per cent of Shein ’s initial share float, last month as part of its role as an underwriter that lets it buy shares in the open market to “stabilise” a stock shunned by investors.

Goldman said it bought the shares, colloquially known as the “greenshoe”, for between HK$35.90 and the listing price of HK$48.56 in a filing to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.

At an average purchase price of HK$42.23, Goldman’s purchases would have produced a trading profit of about $34mn.

Shein’s long-awaited $26bn initial public offering was labelled a “disaster” by analysts after shares plunged as much as 10 per cent on the first day of trading.

The stock has now fallen 38 per cent, valuing the company at $16.3bn.

Underwriting banks sell more stock at the issue price than they are given by the company. They then cover their short position either by exercising an option to issue more shares — known as the overallotment option — or buying them on the open market below the listing price if they fall.

Buying back shares on the open market allows Goldman to prop up the share price to some degree by increasing demand.

The standard agreement among underwriters, as set out by the International Capital Markets Association, states that any profits from stabilisation would be shared between the banks responsible for underwriting the IPO.

Goldman declined to comment.

In some cases, as with Deliveroo’s disappointing London listing in 2021, the underwriters agreed in advance to surrender any stabilisation trading profits to the company.

Shein had cash and cash equivalents of $15bn on its balance sheet as of June 30 according to its latest results, just $1.3bn under its market capitalisation.

Shein’s IPO value represents a sharp fall from its peak. Pandemic lockdowns and social media hype from “Shein hauls” drew young consumers to its affordable fashion and earned the company a valuation of about $100bn following a 2022 private fundraising round.

rows.title: The Burnham tell
rows.content:
Jennifer Williams in Manchester

Published October 2 2026

This article is an on-site version of our Inside Politics newsletter. Subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every weekday. If you’re not a subscriber, you can still receive the newsletter free for 30 days

Good morning from Manchester.

I returned from Andy Burnham’s homecoming conference in Liverpool to find people here mulling the broader reputational impact on the city of the Premier League’s findings against Manchester City.

The prime minister has been thinking about that too. It was a little surprising to see him highlight Abu Dhabi’s investment in Manchester at this particular moment after tending to sidestep it up to now in his narrative about the city’s growth model.

While Abu Dhabi’s investment here has undoubtedly transformed huge swaths of post-industrial Manchester, it was also contentious long before the Premier League’s conclusions, be it for the price of the homes developed in partnership with the council, the opaque nature of the public-private relationship or general antipathy towards the rights record of the United Arab Emirates.

So it hasn’t always felt as though Burnham particularly wanted to dwell on that aspect of the city’s economic turnaround — until, unexpectedly, the club’s finances hit headlines for the wrong reasons.

Anyway, with growth models in mind, on to Tuesday’s extraordinary conference speech.

Inside Politics is edited by Harvey Nriapia today. Follow Stephen on Bluesky . Read the previous edition of the newsletter here . Please send gossip, thoughts and feedback to [email protected]

I’ve written before about how responsive Burnham is: you can often spot when someone absorbs a criticism by how often they repeat it back to you.

“He’ll be down in London more than here and his attention will change from Ashton,” said one woman out doing her shopping in Ashton-in-Makerfield the day after the by-election was declared. She had voted Reform in the local elections a few weeks earlier and was yet to be convinced by Burnham.

He responded to such critiques, which were common online, in vox pops and while canvassing, very quickly.

First came the social media videos and posts in which he promised to make Makerfield the most important constituency in the country; then there was the “Makerfield Test”; and finally there was the linguistic tell: over and over again, including in his acceptance speech, he stressed that the by-election was no “stepping stone”.

By his conference speech, he had a new tell.

Manchester doesn’t quite answer enough questions to function as a national growth narrative, and it isn’t apparent what philosophy is likely to guide any painful fiscal trade-offs coming down the track at this month’s Budget.

Why do we know Burnham has clocked this? Because he’s already told us.

“I have to evolve it,” he told the New Statesman of “Manchesterism” in an interview published a few days before conference. “It was right to . . . localise it when I was the mayor of that area, but now I think you can broaden it out . . . it is about broadening it out into a theory of growth.”

Less than a week later, he told conference: “I have a theory of growth.”

He repeated, later in the speech, that he and other mayors had a “theory of growth”, after telling chief executives the same thing at Monday’s business day.

According to his remarks this week, his theory starts with public control and devolution.

Burnham believes that only strong institutions on the ground can understand what makes a place tick and therefore create the necessary conditions for growth and investment, whether that’s skills or housing or infrastructure; and that privatisation and deregulation have resulted in an extractive economy that gives the taxpayer and communities poor returns, leaving the country overexposed to the whims of bond markets.

I think he probably knows that this is only a partial answer, though. Repeating “I have a theory of growth” feels like the September version of May’s “this isn’t a stepping stone”, almost as though he is trying to convince himself as much as his audience.

One government figure agrees. “That is absolutely his tell,” they say, admitting that he still needs to fill in some “blanks” on the economy.

One such opportunity may arise at a Gordon Brown-organised summit on innovation in Manchester next Friday, at which Burnham is set to speak. Brown is keen to see the agenda promoted ahead of the Budget.

Watch this space. We’ve heard little from the prime minister so far on innovation (or indeed competition), but under Burnham there was nonetheless a significant agenda in Manchester on that front.

He worked closely with universities, including on a reciprocal research and development partnership between Manchester and Cambridge; Jim O’Neill, his erstwhile informal adviser, has a successful venture capital outfit busy investing in university spinouts across the north of England.

Indeed the original “northern powerhouse” agenda that gave birth to the mayoralty, of which O’Neill was an architect, had R&D at its core. Immediately prior to Burnham’s arrival as mayor, George Osborne seemed to be here every five minutes opening a new advanced materials institute.

Burnham himself published Greater Manchester’s new growth strategy last year — “a concrete plan to reindustrialise the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution” — outlining the city-region’s existing and emerging growth clusters.

Some of this was very much focused around the strengths of the Oxford Road research corridor, even if the vibes imply a new era of mills and factories.

Nonetheless, he still always seemed more at home, to me, selling Atom Valley on the edge of Rochdale and Bury. This vast brownfield site is his vision for how Oxford Road’s growth can reach out into the former mill towns on the fringes of Manchester, translating the city’s abstract but fast-growing knowledge economy into tangible change in places much like Makerfield, where he instinctively wants to revive the sort of employment that anchored those communities when he was growing up.

That is probably more what he feels in his political bones than the whizzy economy of the university ecosystem, even though he knows its value on an intellectual level.

Tuesday’s speech was therefore authentically Andy: more the stuff of emotional instinct than of growth theory. It was partly why it jumped out of the TV screen and transfixed the conference hall.

It was also so well delivered that its strengths went a long way towards masking its weaknesses — even as the prime minister himself subconsciously signposted where they were.

You can’t actually try this until they next go on tour, but the highlight of my conference was watching the Sugababes do a brief turn at a Labour Students event at Camp and Furnace, just over a year after I saw them at the Salt and Tar in Bootle (which was right up there with the most fun I’ve ever had at a gig).

Back with the original line-up, in my view they have more than stood the test of time, quietly packing out bigger and bigger stages at Glastonbury, and they are one bit of 1990s nostalgia I am more than happy to indulge in.

It’s not easy being green | Green leader Zack Polanski faces two critical tests that will define his grip on his party: the conference in Brighton, where an anti-Zionism motion risks turning off many moderate voters, and the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, where bookmakers say he is likely to lose to Labour’s candidate.

Alternative suppliers | The government is searching for a UK alternative to Palantir as part of the prime minister’s “Buy British” push.

rows.title: Set designer Richard Peduzzi takes centre stage
rows.content:
Alice Cavanagh . Photography by Delphine Chanet

Published October 2 2026

On a Tuesday afternoon in midsummer, the French artist and scenographer Richard Peduzzi walks into the petite Théâtre des Bouffes-Parisiens dressed in pressed chinos and a white made-to-measure button-down. At 83, he still has a full head of hair, greying only at his sideburns. He surveys the stage, pauses, and says: “It’s a catastrophe,” staring at the large, draped mound of blue fabric that sits, volcano-like, in the centre of the stage.

It’s a set for Samuel Beckett’s absurdist drama Happy Days . The “mound” will bury the play’s protagonist, Winnie – first up to her waist, later to her neck – but Peduzzi is not happy with the form. It’s too flat on top, and there is an issue with the architecture underneath. The colour, however, is spot on. “This blue is the story of infinity, space, night and dreams, but also of confinement,” he says.

Peduzzi is one of Europe’s most celebrated scenographers, best known for his productions with award-winning directors Patrice Chéreau and Luc Bondy. His 58-year career spans monumental stage sets for countless operas – Strauss’s Elektra , Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde , Verdi’s The Sicilian Vespers – and, more recently, fashion shows. He collaborated with Chanel on both the brand’s AW26 collection, which featured towering crayon-coloured cranes, and its Métiers d’Art 2026 presentation in a disused New York subway. According to the brand’s artistic director, Matthieu Blazy , Peduzzi is “legendary”.

“Richard has revolutionised the practice of scenography, elevating it to a true art form,” he says. “It was after listening to a podcast with him that I immediately felt a strong connection. I was struck by his words, by his sensitivity and sense of emotion, and by the subtlety he always brings to his work, despite the grandeur of his set designs.”

But the full arc of Peduzzi’s output also includes paintings, furniture and interior design – much of which will be spotlit across three Paris exhibitions this autumn. The first, opening at the Musée d’Orsay on 6 October, is Vertige : a solo show that pairs a large-scale architectural model, made by Peduzzi for the museum’s inauguration 40 years ago, with 31 of his set-design “studies”. The artworks, in oil, gouache and watercolour, reveal an essential part of his process: his imaginings for “truly exceptional productions that have rightly gone down in history”, says Clémence Raynaud, general curator of architecture at the Musée d’Orsay and one of the exhibition’s curators. But they are also beautiful images in their own right: metaphorical architecture featuring recurring motifs such as archways, columns and blocks, cast in a misty palette of midnight blues and blacks, and sometimes a flash of vivid red.

Next up is a group show at the Opéra Garnier library; opening this month, it includes three paintings of Peduzzi’s set design for Richard Wagner’s epic Der Ring des Nibelungen , which premiered at the Bayreuth Festival in the summer of 1976. In November, Galerie RX will dedicate its Marais space to new work: paintings, tapestries, sculpture and furniture.

In almost all his creative outlets, Peduzzi has wrestled with themes of confinement and escape. “There’s always the idea of the box,” he says. “I like the line that Faulkner wrote: ‘His own flesh as well as all space was still a cage.’” In his 2014 book Là-bas, c’est dehors ( Over there is outside ), Peduzzi writes that since his early childhood in Normandy, he has been searching for an exit door.

After the second world war, his mother was imprisoned and his father deported to Germany – he was part of the Resistance and, in his absence, she, a vulnerable 18-year-old, was linked to a German officer (but was later pardoned). Peduzzi was raised between the homes of his maternal and paternal grandparents. “I was sort of carted around,” he says, adding that his memories of the time have indelibly shaped his visual universe. The war-torn port of Le Havre “was dark, but it was fascinating”. Of visiting his mother in prison, around the age of five, he still recalls the sprawling corridors, a labyrinth of high, featureless walls. He writes: “Ever since then I have felt cramped wherever I am, haunted by the feeling of being stuck in a dead end, trapped.”

Peduzzi’s mother was released from prison when he was a teenager, “but we never had much of a relationship”, he says. It was his father (though never very present either) who introduced him to drawing. At the age of 15, he moved to Paris to live with his paternal aunt; he studied for two years under sculptor Charles Auffret and worked for a time at an industrial design firm.

In 1968, at the age of 25, he met the young theatre director Chéreau through costume designer Jacques Schmidt. The connection was instant. “We talked about literature, books, painting,” recalls Peduzzi. “And the story has lasted 50 years.” They staged shows across Europe, covering Shakespeare, Molière, Neruda and Mozart. Their most notorious outing was Der Ring des Nibelungen , which outraged audiences for reframing the timeless mythical saga as an allegory for 19th-century capitalism – Peduzzi’s scenography included a 20th-century hydroelectric dam. Yet the final cycle of the performance in 1980 received a one-hour standing ovation. For Peduzzi, his sets are living entities. “I always say that a stage set is an actor – it must accompany, dream, precede, move with the other actors,” he says. “It should be a fully fledged character, in its own right.”

At Peduzzi’s atelier in the ninth arrondissement, the long, light-filled space is crammed full of books, paintings and wooden maquettes – meticulous constructions of theatre sets and doll-house-sized furniture. He and his wife, photographer Pénélope Chauvelot, have lived in an apartment above since the late ’90s. Long before that, “Charles Dullin [the French theatre director] lived here and would organise get-togethers with Sartre and Camus”, says Peduzzi. “It’s where Camus met María Casares.” At the home’s centre is a striking rotunda-style room painted a deep turquoise: a sculptural wooden rocking chair is his own design, as is a colourful geometric vase – both part of a 100-piece collection commissioned by Paris’s Mobilier National between 1988 and 2013.

“Richard never really changes his approach, whether he’s working on a stage set or a chair or a painting,” says Hervé Lemoine, president of the Manufactures Nationales, who worked with Peduzzi on a retrospective dedicated to his furniture in 2024. “He is a man of space, first of all. The one question he keeps asking himself is: how much can you leave out, and still say something.”

In his ninth decade, Peduzzi remains busy. “My father is always working,” says his daughter Antonine, who co-founded and runs the fashion label TL 180 . “For him, a holiday is a nightmare. If he stops, he gets anxiety. His work is his way of surviving.” His son Nicolas, a film director who is currently working on a documentary about his father, adds: “Even now, he is always drawing, on everything – in a restaurant he would draw on the napkin. It’s a compulsion.”

Currently, he is immersed in painting. A new series of canvases have a dreamlike quality; the same themes appear, but he looks at them with new eyes, he says. “There is a sense that things appear, disappear and come back again.” After taking on only a handful of theatre gigs in the past decade, he is also thrilled to be working on a stage design again – as well as the Beckett play, he is involved with a production of Così fan tutte showing in Vienna next year. “After [I stopped working with] Patrice Chéreau and Luc Bondy, I didn’t feel like doing any more theatre,” he says. “Now I think we can be reborn.”

Vertige, Musée D’Orsay , 6 October to 17 January; Les Revolutions du Ring, Bibliothèque-Musée du Palais Garnier , 27 October to 20 February; Galerie RX , 20 November to 13 January; Happy Days is on at Théâtre des Bouffes Parisiens until 1 November

rows.title: A trip to Lerryn, the mystical heart of Cornwall
rows.content:
Fiona Golfar . Photography by Cathy Kasterine. Styling by Kate Phelan. Model, Iris Lasnet

Published October 2 2026

Follow the autumnal blaze of bright red hawthorn and holly berries, blackberries, tangled stems of old man’s beard and dark elderberries that spring from the winding, hedgerow-lined lanes that lead from the ancient town of Lostwithiel, once the thriving trading capital of Cornwall, to the seemingly sleepy creekside village of Lerryn. Pause on the two-arch packhorse bridge spanning the still silver waters of the tidal River Lerryn, which flows towards the historic harbour town of Fowey, and take in the view. Within the river’s quiet surface and the ancient Ethy Woods that line its mossy banks lies a rich vein of history and local folklore.

The name Lerryn is said to derive from the old Cornish word lerion or leryan , meaning “waters”. The first written evidence of the village appears in the Assize Roll of 1284, a legal record of the period. Where there was water, there was trade, and Lerryn once enjoyed a bustling river economy. The bridge, which dates back to medieval times, was rebuilt on the orders of Elizabeth I to support the transport of silver from a local smelting works established by Burchard Cranach, a German silver smelter who was said to have “cured” the queen of smallpox. Two thousand ounces of silver were reportedly smelted there between 1556 and 1583.

Past the stepping stones that cross the fording place – which predates the bridge – beyond the swans and small river boats, and along the sandy banks where smugglers once brought their contraband inland by way of Brandy Lane, the creek still seems to carry an air of secrecy. French brandy, tea and tobacco were said to have been hidden in the cellars of the local manor Ethy House. The folds of the land, the hidden inlets and the sheltering woods make this place well-suited to concealment. It takes little imagination to picture small boats gliding in beneath the cover of darkness, their cargo swiftly carried into the tangled lanes.

In the early light, when mist still clings to the densely wooded valley, there is a magical stillness to this place, said to be an inspiration for Kenneth Grahame ’s The Wind in the Willows . Trees sweep down to the damp tidal banks of Lerryn Creek where little egrets, grey herons, cormorants and kingfishers gather. A humid microclimate allows lichen and rare ferns to grow abundantly on the bark of ancient oaks, their trunks twisting between the moss-covered rocks that line the water’s edge. When the tide rises, the river fills. It was not only smugglers who found their way to the village: historically, small barges, ketches and lighters sailed up from the Fowey estuary to deliver coal, timber and lime, as well as coastal sand rich in organic matter, broken shells and natural mineral salts. Local farmers valued it as a fertiliser and soil conditioner.

It is not hard to imagine why the stories given up by these sheltered waters – seemingly so little changed by time – inspired the first of a multitude of novels by Daphne du Maurier , who came to Fowey with her parents in 1926 and became enchanted with Cornwall. Her first novel, The Loving Spirit , a multigenerational saga of a family of shipbuilders, written when she was just 23 years old, was inspired by the masthead of an abandoned wrecked schooner, Jane Slade , in a secluded creek just a few miles from Lerryn. That recovered masthead remains on the side of Du Maurier’s family home today.

In these pictures, Iris Lasnet, an agricultural student and model, embodies the bold spirit of the Land Girls, the women who flocked to Cornwall from the cities during the second world war to take up work in the fields while the men went to war. She embodies the kind of woman who would be happy to dig her hands into the rich dark soil and enjoy the Cornish mizzle on her face as she strides through the verdant countryside.

Standing by the river, one can picture Kenneth Grahame imagining a world where Ratty’s boat noses along the bank or Mole discovers some small and secret wonder within the rich soil of the countryside. Here, there is a sense that the ordinary world has left this tiny corner of England untouched, yet enriched by nature, history and literature.

rows.title: Global bond market steadies after sharp sell-off
rows.content:
Emily Herbert in London and William Sandlund in Hong Kong

Published October 2 2026

Updated October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Global bond markets steadied on Friday after a sell-off that pushed US borrowing costs to their highest level since 2002 and sparked volatility in European sovereign bonds.

Yields on 10-year US Treasuries nudged 0.01 percentage points higher to 5.24 per cent during early trading in London, and European assets also stabilised after a volatile day of trading on Thursday. Bond yields rise when prices fall.

The 10-year French government bond yield fell 0.01 percentage points to 4.91 per cent, having jumped as much as 0.1 percentage points on Thursday after the release of a draft 2027 budget reignited concerns over the state of France’s public finances.

Equivalent Italian bonds had been caught up in the selling on Thursday but were flat on Friday morning at 4.71 per cent.

The euro, which took a sharp drop on Thursday amid the volatile trading, rose 0.1 per cent against the dollar to $1.126. Gilts and Bunds also both rallied in early trading.

Thursday’s moves “were reminiscent of the euro crisis in many respects, with sovereign contagion a big talking point,” said Henry Allen, macro strategist at Deutsche Bank.

Rates strategists at Dutch bank ING said market sentiment was “turning sour” on Europe’s debt dynamics.

The stabilisation in markets on Friday was helped by a fall in oil prices. The global benchmark Brent crude was down 1.1 per cent at $101.23 a barrel.

Investors will be watching Eurozone inflation data on Friday for the latest sign of how the European Central Bank might respond to the energy crisis unleashed by the conflict in the Middle East .

Bonds also stabilised in Asia. Japan’s 10-year yield fell 0.01 percentage points to 3.1 per cent.

Global stocks rose on Friday, with the Stoxx Europe 600 climbing 0.3 per cent in early trading and futures tracking the S&P 500 also up 0.3 per cent, although banks remained under pressure globally.

HSBC’s Hong Kong-listed stock fell more than 5 per cent, while in Japan Mizuho slipped 1.9 per cent after dropping 2.8 per cent the previous session. In Europe, Société Générale was down 0.6 per cent, adding to a 5 per cent fall on Thursday.

Kenny Ng, a strategist at brokerage Everbright Securities International, said the weakness in banks was related to the bond sell-off, “as they hold global bonds in their asset portfolios”.

Investors said they remained on high alert for further selling, and the impact of higher bond yields on global markets.

“We could see further spikes in yields,” said Grace Tam, deputy chief investment officer for Asia at BNP Paribas Wealth Management. “That could tighten financial conditions. That doesn’t bode well for risk assets, especially equities.”

rows.title: Shares in spreadbetter IG Group plunge by a quarter
rows.content:
Philip Stafford

Published October 2 2026

IG Group shares plunged as much as a quarter on Friday after the spread betting group sharply cut its annual growth forecast following a tough summer.

The FTSE 100 group cautioned that “less supportive market conditions” in the three months to September had hit revenue growth.

Global markets have been turbulent in recent months due to rising global borrowing costs, a volatile oil price and currency interventions by central banks — factors that typically encourage customers to use platforms such as IG’s.

But London-based IG said changes to the ways it priced and hedged the risks from customers’ trades, intended to boost the amount of income it retained, had left it with less revenue.

IG Group said revenue growth this year would be in a “mid-single-digit per cent range”, down from a May upgrade of between 10 per cent and 15 per cent.

Shares in IG fell more than 25 per cent in early trading before recovering slightly to trade 21 per cent lower, giving the group a market capitalisation of £3.4bn.

The changes by IG, designed to improve its market-making operation and boost so-called revenue retention, have been running for more than a year. IG said it had taken only a 70 per cent share of the gross income from trading in the third quarter, compared with an average of about 80 per cent before the schemes were introduced.

IG forecast that total revenue for the third quarter would be down about 14 per cent year on year, to about £240mn.

It also said it would incur one-off costs of about £30mn relating to its move to redomicile in Jersey, announced in July.

Breon Corcoran, chief executive, said growth in first trades and active customers remained strong in the quarter, and that he was “confident” the company would still meet its medium-term guidance.

In the summer IG announced plans to join the rush into the fast-growing US prediction markets with the $1.3bn purchase of Underdog Sports Holdings, the third largest in the regulated venue in the US behind Kalshi and Robinhood.

Underdog traded “strongly” in the quarter, IG said, with third-quarter net revenue more than doubling year on year to about $105mn.

rows.title: UK watchdog signals it may block major broadband deal
rows.content:
Kieran Smith in Brussels and Suzi Ring in London

Published October 2 2026

The UK’s competition watchdog has indicated that it may block a planned £2bn deal by Virgin Media O2’s shareholders to buy the country’s fourth-largest broadband operator, potentially delaying consolidation in the highly fragmented sector.

The Competition and Markets Authority said the plan for Nexfibre to buy Netomnia could “result in a substantial lessening of competition” in the wholesale supply of fixed broadband services due to the overlap between the companies’ existing networks.

The regulator also warned that it could impact prices for end consumers, particularly in the north of England. Its decision is provisional and follows an in-depth review .

The move is a blow to Nexfibre — a joint venture between VMO2 shareholders Liberty Global and Telefónica alongside private equity firm InfraVia Capital — which had argued the deal would create an 8mn-home fibre broadband network to challenge market leader BT’s Openreach.

However, the CMA said it did not believe the deal was necessary to achieve that, as Virgin Media O2 was already in the process of expanding its own fibre network.

The decision is set to delay consolidation in the highly fragmented UK broadband market, which has seen more than £31bn raised by “altnet” challengers set up to compete with established players including BT’s Openreach.

However, the cost of building out networks has left many providers saddled with high debt levels. The sector as a whole posted £1.5bn in losses in 2024, according to calculations by Enders Analysis, as consumer uptake of services also fell short of expectations.

Shareholders of Nexfibre, which agreed to acquire Netomnia from Substantia Group in February, have previously expressed a desire for further acquisitions in the fragmented sector, which has more than £9bn of net debt, according to Enders Analysis.

Goldman Sachs-backed CityFibre, which bid for Netomnia and lost out to Nexfibre, called for the deal to be blocked at an industry event in May. CityFibre would consider a rival bid should the deal collapse, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Nexfibre said in a statement that the CMA’s interim report “ does not reflect the commercial and competitive reality of Britain’s fibre market. It fails to prioritise the fibre investment the country needs, and the creation of a scaled, sustainable challenger to Openreach”. CityFibre said that “after recognising that harm, it is vital that the CMA takes the next step and blocks the deal”. It declined to comment on any future bid.

The companies have until October 23 to make further submissions. A final decision is expected by December 15.

rows.title: Putin has told military leaders to abandon rules of war, Zelenskyy says
rows.content:
Christopher Miller in Kyiv

Published October 2 2026

Updated October 2 2026

Vladimir Putin has instructed his military leaders to abandon the rules of war, prompting a steep increase in strikes on civilian targets amid a major push to regain the advantage in the conflict, according to intelligence intercepted by Kyiv.

Speaking in a bomb shelter inside a school that had just been hit by a Russian jet-powered drone, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the FT on Thursday that Ukrainian spy agencies had obtained information that the Russian president had scrapped the constraints that governed earlier air campaigns.

“He said there are no rules now,” Zelenskyy said, referring to the intelligence that included intercepted communications from Kremlin officials.

Zelenskyy said Putin gave the order in September, as Russia began intensifying its air strikes on Kyiv, hitting schools, hospitals and data centres. The Ukrainian president said the bombed school underscored how widespread such targeting had become.

Specifically, the president said, Russia was gearing up to intensify attacks on Ukraine’s largest cities with the aim of isolating them from the rest of the country as winter sets in.

Kyiv, the eastern stronghold of Kharkiv and the southern port city of Odesa are the main targets, according to Zelenskyy and a Ukrainian intelligence assessment described to the FT by Ukrainian and European officials.

The western city of Lviv, a crucial logistics hub near the Polish border, also features in Russia’s plan, according to Ukrainian and European security officials familiar with the intelligence.

Ukrainian officials said Moscow intended to strike nuclear facilities to sever them from the energy grid, increasing pressure on Kyiv to cave in to Russia’s demands in early 2027.

A new refugee flow towards the EU was also part of Moscow’s strategy, officials said, adding to concerns that a large influx of Ukrainians would strain countries where anti-immigrant sentiment is on the rise. Tensions with neighbouring Poland have increased this year, leading to more attacks on Ukrainians.

The Russian campaign comes in response to Ukrainian strikes on refineries, ports and warehouses deep inside Russia, which have caused fuel shortages and heightened a sense of insecurity in the country’s cities and tourist resorts.

The escalating air war contrasts with the largely static front line in eastern Ukraine, where Russian forces have struggled to advance and taken heavy losses. Kyiv and other cities are bracing for a harsh winter, however, as they lack sufficient air defences — mainly US-made Patriot interceptors.

The Kyiv school’s director, Valentyna Chorna, told the FT that 104 students and 60 teachers survived the attack because they had managed to get to the underground shelter before the drone hit the building just after 9am local time.

Zelenskyy said that earlier in the war, Moscow largely focused its attacks on energy and military facilities, to which Ukraine has responded in kind.

Now, he said, Russian drones were going beyond hunting civilians in Kherson and Sumy to strike schools, telecommunications hubs and data centres .

On Monday, one struck Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv. Around the time the school was hit on Thursday, two Russian drones exploded into one of the Ukrainian capital’s main bridges. Authorities said a third drone struck the bridge Thursday evening, sparking a fire and damaging a support column, the road surface and a crash barrier.

Zelenskyy said the attacks are intended not simply to destroy infrastructure but “to pressure people” and instil fear through relentless bombardments.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said: “Russia’s armed forces do not strike schools or hospitals.” Deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure is a war crime according to international law.

But videos from social media, verified by the FT, show that civilian sites have been hit.

Drone debris recovered from the site of Thursday’s strike on the Kyiv school and viewed by the FT bore Russian manufacturers’ markings and handwritten Russian text. Some components indicated that they had been manufactured in Russia on July 28, while some showed they were produced in the west.

Ukraine’s education ministry has documented more than 4,700 Russian attacks on educational institutions, while the World Health Organization has verified strikes on more than 3,000 healthcare facilities, since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022.

The aftermath of a Russian drone attack on a Kyiv school

As he strolled down empty classrooms adorned with children’s arts and crafts, the smell of smoke still heavy in the air, Zelenskyy said that because Putin could not capture the territory of the Donbas, he was now pursuing “massive attack[s], massive killing”.

“They couldn’t organise occupation, and that’s why they do now the same massive attack, massive killing,” he said in English, describing the campaign as an attempt to frighten civilians, force them from cities and weaken Ukraine’s ability to sustain the war.

Russia has in recent weeks intensified its aerial assaults on Kyiv, deploying faster jet-powered drones that have challenged Ukrainian air defences. The attacks have been relentless and have often continued through the night, disrupting daily life for the capital’s more than 3mn residents.

Zelenskyy said Russia had launched some 500 drones in the last day, of which about half were jet-powered and much harder to shoot down. He said Ukraine was destroying about 57 per cent of the jet drones and 85 to 90 per cent of conventional drones.

Ukraine is rushing to produce a high-speed interceptor drone capable of shooting down the Russian jet-powered weapons. Zelenskyy said there are five interceptors currently being tested. By the end of October, he said, Ukraine will be able to produce around 400 of one of those models. The four others remain in the testing stage.

The president said the race to counter the Russian drones faced hurdles, including a shortage of engines for their interceptors. “Engines [are] the key, we really import a lot of engines,” he said. “There are some engines of our production, but not enough.”

He said that Ukraine also faced a budget hole that was preventing the development and mass production of crucial defensive arms.

Zelenskyy said US-made F-16 jets were proving effective against Russia’s new jet-powered drones, but that too many of the aircraft — around half — were spending lengthy periods in Europe for repairs and maintenance.

Some jets, he said, were taking so long to return that Ukraine was losing valuable time when the fighters were most needed to defend its skies.

He said Kyiv wanted its western partners’ help to move more maintenance work inside Ukraine, arguing that keeping the aircraft closer to the battlefield would allow them to be returned to service faster.

Zelenskyy criticised the US and European governments for what he described as insufficient political will to force Putin to end the war, arguing that Ukraine’s partners had the economic and diplomatic leverage to exert greater pressure on Moscow.

When asked whether his partners were doing all they could to help Kyiv, Zelenskyy said: “Not enough, of course not enough.”

Additional reporting by Katya Arenina in Berlin and Henry Foy in Brussels

rows.title: Donald Quintin: ‘We’re entering a different market now’
rows.content:
Robert Armstrong

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

This article is an on-site version of our Unhedged newsletter. Premium subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every weekday. Standard subscribers can upgrade to Premium here , or explore all FT newsletters

Good morning. The S&P 500 has been all but unchanged for four months. Look under the hood, and you will find that earnings expectations for the coming year have risen 7 or 8 per cent over that period — but that this has been neatly offset by the price/earnings ratio index falling from 22 to 20. This is exactly what one would expect to happen in an environment where a combination of real economic growth and inflation are driving interest rates up: future earnings increasing while the valuation of those earnings falls as the discount rate rises. Once in a while, markets make sense. If you spot anything else making sense, email us: [email protected] .

Donald Quintin joined Lone Star Funds in 2010 and became its CEO in 2024. Previously, he worked at Merrill Lynch and Salomon Brothers. Lone Star, founded in 1995, invests across private equity, credit, and real estate. Headquartered in London, the group has offices around the globe, from Dallas to Tokyo. It had about $36bn in assets under management as of the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings .

Unhedged: How do Lone Star’s three strategies — buyout, commercial real estate and credit — fit together?

Donald Quintin: The fund started in commercial real estate during the savings and loan crisis, and pivoted through time to respond to the Japan banking crisis, then moved to Europe. As investment opportunities expanded it made sense to break the fund into commercial real estate and an opportunistic strategy, which we did during the early stages of the financial crisis. Subsequently, we took the opportunity strategy and split it between credit and traditional buyouts. But across all those strategies we remain dedicated to value investing.

Unhedged: What do you mean by value?

Quintin: We focus on transactions where there is a preponderance of asset backing or some sort of reliable cash flow. So, being disciplined on entry price and looking at the companies where there are opportunities to make changes — where the return is predicated on what you can do to improve the business, rather than on market growth or multiple expansion.

We tend to focus on those situations where there could be, for example, a corporate carve-out, or you have a global corporation that is looking to shed a business. These are complex situations — they require a lot of work desegregating that business from the parent. Those situations require a lot of muscle memory, setting up new management teams, addressing technological shortfalls and really trying to define what the business should look like on a standalone basis.

Unhedged: Is it too crude to say that where a lot of buyout shops think about revenue growth, you think more about margin or return on capital?

Quintin: The broader market has historically focused on either revenue growth or multiple expansion. How we think about investing, that is really a small part of the value proposition. The real alpha is coming from either improving the underlying margins of the business, or focusing on the cash flow.

Unhedged: The last time we spoke you talked about how you made your bones picking through the wreckage of the great financial crisis — loans in distress, CDOs on the rocks. What did that teach you?

Quintin: Having gone through the financial crisis gives you an appreciation for things like excess leverage, and focusing on how things can go wrong . . . I started my career at Salomon Brothers in fixed income, in the mortgage division as a trader. I moved to Merrill Lynch just at the onset of the financial crisis and worked closely with management there — John Thain, Greg Fleming — culminating in the sale to Bank of America. That was a huge learning opportunity, with many sleepless nights and difficult situations during the day.

Unhedged: We’ve seen lower returns and longer hold times in the buyout industry. Are industry returns permanently lower now?

Quintin: I think what’s happening is a separation in the market, which will force a return to what private equity was in the beginning, in the nineties — where the quality of the business, the quality of the management and a realistic view as to what one can do to improve that business are really important. A respect for how you’re going to exit that business before you ever buy it. When money is cheap, rates are low and multiples are expanding, that kind of stockpicking attitude isn’t as relevant because a rising tide raises all boats. Now we have high interest rates relative to recent history, and those rates are likely going to be higher for longer. That puts pressure on the assumption that growth is what’s going to drive your returns . . . We’re entering a different market now.

Unhedged: 2021 was a euphoric peak in private equity. That’s five years ago now — time for that vintage of buyout to grow up and move out. Are they going to struggle to do so? And does that create opportunities for Lone Star — helping with companies’ balance sheets or on the equity side? Are you licking your chops?

Quintin: I think we are. It will create opportunities. Broadly, I agree with your timeframe, 2021, that period had really kind of peak multiples. And you had post-pandemic inflated Ebitdas, you had a significant amount of cheap debt available that wasn’t hedged at the operating company level from floating rate to fixed rate. Because nobody was anticipating that rates would go up — they’d only seen them stable to down. Those situations are now manifesting themselves into credit opportunities. You have good businesses that are under capital structure pressure . . . with companies where the purchase prices were elevated, the challenge is really if those positions haven’t been marked low enough. I’m struck by the fact that we’re in a time now where you have a huge amount of debt capital available through private credit and through the bank market. You have a healthy banking system, generally. And there’s a lot of dry powder. So you have the tools for transactions, right? You are starting to see asset-by-asset transactions happening, but you’re not seeing portfolio sales, and a lot of it is because those companies didn’t grow into the elevated prices they were acquired at, they didn’t hit their growth projections.

Unhedged: So if they mark to market, it crystallises a bad return.

Quintin: You could make that argument. If they’re willing buyers, and transactions don’t happen, it’s often because the expectations are not being met by the seller.

Unhedged: What about retail distribution of private equity investment? Lone Star hasn’t done it, but what do you think? Where is it appropriate? Is there an opportunity here?

Quintin: It’s not something we anticipate doing in the future. Raising money in the retail space requires a significant apparatus. And I think where you’re seeing a prevalence of that is in those institutions that have become quite large and they have many different channels for fundraising. It’s not something that we have spent time thinking about.

Unhedged: What’s the best deal you ever did?

Quintin: I feel quite proud of the Novo Banco transaction, which was the acquisition of the good bank from Portuguese central bank Fundo, the rescue vehicle. At the time, there were those calling for the liquidation of the bank, and the Portuguese state had difficulties selling the bank. It was a very complicated transaction. It required a significant amount of work on the balance sheet, the structure and the needs of the state. We presented them with a very novel proposal that enabled the state to sell the bank, and we bought a 75 per cent stake. What I’m really proud about is that we really refocused the bank, we improved the governance, we introduced technology, we expanded its lending footprint in Portugal. When you are buying a bank, particularly post-financial crisis, you have a lot of stakeholders, whether it’s the ECB, the Central Bank of Portugal, the Portuguese government. And an incredibly important stakeholder in the citizenry of Portugal. We successfully exited the bank, selling it to BPCE, a French bank. And I think it was a great success story for Portugal.

Unhedged: Lately there has not been a lot of distress in the credit world. So what’s keeping you busy in the credit business?

Quintin: Credit is something that we do on an opportunistic basis, and it hasn’t really been a big focus of ours given where we are in the cycle. That being said, there are opportunities coming up because some of it is a situation you described before — the high prices paid and the excess debt used in the 2019 to 2021 timeframe. I also think the elevated rates are creating issues . . . there are operating businesses that didn’t hedge their debt and where things were priced to perfection. Debt starts to impact cash flow. That’s something that we’re clearly seeing. Also, private credit has been a complement to the existing bank loan market and it complements private equity very well, but when you start to enter a credit cycle, if there’s an element of bad underwriting, you can’t escape that. And we’re starting to see instances of that crop up. But I still think it’s early days.

I do think that the market will start to separate between those that have experience handling stressed and distressed credit. Private credit that’s been assembled without proper workout teams, anticipating potential issues, will have to scramble to catch up, just to find the expertise.

Unhedged: Where are we in the credit cycle?

Quintin: It’s early days, but we are starting to see a trend. I think the reported figures from folks like Fitch and others are starting to increase. I think it is different than the financial crisis . . . to this point the economy has continued to do well, and in the industrial manufacturing space order books are still holding up fine. But there has been an impact from the prolongation of a higher-rate environment.

Unhedged: Turning to the real estate business, rates were nothing and now they’re 5 per cent. How does that change how you manage that business?

Quintin: We’re obviously not immune to the higher-for-longer interest rates. But I think those also create opportunities for investors in that opportunistic space, as higher rates put pressure on individual situations. In the financial crisis, we had a concentration of large pools of assets that are under stress at the same time. Now you have more idiosyncratic situations, and those in and of themselves are creating opportunities for investors. You also have a different banking environment, and private credit. The positive side of private credit is that it’s very patient capital.

Unhedged: When asset values are high and rates are rising, everybody wants to know, is there going to be a big dislocation? I’m not going to ask you that, but I will ask: if there is a dislocation, where will the opportunities be?

Quintin: I think it’s about being very disciplined, pragmatic and able to move quickly and handle complex situations. You don’t want to be learning on the job in those types of markets. You want muscle memory to kick in. That’s where experience comes into play. It prevents you from making decisions that you will come to regret later.

In yesterday’s letter we incorrectly stated that the 10-year Treasury yield was 4.29 per cent, rather than 5.29. This was a careless error — and one committed by Rob, not Katie, despite Katie’s byline being at the top of the letter. Rob regrets both misleading readers and damaging Katie’s reputation.

A tough guy .

rows.title: Pro-Russian parties jostle with Kyiv supporters in crowded Latvian election
rows.content:
Henry Foy

Published October 2 2026

Good morning. A scoop to start: Vladimir Putin has instructed his military leaders to abandon the rules of conflict, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the FT in an interview , citing intelligence briefings that the Russian president had told his generals: “There are no rules now.”

Today, we preview tomorrow’s parliamentary election in Latvia, and the Netherlands’ justice minister says a freeze on EU funds to Sierra Leone is a triumph for justice.

Have a cracking weekend.

This article is an on-site version of our Europe Express newsletter. Premium subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every weekday and fortnightly on Saturday morning. Standard subscribers can upgrade to Premium here , or explore all FT newsletters

Latvians head to the polls tomorrow following a government crisis in May, in an election that’s likely to deliver further uncertainty for the Nato member on the alliance’s eastern flank as Russia escalates its threats, writes Paola Tamma .

Context: Polls open on Saturday and seven parties are forecast to clear the 5 per cent threshold necessary to enter the 100-seat parliament, according to a poll released last month and commissioned by Latvian public broadcaster LTV. The campaign has been dominated by socio-economic issues, although parties still largely position themselves around Latvia’s ethnic-linguistic divide.

United List, the party of Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, a staunch Ukraine supporter, has a comfortable lead, polling at 14.4 per cent.

Coming second and third, with over 9 per cent of the voting share each, are two parties courting Latvia’s substantial Russian-speaking minority — Sovereign Power and Latvia First — which are either openly pro-Russia or call for an easing of sanctions against Moscow.

Trailing them with around 5 to 6 per cent of the vote each come the Progressives, a green-affiliated party, National Alliance, a staunchly anti-Russian party, and the Union of Greens and Farmers.

In a spectacular fall from grace, New Unity, the centre-right party of former premier Evika Siliņa, is polling below the threshold at 4.3 per cent. Siliņa resigned following the mishandling of Ukrainian drones crashing into the Baltic country. Almost 15 per cent of Latvians polled said they would not vote.

Kulbergs has ruled out an alliance with Sovereign Power, the more outspokenly pro-Russia party, whose leader Jūlija Stepaņenko has faced scrutiny over financial gifts of €420,000 from her father, a Russian-based businessman whose company supplied concrete anti-tank barriers used by Russian forces.

But he has been more nuanced on other potential coalition partners. Analysts agree that no single party will win an outright majority; the most likely outcome is a coalition government built around Kulbergs’ party, although coalition partners depend considerably on who clears the 5 per cent hurdle for parliamentary representation.

Europe should take Donald Trump’s diesel ban seriously, if not literally, writes Lex — it is a sign that the continent can no longer rely on the US being an unconditional supplier of energy.

The EU has postponed aid for Sierra Leone after the Dutch government pressured Brussels to cut off money to Freetown unless it extradited a wanted drug lord, writes Laura Dubois .

Context: Dutch authorities have said Sierra Leone should not receive EU aid unless it extradites Jos Leijdekkers, a Dutchman who was sentenced for cocaine trafficking and other charges in the Netherlands and Belgium. The Hague believes he is hiding out in Sierra Leone under the protection of the authorities.

The European Commission this week said it would postpone €18mn in direct budget support to Sierra Leone’s government planned for this year — a move immediately celebrated as a success by Dutch justice minister David van Weel.

“I’m very happy with that,” van Weel told the FT. “I think that every pressure we can apply to Sierra Leone to finally co-operate on the extradition of Mr Jos Leijdekkers should be used.”

According to the Commission, the aid was suspended because certain conditions for it to be paid out could not be met. “It’s due to technical reasons that the disbursement for 2026 was suspended,” said home affairs commissioner Magnus Brunner yesterday.

Commission spokesperson Guillaume Mercier said the aid was “currently under assessment and no disbursement is currently planned” and added that the EU was “closely monitoring drug trafficking and, more broadly, trends in transnational organised crime in Sierra Leone and across the wider west Africa region”.

Van Weel, however, waved these technicalities away. “It’s up to the Commission to do their own spokesperson [work],” he said. “I consider this a very welcome event in light of the pressure that we’re trying to build up towards Sierra Leone.”

rows.title: Black voters rally against new electoral maps in the US South
rows.content:
Guy Chazan in Baton Rouge, Louisiana

Published October 2 2026

Like many Black voters across the South, Asti Robins is furious. And the anger is so powerful, she says, it could shape the outcome of November’s midterms.

The cause: new Republican-backed electoral maps that critics say will dilute the voting power of African Americans. There would be a reckoning, Robins predicted. “Black voter turnout will be huge. People are energised.”

An environmental campaigner, Robins lives in Louisiana’s sixth congressional district, a majority-Black constituency that was redrawn by the state’s Republican-controlled legislature.

Louisiana was a bastion of the slaveholding economy before the civil war and Black people still make up 32 per cent of the state’s population. It had two majority-Black districts to represent them, out of the state’s total of six. Now it has just one.

“Without representation, what is citizenship?” asked Ashley Shelton, founder of Power Coalition, a Louisiana non-profit focused on voting rights and civic engagement. “What is citizenship when my values, my experience of this country as a Black woman aren’t reflected in the halls of Congress?”

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The boundary change came after a landmark April Supreme Court decision, Louisiana vs Callais, that ruled Robins’ district was an “unconstitutional racial gerrymander”.

Critics said the ruling gutted the 1965 Voting Rights Act, a central achievement of the civil rights era, which prohibited racial discrimination in voting. Supporters said the US constitution did not allow states to sort voters by race .

Electoral boundaries were traditionally redrawn every 10 years based on the census, but recently Republican- and Democratic-controlled states across the US have been remaking their electoral maps with increasing frequency in a tit-for-tat race to derive maximum partisan advantage. This year the process has been accelerated by President Donald Trump.

Republicans have been the main beneficiaries of the changes and are projected to net about four seats, according to the Cook Political Report.

But with Trump’s approval ratings at record lows and Republicans trailing Democrats in the polls, that advantage may not be big enough to preserve the party’s House majority in November.

Redistricting has largely been driven by politics. But in the South, race is never far from the surface. Over the past few months, Black communities in Louisiana, Alabama and Tennessee were “cracked”, or broken up and combined with larger white populations into new gerrymandered districts that critics say will reduce their ability to elect candidates of their choice.

The process means Cleo Fields, the Black Democratic lawmaker representing Louisiana’s sixth district, which is now majority white and overwhelmingly Republican, will soon be out of a job. He is retiring from national politics and will seek a state senate seat instead.

Fields is convinced the gerrymander will backfire. “People are going to show up in greater numbers [in November], particularly African Americans,” he said in an interview. “They are determined not to let their voices be silenced.”

It is unclear how much impact a Black voter surge in the South will have. The region is deep red: even in 2008, when a rise in Black turnout helped propel Barack Obama into the White House, all but three southern states voted Republican.

Black voters do not always vote Democrat, however. Republicans made big inroads in 2024, when Trump received 15 per cent of their vote, according to Pew Research, compared with 8 per cent in 2020.

But this year Black Democrats, backed by a newly galvanised base, are running across the South in places that were long seen as impregnable Republican strongholds.

Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Black former mayor of Atlanta, is in a close race with Republican Rick Jackson for the governorship of Georgia, an office held by Republicans for the past 23 years. In Mississippi, limited polling has put Scott Colom, a Black state prosecutor running for Senate, within striking distance of Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Voter apathy has long been a problem in deep southern states such as Louisiana. But Shelton believes that might be changing.

“You’re giving people something to stand up for,” she said. “You’re giving them a reason to say, ‘I have to pay attention, I need to understand.’

“The only answer to people taking away your voice and your power is to show up.”

For Black community leaders, the gerrymandering evokes dark memories of Jim Crow, the system that enforced racial segregation after the end of Reconstruction in 1877.

Leona Tate personifies the struggle to overcome that legacy. As a six-year-old girl in 1960, she had to be escorted by US federal marshals into her newly desegregated school in New Orleans through a crowd of yelling and cursing white people held back by police.

She remembers not being able to eat in the school cafeteria. “[The white students] were going to either knock the food out of your hand or they was going to spit in it,” she said in an interview. “Every school that I went to was the same thing, all the way through high school.”

The civil rights movement overcame the worst excesses of Jim Crow. But with redistricting, Tate says its gains are threatened. “I see a regression,” she said. “It feels like they’re just trying to erase all people of colour.”

In its April ruling, the Supreme Court’s conservative majority argued that the US had fundamentally changed since the 1960s when Black voters were blocked from voting by literacy tests and other obstacles. The legacy of that unequal treatment, the justices said, was no longer enough to justify drawing electoral districts along racial lines.

Fields agrees that the lot of African Americans has indeed improved. “But have we overcome all of the vices of discrimination? Absolutely not,” he said. “They need to walk in my shoes one or two days . . . just come and live my experience.”

Critics said the court’s ruling marked the culmination of years of legal efforts to unpick the VRA, a law that Justice Elena Kagan said in her dissent was “born of the literal blood of Union soldiers and civil rights marchers”.

Conservatives insist that most of the VRA remains intact. But detractors say that in purely practical terms the court’s ruling makes it much harder to challenge electoral maps that diminish Black voting power.

Louisiana was quick to enforce the judgment. Jay Morris, a Louisiana state senator, was one of the architects of the state’s new map, which he has admitted was “drawn to maximise Republican advantage”.

In an interview, Morris accused Democrats of doing the same. There were some blue states in the north-east where “30 or 40 per cent of the population votes Republican”, yet “there are zero Congress members from the Republican Party” being elected there, he said.

Morris said there was nothing undemocratic about the way Louisiana had changed its map. “That’s how democracy is defined — majority rules,” he added. “And we’re a majority-Republican state.”

Robins said the dissolution of the sixth district was a “gut-punch”, both for herself and her relatives. Her family hails from Alsen, a small community just outside Baton Rouge settled by former slaves who fought on the Union side during the civil war. The childhood summers she spent there, among the chickens, cows and pecan trees, were idyllic. But in recent years, it has become a tougher place to live.

The community sits at the northern end of a heavily industrialised corridor along the Mississippi River nicknamed “Cancer Alley”. It is hemmed in by a massive Exxon polymer plant and a sprawling landfill site. Locals complain of respiratory problems. “The smell will burn your nose,” Robins said.

Residents often felt overlooked. That changed in 2024, she said, with the creation of the new sixth district, of which Alsen was a part. The community felt newly hopeful. “We were sending a hometown guy from Baton Rouge to Congress,” Robins said. “People thought their voice would be heard on the federal level.”

Then came the Supreme Court decision and the new map. Robins said she felt deceived. “The state sends six representatives to Congress and this now means that only one of them [will] care about people who look like me — the descendants of slaves,” she said. “It felt like we’d taken two steps forward and been pushed back six.”

rows.title: Meet Man City’s powerbroker
rows.content:
Published October 2 2026

One thing to start: Monzo Bank is stepping up its efforts to court private equity investors after takeover talks with the Brazilian fintech giant Nubank collapsed over the up-to £10bn valuation the UK group was seeking.

And a scoop: Petrol station empire EG Group is delaying plans for an initial public offering until next year, opening up the possibility that the group will explore a sale.

In today’s newsletter:

Khaldoon al-Mubarak’s big test

Will UBS ever leave Switzerland?

The go-to firm for corruption scandals

For eight years, the Premier League ’s probe into Manchester City’s finances has cast a pall over the club. And this week, those inquiries broke into explicit charges and allegations.

So when longtime former coach Pep Guardiola posted a message of solidarity to supporters of the club, his choice of image was telling: a picture of him next to City chair Khaldoon al-Mubarak , in a warm embrace.

Mubarak has been the face of Abu Dhabi investment in the football club, as royal owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan has stayed in the shadows.

The FT’s Chloe Cornish and DD’s Arash Massoudi profiled Mubarak, the Abu Dhabi power broker, and how the scandal for City has forced him into a position of now having to defend both the club and his own reputation.

During Mubarak’s tenure, the club has gone from mid-table plodder to one of the most successful teams in European football. Mubarak has been there for all of it: he regularly attends games at the Etihad Stadium , where he’s been seen lifting trophies from eight Premier League title wins as well as the Champions League .

But after a damning verdict last week found City guilty of more than 100 violations of the Premier League’s financial rules, Mubarak must manage the firestorm of reputational damage to Abu Dhabi, whose image has become tightly intertwined with the club’s.

An independent commission found that the club had inflated its income and hidden its costs to the tune of more than £900mn over a period of almost a decade.

The club has until Friday to lodge a formal appeal against the findings of an independent commission. Meanwhile, Etihad Airways , the team’s biggest sponsor, has threatened legal action against the Premier League.

Mubarak and City have vowed to fight the charges, which they strenuously deny. And attention will return to the pitch soon. When the Premier League kicks off again on October 10, City will be sitting top of the table.

But chairing City is far from Mubarak’s only job.

He’s one of the United Arab Emirates’ most powerful non-royals as chief executive of Mubadala and as the point person for several important diplomatic relationships, including with China. As a sign of just how powerful he is, when Abu Dhabi secured a seat on Donald Trump ’s Board of Peace this year, Mubarak got the slot.

At Mubadala, Mubarak’s not only the world’s longest-serving head of a sovereign investment fund but one of the main figures overseeing Abu Dhabi’s more than $1.5tn in wealth.

For the heads of hedge funds and investment firms globally, that makes him one of the most important people to know.

“The power he holds is massive,” said one executive at a large global investment firm. “But he does it from behind the scenes.”

But despite all of the allegations levelled against the football club in recent days, Mubarak, at least personally, appears to have some protection. He was placed on the UK’s official list of approved diplomats in 2020, which automatically gives immunity from any criminal investigation and in most cases shields the person from civil proceedings on UK soil.

The political battle over UBS ’s future in Switzerland is already heated. Now one of its influential shareholders has entered the fray, with a simple suggestion: leave.

Artisan Partners , whose funds own 1.8 per cent of the bank, wrote to the Swiss bank’s board this week arguing that Switzerland was “no longer an attractive or desirable location” following moves to impose tougher capital requirements.

The Milwaukee-based asset manager reckons the rules could force UBS to hold an additional $16bn of common equity and cost shareholders as much as $36bn in foregone market value.

UBS politely pushed back, saying its “goal is to continue operating successfully as a global bank from Switzerland”.

But leaving is not entirely theoretical. UBS has explored contingency plans for moving abroad if the rules prove too onerous. Chair Colm Kelleher has even privately discussed with US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent what shifting the bank’s headquarters to the US could look like.

And Artisan is worth watching. It’s not an activist investor by trade, but the long-only fund manager has form when it decides to speak up.

In 2021, it publicly criticised Danone ’s strategy and governance and pushed for changes at the top. Chair and chief executive Emmanuel Faber was ousted weeks later from the French consumer goods company amid mounting shareholder pressure. Artisan has made itself heard in Switzerland before, too. That same year it backed activist investor Third Point ’s push for change at Richemont , arguing there was “significant unrecognised value” in the Cartier owner.

Artisan has not gone full activist at UBS — at least not yet. But its intervention adds another complication to an increasingly febrile debate over the bank’s Swiss future.

For corruption in the basketball world, Wachtell Lipton may now be the go-to law firm. In August, the report prepared by the firm for the National Basketball Association on the topic of alleged salary cap misconduct at the Los Angeles Clippers was so damning that the team’s owner Steve Ballmer was suspended for the year.

The FT on Thursday scooped that Wachtell had hired Joon Kim , a Cleary Gottlieb white-collar litigation partner who previously had a distinguished run at the US Attorney’s Office in Manhattan.

His famed cases as a federal prosecutor include the high-profile charges he brought in 2017 against US college basketball coaches accused of a wide-ranging kickback scheme.

In other Southern District of New York matters, Kim took on Steven Cohen , the hedge fund manager, and Ross Ulbricht , the mastermind of Silk Road , the illicit online marketplace.

Wachtell’s litigation group had been looking for a rebound.

Over the summer, its ace litigator and firm co-chair abruptly left for Gibson Dunn with several colleagues. Kim’s hiring shows the M&A powerhouse isn’t throwing in the towel when it comes to putting lawyers up for clients’ court fights.

The firm very rarely makes outside lateral hires so landing Kim is a big deal and shows that Wachtell wants to play offence.

The firm is down to roughly 20 litigation partners, almost half its corporate partner roster. Don’t be surprised if there are more free-agent signings at Wachtell coming.

KPMG’s global general counsel Anne Collins has left the firm as part of a wider executive reshuffle. She attracted scrutiny for her handling of whistleblower allegations that rocked the accounting firm in Australia.

JPMorgan executive chair of global investment banking Hernan Cristerna is retiring from banking after 30 years at the bank and will step down at the end of the year.

Linklaters has hired Mohammed Almarzouki as a corporate partner in Riyadh. He joins from Clyde & Co .

Houlihan Lokey has hired Jacques Bitton as a senior adviser in France. He previously worked at Société Générale .

Living large Changpeng Zhao, the former Binance chief executive who was jailed in the US, is now living a gilded life in the United Arab Emirates, the New York Times reports .

Who’s who In a deep dive about the secretive trading house Jane Street, Bloomberg digs into the relatively unknown people behind the firm, including the management committee, decision makers, founders and notable alumni.
