rows.title: UK universities comb records for China links after MI5 warning
rows.content:
Michael Peel , Charles Clover and Lucy Fisher in London

Published October 2 2026

UK universities were racing on Thursday to meet an MI5-driven order to cut ties with a Chinese research organisation, prompting fresh calls for official help to cover national security compliance costs as geopolitical tensions rise.

The educational institutions have been combing their records since Wednesday’s espionage alert , which said the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) secretly channelled funding from Beijing’s intelligence apparatus to more than 100 UK-linked academics.

The UK domestic security agency’s unusually specific alert highlights growing pressure on the country’s leading universities to carry out deep vetting of collaborations with Chinese institutions, particularly in sensitive technological fields with potential military uses.

“[Universities] have become very much better at this over the past few years, but we still have to recognise that it’s patchy,” said Sir Peter Mathieson, the University of Edinburgh’s vice-chancellor. “Not every university has the same level of sophistication around national security — and not every university has the same needs.”

MI5 was “very respectful of academic freedom and institutional autonomy” but the security agency did not “necessarily show us its workings”, Mathieson added.

None of the universities or sector representative bodies contacted by the FT since the MI5 alert has said it has found evidence of a relationship with the CGTRI.

However, MI5 has not identified the more than 100 academics it cited nor said how many of the cases were current and which were historic, university representatives said.

The MI5 alert also acknowledged universities might have “engaged with CGTRI in good faith”, as the Chinese body had “obfuscated” its links to the Chinese Ministry of State Security.

The announcement triggered a letter by security minister Dan Jarvis to all UK university vice-chancellors asking them to end arrangements with CGTRI.

The security agency’s work on CGTRI had exposed Chinese intelligence efforts to “covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies”, Jarvis said.

China’s embassy in London has condemned what it called “baseless allegations”.

“The accusations made by the UK intelligence agency against the relevant Chinese entity are imaginary and purely fabricated,” it said in a previous statement.

In 2024, the previous Conservative administration summoned university vice-chancellors for a briefing from the intelligence agencies on hostile powers targeting British academia.

It came after the creation in 2021 of the Research Collaboration Advice Team, a government unit that provides advice to universities on national security risks linked to international research.

George Freeman, an MP and a former minister for science, said a government review he commissioned in 2022-23 identified about 400 links between China and Britain’s research and innovation system. This included 40 collaborations that were “red-flagged” by the research collaboration advice team.

He said the MI5 public warning “suggests these red-flag exposures have still not been properly reviewed. They need to be, urgently.”

The current Labour government is planning to publish a fresh research security strategy, bolstered by a new research security fund, in the coming months.

The fund is a recognition of the increased compliance costs universities face in analysing proposed Chinese partners, including whether they have other affiliations with the country’s military and security agencies.

Ben Moore, associate director for international policy at the Russell Group of 24 research-intensive universities, said the association had long called for such a fund to “protect sensitive research and proactively tackle threats as they emerge”.

He added: “It’s encouraging to see government taking steps towards this and we’ll continue to work with them closely as more details are confirmed.”

rows.title: Monzo courts private equity after Nubank walks away
rows.content:
Laith Al-Khalaf

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Monzo Bank is stepping up its efforts to court private equity investors after takeover talks with the Brazilian fintech giant Nubank collapsed over the up-to £10bn valuation the UK group was seeking.

The digital bank has in recent weeks held early-stage discussions with the European buyout group CVC and US private equity firm Advent International about selling a significant stake in the group. People familiar with the matter said Monzo was seeking to sell a stake of up to 15 per cent.

They added that a sale to a private equity fund was now the preferred option for Monzo after takeover talks with Nubank fell through and that Monzo’s advisers would turn their efforts to engaging with more fund managers.

Monzo had been trying to clinch a sale to Nubank in a deal that would have valued the UK fintech at £10bn. New York-listed Nubank, which has a market capitalisation of about $65bn, said on Wednesday that it would not be pursuing a deal.

People familiar with the matter said that the sides were unable to agree a price and that Nubank had instead decided to concentrate on growing in its home market and the US, where it has recently secured a banking licence.

Monzo could yet pursue a third option: tapping venture capital investors for a more traditional fundraising round. However, one person familiar with the board’s thinking said Monzo would prefer the private equity option as it would probably be a far larger investment and give Monzo access to more cash for growth.

Monzo, Nubank, Advent and CVC declined to comment.

Monzo has endured a difficult year, with a bruising fight between its board and investors over the company’s international expansion plans and long-awaited initial public offering.

The fintech’s board ousted then-chief executive TS Anil because of concerns about the pace of growth and whether he was committed to the business for the long term — a move that angered the company’s biggest investors.

Anil ultimately remained on the board, but was replaced as CEO by former Google executive Diana Layfield. Since taking the helm in February, Layfield has closed Monzo’s US offices and switched the focus of expansion plans to Europe, opening offices in Spain and securing a European banking licence from Irish authorities.

Anil — who stayed on as an adviser to Layfield — along with Monzo’s chief financial officer and former Nubank executive Tom Oldham helped broker the takeover talks, according to people familiar with the deliberations.

When asked last month about whether there would be more consolidation among direct-to-consumer fintechs, Oldham demurred. “I’m not sure on the consolidation point,” he told the FT. “I think we’re really just focused on growing our customer base at pace.”

He added: “If we see other great companies that are delivering against one of our customers’ needs, and we think that’s a good cultural fit for us, that’s a company that we like, then for sure we would look.”

But behind the scenes, São Paulo-based Nubank had identified Monzo as providing a potential foothold in Europe.

“You cannot look at the deal without looking at Revolut,” said one senior technology banker of Nubank’s interest in Monzo.

“If you’re looking at it from a financial point of view, the deal doesn’t make sense for anyone. But Monzo as a platform could turbocharge Nubank into developed markets, handing them a banking licence and more customers than Revolut in its own market.”

Although Monzo is a similar age to Revolut, it has long since been overshadowed by its larger rival. Revolut has grown to become a global player with 80mn customers and a $115bn valuation. Monzo reported just 15mn customers this year.

Nubank, which launched in 2013, has 140mn customers. But they are mainly in Latin America, and the company is seeking to take on Nik Storonsky’s Revolut to become the world’s dominant fintech.

Both have already secured US banking licences in recent months, while Revolut has also made moves in Colombia, Mexico and Argentina.

John Cronin, an independent banking analyst, said there were “only two ways” for Nubank to expand in Europe: “You buy your way in . . . or you build organically, which takes ages, and you’re behind in the race versus Monzo, Revolut and others scattered around the continent.”

Nubank’s top executives are aware of the difficulties around European expansion. David Vélez, the company’s billionaire co-founder, told the FT last month that UK growth would be costly and posed its own challenges.

“I would say there are more digital banks, it’s a very big market, [but] you still have access and cost problems . . . there’s still a significant lack of access to certain products, specifically on credit.”

The price tag for Monzo attached to its talks with Nubank had sparked scepticism, however. In a note to clients, equity research company Autonomous labelled the deal “financially questionable”, noting that a valuation of between £8bn and £10bn would be seven times Monzo’s tangible book value, far higher than competitors.

Autonomous added that in the mature UK market, it would be hard to monetise Monzo’s customers to make the transaction pay off. The $9 per month Monzo generates from each customer is only half the monthly average revenue per Brazilian Nubank customer, Autonomous said.

“Nubank would be paying a premium to its own valuation to acquire something that doesn’t generate the same returns as it’s currently generating,” the independent analyst Cronin said.

A venture capital adviser said Monzo and Nubank also served starkly different customers, with Nubank providing lending and banking services to underbanked customers in Latin America.

“Nubank is more mass-market and not necessarily known for higher-value customers. There are not a large number of underbanked people in the UK or Europe.”

But if Nubank balked at Monzo’s desired valuation, private equity firms without the same strategic rationale for a deal or operations to merge were likely to be even more price sensitive, making a deal difficult to pull off.

That could mean that rather than cashing out via a sale to Nubank, Monzo’s existing investors have to inject more cash into the UK fintech to fund its growth plans in pursuit of an exit at a later date.

Still, speaking to the FT last month, Oldham seemed unperturbed. “We’re super hopeful about bringing that sort of Monzo magic, as we like to say, to other markets,” he said.

Additional reporting by Michael Pooler and Akila Quinio

rows.title: Amazon seeks to offload $8bn of Nvidia chips to investors
rows.content:
Michelle Chan in New York and Rafe Rosner-Uddin in San Francisco

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Amazon is seeking to offload about $8bn of advanced Nvidia chips to external investors through a new vehicle aimed at strengthening its balance sheet, according to people familiar with the matter.

The Seattle-based cloud giant has held talks with investors in recent weeks to gauge interest in the deal, which would allow the company to spin off thousands of Grace Blackwell chips it is deploying in data centres across the US into a special-purpose vehicle.

Amazon will then lease the advanced AI chips back from the SPV, which would tap outside investors through debt issuance. By unloading the expensive semiconductors to investors, the company could adopt a more asset-light approach to its balance sheet.

Amazon declined to comment.

The proposed move comes as tech giants seek creative ways to finance massive spending on data centre infrastructure. Much of the cost associated with the build-out of these facilities is tied to the chips used to train advanced AI models.

Tech companies are pursuing a range of strategies to move debt off their balance sheets to preserve their creditworthiness. They have used residual value guarantees , providing lenders with assurances about the future value of chips or data centres, without borrowing cash to finance projects themselves. The approach has obscured the amount of risk that tech giants are taking on.

Investors expect the entity will receive an investment-grade credit rating based on Amazon’s current double A rating, paving the way for a broader base of investors such as insurance and pension funds to join the deal.

Amazon also plans to offer an equity stake of up to 10 per cent in the vehicle, meaning that it will not own any stakes in the entity. Discussions between Amazon and investors are ongoing and are subject to change, the people added.

Amazon bought or leased the chips involved in the proposed deal and they have been deployed in more than a dozen US data centres across five states, including Nevada and Virginia, the people added.

Nvidia’s Grace Blackwell chips are some of the semiconductor group’s most advanced but will soon be superseded by its latest Vera Rubin offering.

Leading AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic — in which Amazon has committed to invest as much as $83bn — use the latest chips to train their models. Previous generations of silicon continue to be used for running applications. Amazon expects each series of semiconductors to last at least five years, according to regulatory filings.

Amazon is expected to spend $220bn in capital expenditure this year, the majority of which will be allocated towards its cloud unit AWS for the purchase of advanced chips and the wider build-out of AI data centres.

The company has tapped the market to help fund this investment. In March it laid out plans to raise about $50bn through corporate bond issuances, increasing the offering from $37bn following strong demand. But it faced weakening interest in long-dated debt when it sold $25bn in bonds in July, with investors demanding higher yields.

Financing backed by graphics processing units has proven popular among companies such as CoreWeave, which have used their ready access to chips to fund borrowing.

In order to lower borrowing costs for its clients, Nvidia in August offered to backstop up to $125bn of such debt through a $500bn financing platform with major Wall Street groups.

rows.title: IPO hopeful Zilch needs to prove it’s one of a kind
rows.content:
Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Part of valuing any company when it goes public is working out which existing stocks it most closely resembles. Investors gauge valuation multiples for the so-called peer group , add a discount or maybe even a premium, and presto — an IPO share price emerges. For Zilch, a UK fintech preparing for a London listing, this simple-sounding process poses a grave problem.

Zilch’s main product is a cheaper alternative to credit cards, offering customers a competitive interest rate that is, in effect, subsidised by selling advertising. Five years ago it was valued in a fundraising at $2bn. Peers included Sweden’s Klarna, which had rocketed to a $46bn valuation. But the peer group has gone from help to extreme hindrance: Klarna has shed 90 per cent of its value since then.

Value Zilch next to its Swedish counterpart now and it would be worth, well, close to zilch. True, Klarna had its own idiosyncrasies . But it’s not like other comparisons are less awkward. Affirm, a buy-now-pay-later specialist, still trades above its IPO price but is down 42 per cent from where it closed the day it went public, and 9 per cent this year. Upstart, which focuses on personal loans, has fallen 92 per cent over five years and halved this year so far.

What about earlier generations of consumer finance companies that Zilch hopes to usurp? There’s Vanquis, a subprime credit card lender that has been restyling itself as a fintech, but has been around in various forms since the 1800s. No luck there either: its shares are down almost 40 per cent over the past 12 months, and 80 per cent over five years.

Zilch may argue it isn’t really like any of these. It aims to mix the low interest rates and convenience of companies such as Klarna with the stickier customer relationship of credit card lenders. Since its service can be used anywhere — unlike products that are offered by retail partners at the checkout — it should not be reliant on a handful of large merchant partners, while the quick turnover of its loan book makes it less exposed to interest rate moves.

Its finances do seem to be on the up, too. Zilch reported a net loss of £10.5mn in the year to March 2025, but showed a route to profitability. Revenue nearly doubled, massively outpacing the mere 7 per cent growth in operating expenses, creating what financial analysts call “positive jaws”.

Zilch would be one of a kind in one important way: by listing in London. The City has not always been welcoming for tech groups, but scarcity can be a virtue. The listing of Raspberry Pi in 2024 with a valuation of just over £500mn would barely have registered in the US, but created a sizeable stir in the UK. Its shares have risen almost 150 per cent since.

By the same token, Zilch would be assured attention from exchange executives and politicians desperate to liven up the long-quiet IPO market. And other fintech IPO hopefuls such as Zopa are watching closely. If Zilch can secure a better reception than its ailing listed peers, it may not be a one-off for long.

rows.title: French schools burn as student unrest spreads
rows.content:
Adrienne Klasa in Paris

Published October 2 2026

High school protests across France have turned violent in recent days, with top officials and far-right politicians accusing the hard-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon of fuelling the unrest.

According to the interior ministry, 1,949 people were arrested on Thursday as students, angered by overcrowded facilities, crumbling infrastructure and under-investment in education, protested outside more than 1,000 schools and blockaded 222 of them. Some schools were set on fire, including in Nantes and Lyon. There was also an attempt to set fire to Bordeaux’s city hall. Public transport was suspended in Marseille, as were tram services in Strasbourg.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu earlier this week accused the far-left party of “exploiting [the students’] anger for partisan ends”.

The education minister said 400 schools will be closed on Friday as he called for classes to be held remotely. “Violence will not deprive our students of their fundamental right to education,” Édouard Geffray wrote on X on Thursday.

French students burn bins and gather to block the entrance of their high schools in Aubervilliers

An official in Lecornu’s entourage said intelligence services shared the assessment that the unrest was “a manoeuvre’’ organised by Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise “and its ultra-left proxies”.

This is a “turning point”, the person added. “It is no longer a question of blockades of high schools, but of urban violence.”

Far-right leader Marine Le Pen on Thursday also blamed Mélenchon’s LFI for the unrest.

“These are no longer student protests. These are riots organised by professionals and overseen by members of parliament from La France Insoumise,” she said while calling for a new “anti-rioter” law.

Mélenchon has called for peaceful protests, but said they came in reaction to the “lamentable” state of national education after President Emmanuel Macron’s nine years in power.

“We are appalled by the dilapidated state of our high schools. Such neglect is shameful!” Mélenchon wrote on X. “The Macron government has made a terrible mistake. By blaming us for everything, they think they’re solving the problem.”

The far-left candidate is polling at about 17 per cent of voting intentions, which could potentially qualify him for the run-off against far-right Le Pen.

More than 3,000 people have been arrested in connection with the student protests so far, according to the interior ministry, and more than 100 students and school staff have been injured since the protests began. Some 305 law enforcement officers were injured on Thursday alone, the ministry added.

Video footage circulating on social media shows one incident in which a teenager was hit at close range by a projectile fired from a police grenade launcher. Investigations have been opened into three incidents in which students were allegedly injured by law enforcement, interior minister Laurent Nuñez said on Wednesday.

The protests come as the government announced spending cuts for 2027 — though not in education — in a bid to calm market jitters about the deterioration of France’s finances, which has led to higher borrowing costs. The government said next year’s education budget would increase by €1.1bn compared with the previous year, but teachers’ salaries will be partially frozen.

Earlier this week, French labour unions organised strikes over pay and the rising cost of living.

Governments in France have long feared student protests, which can ignite unpredictably and risk rapidly swaying public opinion. In 1968, a student revolt helped trigger national strikes that nearly brought down the De Gaulle government. More recently, student strikes converged with the 2018 gilets jaunes uprising, compounding the biggest domestic crisis of Macron’s first term.

France’s education system showed a sharp deterioration according to a benchmark transnational study from the OECD released in September, including a continuing decline in student reading skills and an “unprecedented” drop in maths.

The OECD pointed to teacher shortages, poor classroom conditions and inequality between rich and poor students as causes. Lost teaching time due to school closures and absent teachers who were not replaced totalled 10 per cent nationally, according to the education ministry.

rows.title: Paramount picked a bad time to fund a $110bn leveraged buyout
rows.content:
Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

This may not be the absolute worst moment to fund a highly leveraged acquisition, but it’s certainly not the best. Treasury yields are hitting multi-decade highs; risk appetites are wavering. Paramount Skydance, which has a $110bn purchase of Warner Bros Discovery to finance, is forging ahead anyway. It has little choice.

David Ellison’s media company sold $52bn in debt on Wednesday. Paramount won an investment-grade credit rating — albeit the lowest one available — but money managers buying the bonds seem sceptical. Ellison ended up offering yields higher than comparable investment-grade bonds. The same was true of the riskier “junk” part of the offering, sold with a yield of 9 per cent.

It’s not hard to see why. Fixed income buyers are being asked to finance a media company that, for all its streaming ambitions, relies for cash flows on a legacy TV business in long-term decline. The combination has annual ebitda of roughly $12bn, before factoring in cost savings resulting from the deal, compared with net debt of roughly $80bn.

And while the projected cost savings are substantial at $6bn a year, Ellison can’t count on the company keeping them all for itself in what remains a very competitive industry. Netflix chief Ted Sarandos vowed on Wednesday to make his own streaming giant grow faster, suggesting the prospect of a new round of expensive “content wars”.

A downturn in Paramount’s prospects could get messy, quickly. Investment-grade funds would have to sell out of the company if its credit rating fell to junk. And if things get even worse, Paramount’s creditors include some tough negotiators. A big portion of the new debt is held by huge firms like Apollo, Pimco, and Man Group according to a person familiar with the situation.

Ellison can take some comfort from the fact that those funds did not wring out particularly tight covenants, potentially as a trade-off for relatively generous yields. The tighter the covenants, the more protection investors have against borrowers getting creative in order to skirt bankruptcy.

Ideally such protections won’t be put to the test. Paramount certainly isn’t starting from a position of strength, though. Ellison has already come through a series of battles, first with WBD’s board and then with US states that tried to block his deal. A balance sheet laden with debt that is both copious and costly pretty much ensures struggle will be the Paramount chief’s new normal.

rows.title: Zack Polanski faces defining week as UK’s Green surge falters
rows.content:
David Sheppard in London

Published October 2 2026

For some British political leaders, a speech to party conference is one of the landmark moments of the year.

For Zack Polanski , it may be the easiest part of the next seven days.

The Green Party leader faces two critical tests that will define his grip over his activists and his appeal to the country at large.

First is the party conference in Brighton, where an anti-Zionism motion risks turning off many moderate voters.

Then on Thursday comes the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, where Polanski is seeking to become an MP for the first time but where bookmakers say he is likely to lose to Labour’s candidate.

“It’s a perilous moment for Zack,” said Rob Ford, a professor of politics at the University of Manchester.

“Assert control over the more radical activists in his party, and make it to Westminster, and he’ll undoubtedly have regained momentum. Lose, and the knives might be out with older members asking whether he’s really taking the party in the right direction.”

At the conference, a ‘Zionism is Racism’ motion proposes that the party should commit to supporting a single Palestinian state. Critics say the motion, heavily supported by party activists, is tantamount to backing the eradication of Israel.

Polanski will not back the motion unless it is amended to allow for the possibility of a two-state solution, if that is what Palestinians eventually choose, said one person familiar with his thinking.

But with the party flooded with activists enraged by the war in Gaza, he faces an uphill fight.

After Polanski became leader a year ago, the Greens surged in the polls: at one stage, the party was closing in on Labour, threatening a four-horse race with the Conservatives and Reform UK.

Its membership has tripled to more than 200,000, buoyed by supporters of former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, alongside others who thought then prime minister Sir Keir Starmer was slow to respond to the devastation in Gaza.

But in the subsequent wave of attention, less politically engaged voters have not always liked what they have seen.

Polanski has been hit by a fall in his party’s and his own poll ratings. His net approval rating is now minus 24 — the same as Reform’s Nigel Farage — while Prime Minister Andy Burnham has a net positive rating of 11, according to polling by More in Common.

Polanski’s ratings deteriorated sharply in the days after he retweeted a social media post criticising police who had subdued a knife attacker in Golders Green.

Luke Tryl, executive director of More in Common, said that, while Polanski had won a lot of support early in his leadership, the words that came up most often now from voters were “weird” and “dangerous”.

“[The Greens] risk becoming defined by issues where they’re outliers from public opinion rather than issues where people actually agree with them,” Tryl said, arguing Polanski’s early message of “fairness” on economics and the environment had broader appeal.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Green officials say they deserve credit for having forced a shift within Labour on Israel-Palestine, and argue that their victory in February’s Gorton and Denton by-election lit the fuse under Starmer’s premiership.

Polanski had hoped to make a similar noise by winning the by-election in Holborn and St Pancras, Starmer’s former seat. But Labour has been buoyed by its new leader and has won back a number of voters by taking a tougher stance towards Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, including imposing trade sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bank.

The Greens argue that defeat in the seat, which returned Labour councillors in May’s council elections, would not itself be damaging.

“It’s really one of our weakest areas in central London,” one official said.

“How close we get really matters,” another member said.

Polanski appears determined to the point of risking throwing the conference into chaos, telling members to focus on campaigning in London rather than coming to Brighton.

On Friday, Polanski will announce that a Green government would introduce a three-year cap on household rent increases, which he has dubbed an ‘emergency brake’, limiting rises to the lowest of CPI inflation, average earnings or 2 per cent.

After his conference speech on Friday he is expected to return to London that night, with two days of the conference left — including the vote on the ‘Zionism is Racism’ motion.

Jonathan Turner, chief executive of UK Lawyers for Israel, an activist group that has brought numerous legal claims against what it believes are anti-Israeli activities, argues that the motion may violate the Equality Act of 2010 “by discriminating against and harassing members and staff who are sympathetic to Zionism or for whom Zionism is intrinsic to their Israeli or Jewish identity”.

Polanski, who is Jewish, is also backing another amendment that would not discriminate against Jewish members who attend synagogues that consider themselves Zionist as most British synagogues do.

Some members are frustrated that Polanski has not shown stronger leadership or taken a clear stance against the motion, which they argue will appear extreme to voters.

The leader on Thursday focused on the Holborn and St Pancras vote, which he claimed was “on a knife edge”.

“The fact we’re competitive here is already amazing,” Polanski said in an Instagram video. “But we don’t want to come a close second: it’s time to cross the line.”

Additional reporting by Rachel Rees in London

rows.title: Quant hedge funds reap big gains from global bond sell-off
rows.content:
Costas Mourselas and Ian Smith in London

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Computer-driven hedge funds are making big profits out of a rout in global government bonds that has pushed US and European borrowing costs to multi-decade highs.

Funds using computer models to find and latch on to market trends have been running big bets against fixed income this year and have benefited as the Iran war and, more recently, strong US economic data have fuelled investors’ inflation fears.

Yields on 10-year US Treasuries have surged from around 4 per cent at the end of February to more than 5.2 per cent, while French, UK and Italian bonds have also sold off sharply. Yields rise as bond prices fall.

Among funds to benefit is Connecticut-based Graham Capital, whose Tactical Trend fund is up more than 31 per cent so far this year, including a 3.3 per cent gain last month, according to two people familiar with the matter.

London-based Winton, founded by billionaire Sir David Harding, gained 17.5 per cent in the year to last Friday in its Diversified Macro fund, while Aspect Capital’s flagship fund is up 21 per cent so far this year and gained almost 5 per cent last month, according to people who have seen the numbers.

“The embers of inflation are still glowing red,” said a director at one quant fund. “From about July onwards our risk has been pointed towards bonds, energy and currencies.”

All three funds make bets across asset classes and have made gains in other areas too. For instance, both Winton and Aspect made money by betting on energy markets, as the Iran war has kept oil prices stubbornly high.

Driving the surge in global bond yields and expectations of interest rate rises this year have been soaring crude prices, with benchmark Brent crude up around 40 per cent since the war began in February.

Fading hopes for a negotiated end to the Iran conflict have ignited a fresh burst higher in crude prices in recent weeks. Brent settled at $102.31 on Thursday.

The Federal Reserve increased its policy rate last month for the first time since 2023, responding to a jolt higher in inflation, and the European Central Bank has raised rates twice, while the Bank of England is expected by traders to follow suit in the coming months.

The inflationary impact of the war has been compounded by resilient US economic data that has stoked bets on higher US rates, while concerns over record government and corporate debt sales have meant investors demanding ever-higher yields to lend over the long term.

Rising yields have also forced some investors to unwind lossmaking positions, which has exacerbated the moves, according to market participants.

Trend funds tend to do best in years where there are clear, persistent trends across several months. One of the best years for the industry was 2022 when central banks kept increasing interest rates to fight persistent inflation, with quant funds profiting by betting against government bonds.

rows.title: A cathedral for plants: Edinburgh’s newly restored Palm Houses
rows.content:
Nathalie Thomas

Published October 2 2026

This article is part of FT Globetrotter’s guide to Edinburgh

Every one of the 600 plant specimens in the newly restored Palm Houses at Edinburgh’s Royal Botanic Garden has a remarkable story.

Take the Lion’s plant, or Valdivia gayana . The leaves look similar to those of a common primrose but seeds for this perennial with vibrant pink flowers, endangered in its native Chile, were harvested by botanists from plants growing on one surface of a cave in the South American country. They were brought to Edinburgh and propagated “en masse”, says Professor Julia Knights, Regius Keeper of the RBGE, before some seeds were sent back to Chile to boost the Lion’s plant population in other areas of the country.

“This is an example of the conservation efforts that all our team members are undertaking around the world to save plants,” says Knights, who picks out the “unassuming” little plant as one of her favourites in the 19th-century Palm Houses.

The Palm Houses are one of the highlights of the RBGE, a 70-acre garden whose own roots date back more than 350 years and which has long been a favourite among locals and visitors to Scotland’s capital city. Visitor numbers to the garden, one mile north of the city centre, are especially high during the summer months when its tranquillity provides a welcome respite from the joyful chaos of Edinburgh’s famous arts festivals .

The name “Palm Houses” is slightly misleading. Yes, there are many magnificent palms striving to reach the A-listed glass and iron ceiling, which reaches nearly 22 metres at its highest point, making it one of the tallest stone and glass houses in the world. But ferns, begonias, conifers and even liverworts are also housed beneath the daylight-flooded cathedral-like structure, each with their own intrigues.

Just a few metres away from the Lion’s plant, for example, is a deep green Cook pine from New Caledonia in the South Pacific, a conifer with needlelike leaves that grows in the direction of the equator rather than towards the light. “It’s the only plant we know of [in science] that grows towards the equator, which is quite fun,” says Knights. “We call it the wonky tree because it grows in an unusual direction.”

In all, plants from more than 35 countries are contained in the Palm Houses, which have quite the story of their own.

There were originally two RBGE Palm Houses, now consolidated into just one building after a painstaking five-year restoration. The initial octagonal structure dates from 1834. A second, taller structure was finished in 1858 at a time when the Victorians had a craze for ferns — a fashion so widespread that Charles Kingsley, a Victorian novelist, coined the term “pteridomania”.

Walking around the Palm Houses, it’s easy to see why the Victorians were so mad about ferns: the almost alien-like, tightly curled fronds provide an interesting contrast to the exotic, elegant palms.

The RBGE has one of the world’s leading collections of ferns, which, since the height of their popularity in Victorian times, have tended to be “sidelined” in favour of flowering plants, says the RBGE’s glasshouse curator Sadie Barber. Now, though, they are “becoming recognised as a really important group of plants”.

Ferns, which reproduce from tiny spores rather than seeds, are known not only as natural air purifiers but as great survivors, too. There is fossilised evidence of members of the fern family from around 360 million years ago.

“Because they are just spores in the ground, anything could happen to the earth and the ferns would come back,” adds Barber.

During the restoration of the Palm Houses, more than 5,000 panes of glass were replaced, while much of the ironwork and sandstone had to be either restored or substituted as the structures had weathered over time and were damaged by storms.

Another perilous task was moving all the plants — originally 800 specimens — and housing them temporarily in nearby glasshouses to allow for the construction work. Amateur gardeners will be well acquainted with the frustration of moving healthy plants only to find they wilt in their new environment for little or no reason. This was the same task on a mammoth scale.

“We’re the custodians [of the plants] and it’s quite a responsibility,” said David Knott, director of horticulture, when asked about the move.

The Palm Houses light up at the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh

Not every plant made it. Not least the Palm Houses’ best-known former inhabitant: a 200-year-old Sabal mexicana that towered towards the roof but was too tall and elderly to be moved. Fortunately, the Sabal mexicana is a fairly common species of palm. Visitors with fond memories of the old tree are able to see its 10-year-old offspring instead.

Other plants were purposely not returned to allow those that were — and visitors — more space and light.

The RBGE was originally founded as a “physic” garden in 1670 to grow plants for use by surgeons and medical students. These days themes of conservation, resilience and the changing climate are evident throughout the wider garden, which intentionally includes the remains of what was once a 30-metre-tall Himalayan cedar, at the time the tallest tree in Edinburgh, before it was felled by a violent storm in January 2025. The effect is powerful: it is a haunting totem that still looms over the rest of the site.

RBGE staff feel the garden can play a particularly important role in preserving species that are endangered elsewhere because of rising temperatures.

Visitors on a blustery, cold, rainy day may not think so but, as Knights says, “we are really lucky here in Scotland. We have got this wonderful climate, it’s not too hot here in the summertime.”

Next in the queue for renovations will be the research glasshouses, home to a treasure trove of species including rhododendrons, gingers and heathers — other RBGE specialisms. This is also where 120 or so scientists work behind the scenes trying to make sure that the story is not yet over for some endangered species, as well as continually discovering new information about others.

Back in the Palm Houses, the leaves of a potted Begonia dregei with delicate white flowers from South Africa are just turning from green to a pale red.

“Our scientists have identified over 100 new species [of begonia] and counting,” says Knights, calling the tale of the begonia the one that is “closest to [her] heart”.

“We are doing a lot of DNA analysis to try and understand a particular question about begonias, which is why do you have some the size of a fingernail and others the size of a car tyre? Why do we have that biodiversity of even shapes and sizes?

“We’re losing [some] plants at such a fast rate and yet we don’t know everything there is to know about them and that’s why these questions are so important,” she adds.

The RBGE is open daily (except 25 December and 1 January) from 10am; closing hours are seasonal. Entrance is free but advance booking is advised to see the new Palm Houses . An adult ticket for the Palm Houses costs £4.95 or £5.50 with a donation.

rows.title: UK ministers resist union demands to rescue Scottish steelmaker
rows.content:
Ashley Armstrong and Jim Pickard

Published October 2 2026

Ministers are resisting union and industry demands to take control of another chunk of Sanjeev Gupta’s faltering steel empire, amid concerns about the cost of recent nationalisations, according to two people close to the situation.

Liberty Steel Dalzell, which has its main steel plate mill in Motherwell, Scotland, remains owned by the Gupta Family Group Alliance and provides steel for Royal Navy warships.

The business, which employs just over 100 people, has not filed accounts with Companies House for the past six years and its site has been sitting idle for months.

A key trade union and an industry group are pushing for the UK government to take control of the Scottish site and combine it with its other steel businesses: British Steel, which was nationalised from Chinese owner Jingye in July, and Liberty Speciality Steel, which the government said last month that it would take over.

“It is right that there is full consideration of how the strong synergies that exist with other businesses — including British Steel — can be fully utilised,” said Alasdair McDiarmid, assistant general secretary at Community, a union that represents workers at Dalzell.

Together the three companies could strengthen Britain’s domestic supply chain for defence and offshore wind farms. British Steel makes the raw steel slabs which the Dalzell site could heat and roll into metal plates for the navy.

Gareth Stace, director-general of UK Steel, an industry body, said there was a “once-in-a-generation opportunity” to look at the synergies.

Two people close to the situation said officials were aware of the challenges facing the Motherwell business.

One of the people close to the situation said that there were many stakeholders who were pushing for the government to take control, but the question was “whether there’s money to do so”.

A government spokesperson said: “We recognise the importance of the Dalzell site to the workforce, local community and the UK’s wider capability but responsibility for the site remains with Liberty Steel as the private owner.”

Liberty Steel declined to comment.

Speciality Steel had been in the Official Receiver’s hands before the government said that it was considering public ownership — distinguishing its status from that of the Dalzell site currently.

A recent report by the Public Accounts Committee found British Steel had already cost taxpayers £555mn and the site is losing £1.3mn a day.

MPs criticised the government for lacking a plan to put the company on a sustainable footing.

Gupta, once hailed as the “ saviour of steel ”, bought up unloved metals companies around the middle of the previous decade to build a conglomerate stretching from Scotland to Australia and employing about 35,000 people.

But the group has floundered since its main lender Greensill Capital went into administration in 2021, prompting plant and mine closures, thousands of job losses and an effort to refinance more than $5bn in debt.

Gupta is also facing legal action from Companies House for failing to file accounts in the UK while the Serious Fraud Office has an ongoing investigation.

The Scottish government lent Gupta £7mn in 2017 to facilitate the purchase of Dalzell.

The entrepreneur had pledged to also turn around the Alvance aluminium smelter in the Scottish Highlands, and to open an aluminium car wheel factory, with a separate financial guarantee from the Scottish government.

The Scottish government said there was no interest paid on the loan after June 2024.

Dalzell will restart operations this week using imported steel slabs from Kazakhstan, according to a person close to the company.

rows.title: Trump’s diesel threats could go very wrong — just look at the soyabean
rows.content:
Gillian Tett

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Cometh the hour, cometh the panic — and the performative politics. This autumn Chuck Grassley, the longest-serving Republican senator, has watched in dismay as his party’s polling numbers have wilted amid popular anger over inflation and the Iran war.

So, with the midterm elections looming, he and other Republican leaders are urging President Donald Trump to ban exports of US diesel, in a bid to stop record-high prices squeezing voters.

“Why doesn’t Pres Trump put an embargo on diesel exports like presidents in the 70s put embargoes on ag[ricultural] products bc food prices were inflated,” Grassley wrote in a recent social media post, referring to President Richard Nixon’s 1973 embargo on soyabean exports. “High diesel prices ARE KILLING FARMERS INCOME.”

Whether Trump will take this advice is unclear. He has said he is “very seriously considering” embracing a ban. But Chris Wright, his energy secretary, has lobbied against one, as have American energy executives. One person close to the debate admitted to the FT that “we don’t have a firm sense of what he’s going to do” because “this is all about Trump.” Welcome to how Washington works today.

Amid all this, however, there is a bitter historical irony at play. In the Trump administration, it seems almost natural for Republicans to embrace trade controls as nationalist economic tools in order to appease populist political forces.

But for 1980s Republican president Ronald Reagan — who men such as Grassley revere — such trade meddling was anathema. And if you dig into the history of that 1973 soyabean embargo, it was anything but a success.

Yes, Nixon’s export ban did briefly suppress domestic prices; hence why Trump might like to emulate it when it comes to diesel. But it also “raised questions about the US as a reliable supplier of staple commodities”, as Jonathan Coppess at the University of Illinois wrote in a 2019 paper.

The Japanese government, which relied on US soyabean imports, was so furious that in 1974, Coppess says, the Japan International Cooperation Agency began a large-scale investment in the development of the Cerrado region in Brazil for soyabean production.

That worked remarkably well. Indeed, by 2015 Brazil was exporting more soyabeans than America — and, somewhat remarkably, Brazilian sales last year were nearly twice those from the US.

More recently, the US has scored another own goal. Today China is the world’s biggest source of soyabean demand. However, Trump’s US-China trade war has hobbled American sales there, and Chinese purchasers buy from Latin America instead. When Trump met with Xi Jinping, his Chinese counterpart this month, soyabeans were notably excluded from the $30bn worth of tariff-cutting trade deals that were announced — much to American farmers’ fury.

“Trump has been very good for the Brazilian soybean business,” one Chinese importer joked to me last week; he now buys most beans from non-US sources. Or as Philip Verleger, an American energy economist, wrote in a recent Substack : “[In 1973] Richard Nixon sacrificed the US farmers’ future for a few months of lower consumer prices.”

Would a diesel ban repeat that? White House officials tell me not, because America is now so dominant in fossil fuels, and it is harder to switch diesel suppliers. They also insist that fuel supplies will soon move freely through the Strait of Hormuz. Maybe so.

But Trump officials have been talking to allies about a possible export ban and demanding that Europe dip into its reserves to lower prices. So during the recent meeting of the UN General Assembly in New York I heard non-American executives and government officials outlining plans to protect themselves from the fossil fuel squeeze by “diversifying”, ie embracing renewable energy.

That might create new vulnerabilities: renewable energy can be intermittent, and China dominates the green tech supply chain . But these risks look less daunting when set against the dangers of being a hostage to capricious US trade policy or wars in the Gulf.

As Verleger tells me: “What country is going to want to rely on the US for natural gas exports now, if America might suddenly cut these off?” To put it bluntly: one consequence of Trump’s Iran war is an acceleration of the green transition that the president loves to hate — and which will make others less exposed to the US.

The White House should be paying attention. Yes, a putative diesel ban might score short-term political points. But it may also prompt US energy groups to curb production , thus boosting prices in the medium term. And insofar as a diesel export ban will make America seem (even more) unreliable to allies, there will be big long-term costs. Just look at that humble soyabean to see what happens when politics ignores the power of unintended consequences.

rows.title: No, AI is not similar to the Manhattan Project
rows.content:
Adam Tooze

Published October 2 2026

The writer is an FT contributing editor and writes the Chartbook newsletter

To describe the current AI race, the historical analogy of the moment is the nuclear arms race. Trump’s White House has directly tied its Genesis Mission for AI to the precedent of the Manhattan Project — the effort during the second world war to develop the original atomic bombs. This historical association is intended to sound urgent, dramatic and reassuring all at the same time. And that is also why it is unhelpful. As serious as it may sound to invoke Los Alamos, the analogy in fact presents a sanitised image of the drama we find ourselves in.

For those pushing the urgency and national importance of AI, it is obvious why the Manhattan Project is attractive. A spectacular scientific breakthrough owed to the greatest minds of their generation was put at the service of winning the war against fascism. The ethical dilemmas were real, but in figures such as Oppenheimer they can be portrayed as morally serious.

This is not the world that we are in.

For one, the early atomic bombs were comparatively modest explosive devices, suitable for destroying individual cities not entire civilisations, let alone humanity. The sort of apocalyptic risk fitfully debated in Silicon Valley right now did not appear in the nuclear arms race until the advent of the thermonuclear age in the 1950s and the development of the hydrogen bomb.

If you are looking for a narrative from that period, the urtext is Stanley Kubrick’s satire, Dr Strangelove . Tellingly, in that version of nuclear disaster it is rogue agents — not software but actual humans — who take it upon themselves to launch a first strike and thus provoke the Soviet doomsday machine. The analogy is not edifying. Kubrick’s point was to highlight the obvious insanity at the heart of deterrence doctrine. From the cigar-chomping cold war cowboy to the not-so-ex-Nazi ruminating lasciviously about the sex ratios in the atomic bunker, every manner of ideological fixation was mixed into an annihilatory logic of tit-for-tat.

But dark and funny as Dr Strangelove may be, our situation is even more delirious. We have the old framings of autocracy vs democracy and China vs US. We have dark rumours of the antichrist . But this time, the central actors in our drama are not scientists, soldiers or civil servants but businessmen with huge conflicts of interest. When the bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic took it upon themselves to warn of existential risks and to call for “pacing the frontier”, the immediate suspicion was that they were talking their own book. They were seeking to stir up a panic so as to provoke regulation and thus stabilise their precarious oligopoly. “Rocket-makers in clash with Wall Street over nuke safety worries” is not a headline even Kubrick would have dreamt up.

What separates us both from the Manhattan Project and from Dr Strangelove is political economy. Between 1940 and 1996, a Brookings study estimated that the US spent $5.5tn in 1990s dollars on the nuclear arms race. A substantial slice of that went to private contractors, who no doubt did their best to keep the foreign policy “blob” in Washington DC on high alert and the dollars rolling in. But in its overall architecture the Manhattan Project was the paradigm case of technocratic, government-led industrial policy. It inaugurated the era of publicly funded “big university” research, to which the Trump administration and the likes of Elon Musk are so deeply opposed.

What is singular and novel about the current AI threat is that, for all its profound geopolitical implications, it was born out of the private sector, out of the technologically and commercially driven logic of search engines and advertising algos. It is a product of Silicon Valley after the end of the cold war, when R&D budgets had substantially shifted from the public to the private sector. At first it could be funded in-house from the cash-rich tech balance sheets. But in the hyperscaling race for AGI, existential technological risk has been hooked to Wall Street and financialisation.

The world we are in is not that of ascetic bombmakers wrestling with their souls. It is both darker and more mundane. Today’s world-threatening technologies are fuelled by trillionaire greed, junk bonds and jerry-rigged financial engineering. In filmic terms, think Dr Strangelove mashed up with Gordon “Greed-is-Good” Gekko and a dash of The Big Short . If this is the way the world ends, it will be not with a bang or a whimper, but in a whirl of tech jargon, Californian lifestyles and financial engineering.

rows.title: The Abu Dhabi power broker facing his toughest test at Manchester City
rows.content:
Chloe Cornish in Dubai and Arash Massoudi in London

Published October 2 2026

Khaldoon al-Mubarak rarely appears ruffled. One of Abu Dhabi’s most powerful non-royals, he straddles global finance, diplomacy and football with a polished assurance that mirrors the emirate’s meticulously managed image.

But Mubarak has never hidden his frustration over the Premier League’s probe into Manchester City’s finances, an eight-year saga that has cast a shadow over the club’s transformation from mid-table laggards to a trophy-winning machine since Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan bought it in 2008.

The league’s announcement this week that City had been found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges it was facing has plunged the club into crisis.

An independent commission found that City had used “sham” sponsorship agreements and contracts to massage its accounts, inflating its revenues and understating costs by £900mn. City maintains it is innocent and will appeal against the verdict.

Now Mubarak must defend both an asset that has become one of the emirate’s most successful soft-power projects and his own reputation, as his stewardship of the club comes under intense scrutiny.

“There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club,” he wrote in a defiant open letter on Saturday, becoming the first person from City to speak out on the matter. “We will not give them that opportunity.”

City is just one part of Mubarak’s vast remit.

As group chief executive of Mubadala, he is the world’s longest-serving head of a sovereign investment fund and one of the key figures overseeing oil-rich Abu Dhabi’s more than $1.5tn in wealth.

He also handles critical diplomatic relationships, including with China, and chairs the Executive Affairs Authority, an advisory body to United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, Sheikh Mansour’s brother. When Abu Dhabi was given a seat on Donald Trump’s Board of Peace this year, Mubarak was chosen as its representative.

“The power he holds is massive,” said one executive at a large global investment firm. “But he does it from behind the scenes.”

The son of a senior Emirati diplomat who was assassinated in Paris when Mubarak was eight, he comes from a family of religious and judicial experts who served in government and were close to Abu Dhabi’s ruling Nahyan family.

After his father’s death, he grew up partly in the royal palace, later moving to Boston to study at Tufts University before returning to work at Abu Dhabi’s national oil company.

Mubarak was soon among the officials entrusted by Sheikh Mohamed with implementing his ambitious plans for Abu Dhabi.

In 2002 he was selected to lead the newly founded Mubadala Development Company, which was charged with helping diversify Abu Dhabi’s oil-dependent economy and investing its hydrocarbon wealth in new industries and infrastructure.

Fifteen years later it merged with Sheikh Mansour’s larger International Petroleum Investment Company, which had become embroiled in Malaysia’s 1MDB scandal, before adding another wealth fund, the Abu Dhabi Investment Council, a year later.

As chief executive of the enlarged group, renamed Mubadala Investment Company and chaired by Sheikh Mansour, Mubarak now heads Abu Dhabi’s second-biggest sovereign fund, which manages $385bn and is one of the world’s most active dealmakers.

He “is someone whose word you can trust”, said Bayo Ogunlesi, chair and CEO of BlackRock-owned Global Infrastructure Partners, adding that Mubarak had “remained centred and treats everyone with respect”.

As Mubarak’s prominence in international investing has grown, so has the rest of his portfolio, with many in the UAE now regarding him as more powerful than most ministers.

“His responsibility has transcended way beyond finance,” said Diego López, founder and managing director of Global SWF, an industry tracker.

Kristian Ulrichsen, fellow for the Middle East at the Baker Institute, described Mubarak as “suave”, “very articulate” and “incredibly capable”, saying “that’s why he’s been given so many portfolios”.

Mohamed Alabbar, managing director of Dubai property developer Emaar, said he had seen Mubarak in “many, many situations . . . He’s a good human being . . . he’s light-hearted, he’s funny, he’s probably the best friend you can get if you are lucky. And he’s clean.”

During a career tied to Abu Dhabi’s development, Mubarak has taken on projects from bringing nuclear power to the Gulf region to building a Formula 1 circuit while largely avoiding personal association with controversies that have dogged the emirate.

These range from the 1MDB scandal to claims that the UAE has armed a faction in Sudan’s civil war that the US has accused of genocide, allegations that Abu Dhabi had repeatedly denied.

But his role at City has made him Abu Dhabi’s most recognisable non-royal. While Sheikh Mansour has stayed in the shadows, Mubarak has been the public face of the club’s transformation into a footballing powerhouse — a regular fixture at the Etihad Stadium who has lifted trophies as City won eight Premier League titles as well as the Champions League.

He has repeatedly rejected allegations of wrongdoing by the club. But the trust placed in him by supporters, players and team managers will now be tested by the details of alleged misconduct set out by the commission — and by whether City can overturn the decision on appeal.

Supporters and figures associated with City have rallied round the club. Pep Guardiola, head coach from 2016 until this summer, wrote on social media on Wednesday that he was and “always will be behind my club, my owner, my chairman”.

Consequences for UK industry from any breakdown in relations could be serious. The UAE has committed £30bn under a sovereign investment partnership with the UK, overseen by Mubarak.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that the matter could have an impact on both the Premier League and “Brand UK”, adding that he would be “really concerned” if the UAE, which had been “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”, ultimately decided to sell the club.

Ulrichsen said the reputational impact could be worse than that of previous controversies involving the emirate.

“This will probably go global in a way that nothing else has and will associate Abu Dhabi with a club that was systematically cheating,” he said.

Mubarak must manage the fallout at a time when Abu Dhabi’s ambitions to become the destination of choice for the global elite and an internationally significant finance hub are being complicated by the US-Israel war with Iran.

The stakes also extend to Abu Dhabi itself. Although the emirate insists Sheikh Mansour’s investment in the club was private, Mubarak has previously acknowledged that City’s performance and conduct would reflect on the emirate as it embarked on its huge development plans and sought to project itself on the global stage.

“[H]ow we are handling this project is telling a lot to the world about how we are,” Mubarak told The Guardian in 2009. “This is showing the world the true essence of who Abu Dhabi is and what Abu Dhabi is about.”

Additional reporting by Lucy Fisher and Josh Noble in London

rows.title: George Lucas’s $1bn Museum of Narrative Art uses the force of storytelling
rows.content:
James Cahill

Published October 2 2026

In the gardens of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is a heroic bronze sculpture of Jabba the Hutt, surmounted by a bikini-clad Princess Leia. She hauls a chain around the monster’s neck, in a hyper-real recreation of a scene from Return of the Jedi (1983), the third movie released in the Star Wars saga. The bronze statue, a commission by sculptor Mark Newman and digital modeller Giovanni Nakpil, is a disorientating mixture of Las Vegas and high baroque — and an apt prelude to the building facing it.

The museum has materialised in the Los Angeles neighbourhood of Exposition Park like a gigantic spacecraft. It is the billion-dollar creation of George Lucas and his wife Mellody Hobson. The pair first conceived of a permanent home for their art collection some 20 years ago. Originally intended to be in San Francisco, then Chicago, the museum was finally established on a 13-acre site (much of it formerly a parking lot) alongside the historic LA Memorial Coliseum stadium.

Despite Los Angeles being Lucas and Hobson’s third choice (design disagreements and local opposition thwarted the earlier two options), the museum seems to have been made for the city. “I feel like it is the only place it ever should have been,” says Ryan Linkof, the museum’s senior curator, as we tour the building on a dazzling late September morning. Over the street is the University of Southern California, Lucas’s alma mater. Close by are the Natural History Museum, the California Science Center, and the California African American Museum.

Set within landscaped parkland scattered with sculptures, the Lucas Museum is defiantly escapist — an oasis or a folly, depending on how you look at it. The building alone is an almost cinematic spectacle. Designed by Ma Yansong of MAD Architects, the curving, double-domed structure appears to float above the ground. “There are no right angles,” Linkof observes from the cylindrical glass elevator. The exterior, with its white polymer panels, visors of black glass and canopies of turf, inescapably recalls the sci-fi world of Star Wars .

But it is inside that Lucas’s sensibility truly takes hold. Across 100,000 sq ft of galleries, most of them located on the fifth floor, is a vast assortment of paintings, drawings, sculptures and illustrations that reflect the theme of storytelling. There is little to unite them besides that. “Narrative art”, it turns out, is a wide-open field — a means of bypassing traditional categories as much as an organising principle.

The ground-floor galleries — titled “The History of Narrative Art” — offer a theme park-style walk-through of western and world art. This begins with a cavern-like space lined with backlit graphics of the prehistoric Altamira cave paintings of northern Spain, and proceeds through a joyously haphazard array of hologram-style projections of canonical objects and paintings, interspersed with a few originals. Video projections of the Sistine Chapel and Hagia Sophia in Istanbul offer dizzyingly clear recreations of the buildings’ interiors. Michelangelo’s “David” looms — an almost palpable digital model — inside a niche in the wall. It is based on an image of a plaster cast at the Victoria and Albert Museum rather than the real statue.

Originality is beside the point. As Linkof explains: “The thesis statement that George has really clearly articulated from a long time ago, even before the museum existed, is that humans use images to tell stories, and those stories shape who we are and shape the world.” It is a boldly universalising approach, and one that befits a collection shaped by predilection rather than curatorial dictates. “We don’t have wall texts other than just the labels,” Linkof points out, though he adds that the digital guide contains a wealth of information for those who desire it.

Up on the labyrinthine main floor, the emphasis shifts to Lucas and Hobson’s own vast array of artworks, most of them dating from the 19th and 20th centuries. Multiple exhibits blur the lines between fine art and commercial illustration: among the highlights is a substantial collection of comic book drawings, including a 1908 design by Winsor McCay for Little Nemo in Slumberland , a comic strip about a little boy’s dreams. Comics were among Lucas’s own early inspirations; he referred to them in a 1975 interview as “the hieroglyphs or the graffiti of our times”. A drawing for Alley Oop , a strip created in 1932 about a caveman who travels through time, was one of the first works he acquired.

Other galleries abound with fantasy-themed drawings and paintings, featuring characters such as Conan the Barbarian and Vampirella. Amid the inevitable pap, there are reminders of the technical virtuosity that “kitsch” imagery often belies. J Allen St John’s 1922 painting “The Chessmen of Mars”, depicting a dragon-borne warrior, carries echoes of Eugène Delacroix’s more extravagant orientalist scenes. The rose-tinted, classicising fantasies of Maxfield Parrish — which would strike many an avant-gardist as hideous — achieve a perverse kind of loveliness in concert.

Star Wars , unsurprisingly, is a big theme. Several interconnecting galleries house ephemera such as the early painted vignettes that gave rise to movie scenes, and vehicles such as Luke Skywalker’s weather-beaten X-34 landspeeder, complete with a waxwork-style Luke. But Lucas’s own creations form only one — relatively contained — act. “George made this museum in some ways to elevate artists who haven’t had representation in museums and in art history,” Linkof explains.

Cassius Marcellus Coolidge is one such outlier: his 1894 painting of dogs playing poker (one of many on the theme) has become an icon of American popular culture, but is hardly a work of high art. Many other images are lesser known, and have generally been arranged around traditional (faintly idealised) themes such as motherhood, family, love and work, offset by a smaller number of single-artist displays. Not that the collection is lacking in grit. Balancing a newly made replica of a bronze statue of George Washington by Jean-Antoine Houdon (originally dating from 1788-92) is a 2005 collage by Kara Walker that expresses a more ambivalent reckoning with history: a paper silhouette of a Black slave sprints over the top of a civil war-era engraving of jubilant Unionists.

The path to the museum’s opening has been its own protracted saga. The pandemic caused repeated delays to construction. In 2025, the then director, Sandra Jackson-Dumont, and chief curator, Pilar Tompkins Rivas, both exited — leaving Lucas at the curatorial helm. How far these departures altered the museum’s evolution is anyone’s guess; Linkof notes that Lucas “is definitely someone who will continue to tinker”.

The result, however, is exuberantly undogmatic. Not unlike the new Geffen Galleries at LACMA, the displays at the Lucas Museum are an exercise in free-form arrangement. At times the clashes are bewildering: a Batman effigy stands close by a self-portrait by Frida Kahlo. But there are more coherent groupings that might easily belong in a traditional art institution, including an unprecedented range of pictures by Norman Rockwell — homely, subtly haunting fragments of 20th-century American life.

Like the house-sized cornucopia of Sir John Soane in London or the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston, the Lucas Museum is a dream made real, and a testament if nothing else to its creators’ subjective vision. “Narrative art” may be a useful label for unifying the miscellany of Lucas and Hobson’s collection, but it is also a red herring, suggesting a soberness of purpose that the project resists. What Lucas and Hobson have created is not a museum at all, in the academic sense, but an eccentric curiosity — and a riveting story in its own right.
