rows.title: US refiners reap windfall profits as wars push up fuel prices for consumers
rows.content:
Jamie Smyth and Peter Wells in New York

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

US refiners are on course to report a more than fourfold increase in profits due to surging diesel and petrol prices caused by Donald Trump’s Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities.

Eight listed independent US refiners are expected to report combined profits worth $32.4bn in the two quarters since the war began, compared with $6.8bn in the same period last year.

Revenues are forecast at $325.5bn versus $242.9bn last year, according to an FT analysis of each company’s second-quarter results and Wall Street’s expectations for the third quarter.

The Iran war and Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries have pushed up global fuel prices to near-record levels. Despite increasing domestic production, the US has not been immune to the energy shock, with diesel prices surging by more than $2.50 to $6.38 per gallon since the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.

While record oil producer profits have attracted notice, the conditions have also created a windfall for the oft-overlooked refining segment of the energy industry, which has undergone a stunning reversal of fortune after years struggling with tight margins and cut-throat competition from Middle Eastern and Asian rivals.

“We are seeing a drastic change in financial performance for US refiners because of the huge disruption caused to fuel supplies from conflicts in the Middle East and Russia,” said Arne Skjæveland, analyst at Rystad Energy.

He said refiners’ profit margins were approaching levels last seen during the energy crisis sparked by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and were likely to stay elevated because of continued geopolitical instability.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Refiners have faced higher input costs from rising crude prices since the war began, but the value of refined products has risen even more, pushing the price premium — known as “crack spreads” in industry jargon — to record levels.

The three biggest independent refiners, Valero, Marathon Petroleum and Phillips 66, are expected to generate net income of $8.7bn, $10.9bn and $7.9bn respectively in the six months to end September. And for the first time in a year, all eight refiners are expected to make a profit in the third quarter, as they raise output to record levels to meet a global shortfall of diesel and other products. Valero, Marathon and Phillips did not respond to requests for comment.

US refinery output hit a five-year high of 17.4mn barrels per day in August as they ran above 95 per cent of capacity for 15 straight weeks, the longest stretch since 1998, according to Rystad Energy, a research group.

US exports of diesel, petrol, jet fuel and naphtha increased to 2.8mn barrels per day in August from 2.3mn a year earlier, as European and Latin American customers raced to find alternative supplies because of restricted flows from the Middle East and Russia.

ExxonMobil and Chevron, which own a large number of US refineries, as well as oil and gas production facilities, are also enjoying a profits bonanza. Chevron reported its highest quarterly profit on record in three months to end June, while Exxon reported its highest quarterly profit since 2022.

The windfall profits boost has sparked calls for government intervention, such as a ban on diesel exports or windfall taxes that the oil industry warns would cause long-term damage to the sector.

Democrats have called on Congress to pass the Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act, which would impose a tax on oil company profits and redistribute the income raised in the form of tax credits to consumers.

“Big Oil and President Trump don’t care that you are paying 50 per cent more for gas this Labor Day weekend because they are profiting from these prices. It’s wrong. That’s why I’m pushing for the Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act,” Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-sponsor of the bill, said at a public appearance last month.

And in an unusual intervention by Republican legislators, some members of Congress from agricultural states called for a diesel export ban, which they hope would at least in the short term bring down prices for American farmers.

The Trump administration is considering a range of options to tackle soaring diesel and petrol prices, which have dented the president’s approval ratings just five weeks before November’s midterm elections.

But it has so far resisted pulling the trigger on an export ban, which energy analysts have said could prompt refiners to slash production and force up the prices of other products such as petrol and jet fuel.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The oil industry has defended its response to the surge in diesel prices, arguing that it has done everything it can to increase production and is not responsible for the conflicts in Iran and Russia.

Dustin Meyer, senior vice-president of policy at the American Petroleum Institute, said refining was a cyclical business where success was measured in decades, not quarters.

“Today’s higher prices reflect unprecedented disruption to global refining capacity — not the actions of individual companies. US refiners are running near maximum capacity to meet demand while investing in the infrastructure and resilience that strengthen America’s long-term energy security.”

rows.title: What can Burnham learn from Scotland’s social care system?
rows.content:
Simeon Kerr in Edinburgh and Chris Smyth in London

Published October 2 2026

Andy Burnham has pledged to use his political capital to fix Britain’s broken social care system.

The prime minister outlined the creation of a “National Care Service” if Labour wins the next election, promising that it would give “peace of mind” while protecting savings and valuing workers in the sector.

“There is only one real answer: a person-centred, high-quality care service that starts in the home,” he told the Labour conference this week. “A system . . . where everyone contributes and everyone is covered.”

That principle has been in place in Scotland since 2002 when free personal care was rolled out to over-65s before being extended in 2019 to all adults in need.

But the Scottish experience illustrates the limits of the current system.

As with Burnham’s plan, Scots still cover their accommodation and living costs in a care home. Those with assets of more than £36,750 generally have to meet these costs themselves, while those below that threshold receive varying levels of council support depending on their financial circumstances.

Sir Andrew Dilnot, the economist who recommended an alternative system for England that caps care costs, argued the Scottish system leaves families facing potentially ruinous bills.

“It is important to note that the Scottish system does not protect homes and savings — someone in a residential care home in Scotland receives weekly support from the state of £260 against a weekly bill from the care home of £930 or more, leaving a gap of £670 if they fail the means test,” Dilnot said.

“If the prime minister hopes to protect homes and savings, the natural policy is a cap on lifetime care costs.”

Scotland’s divergence goes back to 1999, when Sir Stewart Sutherland’s commission recommended free personal care funded by general taxation. The UK Labour government rejected the proposal for England, arguing that universal care would subsidise those who are better off. After devolution, however, the Labour-led Scottish executive adopted the idea.

“Free personal care does work — it expands entitlement and access and makes a lot of political sense. This idea can resonate with all — help getting dressed or getting in and out of bed, which in a civilised nation is provided for by the state,” said Sebastian Rees, head of health at the IPPR, a think-tank.

“It builds a powerful coalition around a more generous system — so there are lots of reasons to do it in England, but it won’t be easy and wouldn’t solve all the problems.”

Burnham’s vision of a National Care Service to complement the NHS had been considered by the Scottish government, but last year it abandoned a proposed structural reorganisation after the plan lost the support of councils, unions and opposition parties over concerns including centralisation.

Scotland’s system is facing other pressures, including an ageing population, while being constrained by tighter finances for the councils that deliver the services directly and through third-party providers.

The country’s spending per person on adult social care services in 2024-25 was £689, more than a third higher than England’s at £506, according to the IFS.

The growing queue for personal care is also complicated by different eligibility thresholds, leading to a “postcode lottery” for who receives public support. Care is limited to basic personal needs, such as dressing and washing, and does not include tasks such as shopping.

“The benefit of the Scottish model as a universal entitlement is that it is relatively easily understood, but not all have had a favourable experience,” said Camille Oung, a fellow at Nuffield Trust, a health think-tank.

Other models, such as those used in Germany and France, offer more flexibility and choice through needs-adjusted monetary allowances.

The rate of Scottish funding for legally required care delivery has also lagged care costs, said Lynn Laughland, chief executive of Kilmarnock-based HRM Homecare Services.

While the Homecare Association’s minimum price for homecare — through which much free personal care is provided — in Scotland this year is £36.49 an hour, councils are paying on average £24.73 an hour, she said.

In September, more than 6,600 people were waiting for a care assessment and more than 3,300 people were waiting for care at home to begin. The weekly hours of delayed care have risen almost 40 per cent year-on-year.

“The lesson for England is that an entitlement is only as good as the funding of the care that delivers it,” said Laughland.

Expanding free personal care to over-65s in England would cost an estimated £6bn, rising to £10-12bn if eligible adults are included, suggested Rees of the IPPR. A comprehensive system including care home costs would reach an estimated £18.7bn, according to The Health Foundation think-tank.

Beyond funding, forging a workforce capable of meeting care requirements is another challenge.

“When considering funding, we also need to consider who will provide that care, how we value those who do this essential job, and how their skills can continue to be developed, as well as appropriately paid for,” said Professor Susan Shenkin of Edinburgh university.

Scotland has more than 135,000 adult social care workers, with industry surveys suggesting that more than a quarter are staff recruited from overseas.

The ruling Scottish National Party, which has urged Burnham to adopt the Scottish system, has called on him to ensure that proposed changes to visa rules do not hinder the entry of care workers.

Visas issued to main applicants for care jobs fell from 108,000 in the year to December 2023 to just 344 in the year to June 2026 after the UK ended new overseas recruitment of care workers in July 2025.

While England’s workforce continued to grow in 2025-26, the number of posts filled by British nationals fell by 40,000.

Around 360,000 more social care workers will be needed in England by 2035, said Professor Catherine Needham of Birmingham university.

“Government and other care sector bodies have talked about the need for more ‘homegrown’ care workers for years — but there is so little progress towards making this happen,” she added.

rows.title: Emerging markets outperform developed markets as bond rout deepens
rows.content:
Joseph Cotterill and Emily Herbert in London

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Emerging markets are weathering the global sell-off in bond markets better than developed world peers, as investors bet that many countries are now less vulnerable to the threat of higher US interest rates drawing capital away.

Years of painful fiscal reforms, bolstering of central banks and finance ministries and a willingness to tackle inflation early by boosting interest rates have left many developing countries better able to withstand rising yields and a surging US dollar that might have triggered an emerging-market sell-off in the past.

“Basically — a lot more resilient than you would otherwise guess,” said Werner Gey van Pittius, co-chief investment officer for fixed income at Ninety One. “If I had told you at the start of the year that US Treasuries were going to go up 110 basis points, you would have said that EM is going to explode. And it hasn’t.”

Yields on 10-year US Treasuries have surged from 4.8 per cent to 5.3 per cent in the past month. Yet, in South Africa, Chile and other large developing nations, sovereign yields have risen much less and in some cases, such as Brazil, have fallen, reflecting a deep divergence between emerging and developed market bonds in recent years. Bond yields rise when their prices fall.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

“Fiscal discipline has arguably been stronger in emerging markets. They have been pretty good at increasing institutional credibility . . . how they handled inflation post-Covid has given people reassurance,” said Eva Sun-Wai, portfolio manager at M&G.

Sovereign local currency bonds in emerging markets gained 18 per cent over the course of last year and were up 3.5 per cent this year to the end of August, according to a benchmark JPMorgan index.

The global sell-off in September has left the index flat for the year to date. But that still marks a significant outperformance over developed-market bonds, which are down 4.5 per cent in the year to date, according to a Bloomberg benchmark index.

Many investors say a continuation of reforms in emerging markets and underlying strength in the global economy are protecting many countries from a bigger sell-off this year.

“Given the shock, I have to say that [EM] is doing very well,” said Luis Costa, global head of emerging markets strategy at Citi.

“Most of the broad indices for EM debt lost ground over the past month, but if you look at it curve by curve,” or market by market, he added, in many countries yields have not moved up as drastically as they have in the US.

One big risk is that US stocks sell off over the rise in US yields, as they did in 2023, denting demand for all risk assets including emerging markets, Costa said. For now, US stocks are riding high on the AI theme and “we are still getting revisions higher in earnings expectations”, he added.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

“Higher US yields and a firmer dollar raise the bar for EM across local [sovereign bonds] and [dollar sovereign] credit, but contained volatility, stronger fundamentals and resilient spreads point to subdued returns rather than a disorderly sell-off,” said James Lord, Morgan Stanley emerging markets strategist.

In local currency debt, the rise in oil prices and inflation this year has led central bankers in many countries to keep domestic interest rates and hence inflation-adjusted yields relatively high after years of keeping prices under better control than in developed markets.

“Emerging markets [are] holding their own,” said Harriet Ballard, multi-asset portfolio manager at Aviva Investors. She said she was positioned for emerging market local currencies to outperform the dollar because of “a more positive growth outlook for that region”.

“In terms of fiscal credibility and growth, a lot of emerging markets are in a good position relative to developed markets,” she said. “That spread has narrowed.”

Lesetja Kganyago, South Africa’s central bank governor, said this week that reforms to restrain high debts and inflation “have been important in shielding us from the 2026 global bond repricing”, even though the bank has failed to meet its inflation target for the past six months.

“I am not happy that we are missing — but six months is a lot better than 67 months, which is the interval since US inflation was last at target,” he said. The country’s current long-term rand bond yield of about 9 per cent “is roughly where we were at the end of 2025, and well below earlier levels”, even as US Treasury yields have hit their highest in decades, he added.

Some investors have stuck with more niche emerging-market bets, such as oil-rich frontier markets with particularly high interest rates.

A newly launched JPMorgan index for local currency bonds in frontier markets would have gained between 7 and 8 per cent this year based on pricing data. It features crude oil exporters such as Nigeria and Kazakhstan that have posted some of the year’s biggest currency gains against the dollar.

Countries such as Argentina and Egypt are particularly exposed to higher yields because they need to roll over large amounts of short-term debt but in others, such as South Africa, Thailand and Malaysia, deeper pools of domestic capital are replacing the need for dollar borrowing, S&P Global analysts said.

A stronger dollar and rising US yields “will expose a widening divide between borrowers supported by deep domestic markets and policy flexibility and those dependent on external capital with heavy refinancing needs,” the analysts said.

Bank of America analysts recently argued that investors historically have tended to offload emerging-market dollar bonds when the yield on the JPMorgan index hits 8 per cent, as a signal that risks are outweighing the appeal of extra yields. That benchmark yield is currently 7.2 per cent.

“At the moment we [in EM] are somewhat immune to the DM issues. But if there is a significant spread widening in DM, EM will not be immune forever,” said Sergei Strigo, fund manager at Amundi.

rows.title: How to revive the UK’s zombified housing market
rows.content:
Neal Hudson

Published October 2 2026

News that the UK government is launching a revived Help to Buy scheme has baffled some market watchers.

After all, there are many who read the news — or look out of the window at their neighbours’ weather-beaten for-sale signs — and think the decline in UK house prices is exactly what they were after, perhaps thinking of their children being able to buy a first home.

When the FT broke the story about the Your First Home plan last Saturday, one reader wrote “Insanity” in the comments under the story. “Absolute madness,” wrote another, “the market is slowly correcting ”.

And they have a point. In some parts of the country, prices are declining in real terms. In London, they are declining in nominal terms — and affordability is improving as the price-to-earnings ratio also falls.

So why do I imagine the government as George W Bush on the deck of that aircraft carrier with “Mission Accomplished” emblazoned behind him? Because it strikes me that the reality is very different from what it envisaged.

Prices are not falling because millions of new homes have been built; they’re falling mostly because of higher interest rates and the market is braced for yet another round of rate increases.

For borrowers with a 75 per cent loan-to-value ratio, the average two-year fix rose from 3.93 per cent in January to 5.14 per cent in April as the market absorbed the impact of the US president joining a war in the Middle East. Rates eased a little in July, but in the past few weeks have been rising again, with some lenders needing to pull and reprice their mortgage products multiple times in that period.

Since 2022, when rates first started going haywire, we’ve ended up with a housing market where house prices are too high. But, with fewer mortgaged homeowners and lending limited to those with high incomes and big deposits, there has been no trigger for a significant price reduction.

This has left us with a zombified housing market, stuck somewhere between boom and bust.

It’s not the market we knew from the early 2010s. Instead, it is stumbling along in the hope that interest rates fall, while feeding on desperate first-time buyers borrowing many multiples of their income — with some having to pay more in mortgage repayments than they did in rent.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Stagnant house prices have become a permanent feature of this market, especially in more expensive parts of the country. Unfortunately, like Simon Pegg’s bleary-eyed character strolling to the corner shop in the film Shaun of the Dead , policymakers have not quite woken up to the reality of our predicament.

So is the Your First Home scheme evidence that the penny has dropped? Or, rather than revive the zombified market, does it just risk creating another monster by boosting demand and loading young people with even more debt?

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The problem is that much of the way we expect — in fact need — housing to function in this country relies on rising house prices.

The shift to a period of low growth affects almost everything the market touches, including turnover, new building, the housing ladder and government tax receipts. When house prices stop rising, the housing market starts to break down.

While house prices might get the headlines, it’s transactions that really matter. It might sound counterintuitive, but house price growth and transactions are positively correlated. If prices fall, people don’t sell. They wait for the recovery — which, at least until now, has always come along.

Rising prices might make homes less affordable, but falling interest rates can counterbalance this. And a rising market increases borrowers’ equity, which is crucial when climbing the housing ladder, allowing homeowners to unlock bigger mortgages and trade from smaller homes to larger ones.

In the market we have now, where price growth is severely limited, it’s much harder to take the next step up the ladder unless you get a big wage rise or an inheritance.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The result is that the housing ladder hasn’t worked for some years now — especially for those stuck in leaseholds with spiralling service charges or anyone whose flat has been affected by cladding issues. Naturally, this hasn’t stopped lenders or politicians — Andy Burnham, the prime minister, appeared on social media with a ladder as a prop — from dangling home ownership in front of first-time buyers. You, too, could end up with a nice large detached house if you just buy that little flat now.

Thankfully, it appears buyers are becoming savvier. Frequent reports indicate that they’re skipping the lower rungs and moving further afield or waiting longer to buy a bigger home.

But there are downsides to this — notably, the government gets lower tax receipts and fewer homes are built.

This is because the current market squeezes the viability of development — and this does not just affect the building of swaths of swanky flats in London. It’s easier for local and central government to get more affordable homes and amenities built when prices are rising faster than build costs.

When fewer affordable homes are built by developers, there’s a greater reliance on government funding.

With the launch of Your First Home, you can practically hear housebuilders breathe a sigh of relief. But, while it has certainly boosted their share prices , there are uncertainties about how effective it will be — especially as the policy is still light on detail.

The original version of the Help to Buy equity loan was introduced in 2013 to bridge a mortgage market failure — lenders did not want to offer low-deposit mortgages on new-build properties and so a 20 per cent equity loan allowed borrowers to buy a new build worth up to £600,000 with a deposit of just 5 per cent. It took a couple of years to bed in but did increase the number of homes being built — and the scare stories about it inflating house prices were largely based on misleading data.

It wasn’t particularly effective in London, so a 40 per cent equity loan was introduced in 2016. This was much more popular and by far the most controversial part of the scheme — some buyers got trapped by the leasehold and building safety crisis in a housing market that was already showing the first signs of zombification.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

In 2021, following a flurry of scandals over build quality and the bonuses housebuilders were paying themselves, the government introduced the second version of the scheme, which included regional price caps and was limited to first-time buyers. This led to some strange local effects as builders shifted to cheaper locations and smaller property types where caps were more restrictive, such as in the north of England, while the higher caps in London and south-east England meant the market was relatively unaffected.

It’s this second version that Your First Home looks most likely to be based on. We know it will provide a 20 per cent equity loan for buyers with a 2.5 per cent deposit, but there’s also mention of household income caps and local property price caps that will be announced in the Budget.

This is where it could get interesting for analysts like me and dangerous for the government.

The politicians are clearly trying to design a scheme that avoids the pitfalls of the previous versions — and their nasty nicknames: “help to sell” or “help to buy bigger”. But the combination of household income and local price caps could create weird distortions. We could even end up with a situation where the only homes that could be built in an area under the scheme are simply not worth the effort as they would need to sell for less than they cost to build.

It’s a good job the government has done plenty of policy analysis and isn’t rushing in at “breakneck speed” — oh, wait .

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Housebuilders have been keen to point out that the Treasury profited from the original scheme. Because the equity loan element is a proportion of the home’s value, the amount owed to the government has increased as house prices have risen. Government data shows that by the end of March this year, the Treasury had made a £1.2bn gain on repaid loans. A recently published evaluation for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government found a “net present social value” of £25.1bn — mostly because it led to more homes being built.

One big question yet to be answered is where the money is coming from this time. It sounds as though it might be drawn from existing budgets rather than new funding and, while there’s mention of developer contributions, the wording suggests this is just to take part rather than on each individual property — that could cause mortgage valuation problems.

The concern is that the money available falls short of the ambition. If so, it wouldn’t be the first time this parliament. Funding for affordable housing has been underwhelming given the scale of Labour’s housebuilding ambitions.

But while it could be fair to say that the original Help to Buy worked well across most of the country, and that buyers have also gained, positive returns were not universal. Those who bought flats, or who used the 40 per cent equity loan scheme in London, have lost money.

Launching Your First Home into today’s market, therefore, comes with the very real risk that it will end up disappointing both buyers and the government.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Details are still scant, but I wouldn’t expect this new scheme seriously to move the dial on housebuilding numbers over the next year or two. The scheme may work better in the Midlands and north of England, where costs are lower. One London developer was quick off the mark to suggest that a cut to stamp duty would be better.

But, more importantly, it delivers a reassuring message that next year might be better for developers who were facing the prospect of a bleak winter, with the prospect of cutting jobs and output after having held on for the past few years.

Perhaps the better comparison is not with the Help to Buy equity loan, but with its mortgage guarantee — a scheme that failed miserably in terms of the number of people who used it, but one that was incredibly important in delivering a message of hope to lenders. In fact, it kick-started the recovery in 2013.

Clearly the government is tempted to pump up house prices to reanimate the zombified housing market. But it may be letting a good crisis go to waste.

With the market currently lacking a pulse, why not think bigger and try to set it up for success over the next 60 years, rather than trying to return to the past 60? It’s naive of me to wish for a long-term housing strategy, but it might help.

Let’s start with property taxation. Stamp duty is a stupid tax that reduces market turnover. while council tax is outdated and regressive. It’s relatively easy to design theoretical alternatives, but the real challenge is implementing them without inflicting political and economic turmoil on the prime minister who pushes the button.

Still, at least the introduction of Your First Home shows that policymakers are beginning to accept that something needs to be done about the UK’s housing market — and are prepared to spend some of their political capital trying to do it.

Neal Hudson is a housing market analyst

rows.title: Directors’ Deals: Entain’s new finance chief builds stake
rows.content:
Erin Withey

Published October 2 2026

Entain shares are down by half over the past 12 months, which is unsurprising given the wave of regulatory obstacles that have hit the gambling sector in recent months.

It has made for a bumpy start for new chief financial officer Michael Snape, who succeeded his longstanding predecessor Rob Wood this spring, just weeks before UK remote gaming duty almost doubled to 40 per cent in April.

Wood’s parting promise was to offset half of the financial impact from higher UK levies partly by using AI to reduce marketing costs. This cost-focused approach has no doubt informed the new CFO’s strategy to protect earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of between £910mn and £960mn for the 2026 financial year.

But the goal took a fresh hit this week after Brazil provisionally banned all online gambling with immediate effect, in a sudden move that rocked investor confidence in the sector.

While Entain maintained its earnings guidance, the Ladbrokes owner conceded that profit may now sit closer to the “lower end” of its forecast range. Brazil makes up 5 per cent of Entain’s online gaming revenue.

For Snape, who spent £249,992 on 51,815 shares 10 days before the announcement, the 482p a share he paid now looks a little rich.

Still, it’s a purchase that was likely made with Entain’s minimum shareholding requirements in mind rather than a case of opportunistic buying. As a newly minted executive, Snape is required to build a stake equivalent to 350 per cent of his £595,000 salary.

Starting from nil at the time of the group’s 2025 annual report, the finance chief has been quietly adding to his holdings and now owns 64,634 shares. Entain allows its executives five years to build their stakes to the required level.

rows.title: When luxury cars turn electric
rows.content:
Kana Inagaki in London and Christian Davies in New York

Published October 2 2026

Two months after motorsport grandee Luca di Montezemolo deemed Ferrari’s new all-electric Luce model unworthy of the marque’s prancing horse emblem, the group’s chief executive had the last laugh.

“I would not change anything in the launch of the Luce ,” Benedetto Vigna told reporters on an earnings call. “We are very pleased about what has been done.”

When the vehicle was unveiled in May, social media exploded with criticism of its design, the work of former Apple designer Sir Jony Ive rather than renowned automotive studios such as Pininfarina or Bertone. The group’s Milan-traded shares fell 8 per cent as di Montezemolo, a former Ferrari chair, witheringly described the Luce as “a car that at least the Chinese won’t copy”.

But by July, Ferrari had already achieved this year’s internal sales target of just under 500 units, according to people with knowledge of the matter, despite the Luce’s €550,000 base price tag. Todd Blue, a California luxury car dealer, adds that demand for the Luce has been “tremendous”, with his salespeople selling out their allocation.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The new car did not just deviate from Ferrari’s historic design ethos. It was part of a strategy to win over completely new clients that allowed the Italian group to tap into a new generation of young and wealthy buyers, particularly in China and in technology hubs such as Silicon Valley.

“For me, this car has an important meaning for Ferrari but also for the European world and for the western world,” Vigna says of the Luce. “Why not believe that we can do it?” He has previously remarked that the surge in wealth creation due to AI is “a good opportunity for us”.

But it is not a playbook that other luxury manufacturers can easily follow, as they contend with the Trump administration’s hostile stance towards EVs and China’s slowing economy.

Many renowned marques are finding it difficult to decide whether to focus on electric or combustion engines, pushing up their costs and complicating longer-term strategic choices. It is a problem for a sector of the industry that is often at the forefront of advances in design and technology, and in which European manufacturers still enjoy almost total dominance, even as cheap Chinese-made cars flood into the mass market.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

“There is a small market for luxury EVs, but it’s a very different market from your usual luxury or supercar buyer,” says Scott Sherwood, an independent analyst of luxury car brands. “And that’s where Ferrari got it right with the Luce. They targeted a completely new group of consumers.”

In Ferrari’s wake, Bentley has rolled out its first all-electric model and Jaguar will do so next week. Porsche is also going ahead with an electric version of its 718 two-seat sports car.

All are hoping that a foray into EVs could open up a new and younger client base with different tastes for design and personalisation. They, like Ferrari, intend to target the beneficiaries of the tech wealth being generated across the US.

But it is a difficult balancing act. Manufacturers need to navigate their costly transition to EVs while ensuring that combustion-engine loyalists are not left alienated and that profits from higher-margin petrol cars are not eroded.

Sherwood argues that the difficulty in replicating Ferrari’s success comes down to scale and brand strength. “Ferrari doesn’t need to sell 10,000 units to be successful. They can sell 1,000 to 1,500 and declare victory,” he says.

“The problem for Porsche is that they’d need to sell 20,000 or 30,000.”

For decades, the US has been the most attractive market for luxury-car makers because of its deep pool of millionaires and the resilience of its economy.

In 2008, when most Americans had never even seen an electric car, Tesla targeted its two-seater Roadster electric sports car at a small cohort of rich tech entrepreneurs and environmentally conscious celebrities. Early owners included Google co-founder Sergey Brin and film star Leonardo DiCaprio.

That playbook is increasingly being revisited as demand in China, now the world’s largest car market, falters. Overcapacity in the country has led to a flood of exports, but ultra-high tariffs and a ban on Chinese software have kept them out of the US market.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The total US market for luxury vehicles and exotic cars is likely to expand to as much as $215bn by 2035 from $110bn at present, according to recent analysis by Boston Consulting Group and duPont Registry.

Demand is expected to be weaker for higher-end luxury EVs due to the reversals in US climate policy under Trump and concerns about the resale value of battery-powered models.

Separate data from Cox Automotive shows that electric cars accounted for roughly 6 per cent of the overall new vehicle market in the US in the third quarter, down from a peak of 10.6 per cent a year earlier.

BCG and duPont Registry expect the internal combustion engine will continue to dominate sales in the “ultra-luxury” and “hyper-luxury” segments, which include vehicles priced at more than $170,000.

But Felix Stellmaszek, BCG’s managing director, says there is still a market for luxury electric cars, in part because of their exclusivity. “Everyone has his or her car collection in the garage, but if you have something that is electrified, it’s actually quite different from the rest of the buyers and collectors that you meet at the car shows.”

He adds that “range anxiety and all the factors preventing broader adoption of electric vehicles across North America in particular don’t really matter much” in the luxury sector, since high-end cars tend to be bought for personal enjoyment or scarcity value rather than daily use.

Blue, the Californian dealer, adds that what really matters to his customers is “a visceral [driving] experience in a world where we all live on these screens and on our phones”.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Jaguar Land Rover, which like Ferrari was excoriated on social media after a rebranding exercise, is targeting the US as a core market for the $130,000 Jaguar Type 01 electric vehicle due to launch in October. Range Rover’s first electric SUV appeared in September at a starting price of $140,450.

“The amount of wealth transfer that’s going to happen [in the US] over the next five to ten years is . . . by far the biggest [in the world],” says PB Balaji, the UK-based carmaker’s chief executive who has been tasked with reinventing Jaguar as an all-electric brand. “Therefore, we are giving it everything.”

Vigna has expressed confidence that the Luce will be profitable from the start, largely thanks to its high sticker price. But Ferrari is not setting high ambitions for EVs overall. It aims to make 20 per cent of its models fully electric by 2030, half of its original target, while its industry-beating operating margin of 30 per cent will be protected by continuing sales of petrol models and limited edition models such as the €3.6mn F80 supercar.

Bentley, the UK-based carmaker owned by Volkswagen, is also hoping to take advantage of vigorous US economic growth, and broaden its appeal to younger drivers, with its Torcal electric SUV.

“The strength of the US economy is unbeaten in the world,” says chief executive Frank-Steffen Walliser. “The West Coast is a very natural area and we expect that we could definitely grow there.”

But it has taken a different approach to pricing; the Torcal will start at a comparatively modest £173,300, less than half the price of the Luce. At that price point, analysts say Bentley will need to sell large numbers to generate profits, and warn that the Torcal targets the same buyers as the Bentayga, another Bentley SUV that is available in petrol or plug-in hybrid versions. The company argues there will be no cannibalisation, given the Bentayga’s slightly higher pricing.

Walliser has described the Torcal’s debut as “one of the most important product launches in our 107-year history”. It comes as Bentley’s operating profit margin in the first half fell to 4.5 per cent while vehicle deliveries declined 13 per cent to 4,211 units, partly due to its ageing product line-up and the downturn in China.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

For all the recent activity in the sector, the car industry remains deeply divided on how much actual demand there is for high-end battery-powered sports cars.

Product launches so far have tended to be saloons, SUVs or so-called grand tourers — cars designed for luxurious long-distance travel. Jaguar’s Type 01 and the Rolls-Royce Spectre both belong in this category.

Beyond a few models from Lotus and Rimac, a Croatian start-up often compared to Tesla, an all-electric hypercar has proved challenging because of the adverse effect of the battery weight on performance and handling, and the perceived lack of connection between car and driver.

Porsche is busy recalibrating what some regarded as an overly bullish EV strategy. While it enjoyed initial success with the Taycan saloon and could start selling electric 718 models next year, it also plans a new combustion-engine version of its best-selling Macan SUV in 2028.

Michael Leiters, the former boss of British supercar maker McLaren who took over as Porsche chief executive in January, says he still has reservations about the readiness of EV technology for high-performance sports cars.

“There won’t be a 911 electric,” he says, referring to Porsche’s legendary rear-engined model. “The advantages of the technology depend a lot on the customer profile and the use of a car.”

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Others have pivoted to hybrid cars as an interim measure, and to offset the thin margins on pure electric models. McLaren is developing its first hybrid SUV, even though it merged with EV start-up Forseven Holding last year.

Michael Straughan, McLaren’s chief operating officer, says the luxury sector’s transition to electric propulsion is “inevitable” over the long term but cautions that for now, its customers were not “crying out for EVs”.

“The trick is timing it so that the product development start matches the time when EVs are accepted,” says Straughan, who was previously the chief operating officer at Aston Martin. “For a small maker, if you select the wrong technology, it has a dramatic effect on the business.”

Italian rival Lamborghini, another Volkswagen brand, has abandoned plans to launch its first fully electric car by 2030 and will instead roll out two plug-in hybrid models, while Lotus, the Chinese-owned marque known for lightweight and agile sports cars, has also pivoted from an EV-focused strategy to one more focused on hybrids.

“We have very good technology and architecture for both battery EVs and plug-in hybrids. So we are going to do both,” says chief financial officer Wang Daxue. He adds that the US will be “a very important market” for its upcoming Type 135 hybrid supercar, though the vehicle’s Chinese technology content means Lotus will need regulatory approval to sell it in America.

Consumers are warming to EVs at different speeds in different markets, say industry executives. The rise in fuel prices amid war in the Middle East has sparked a surge in sales in Europe, contrasting with the EV slump in the US.

“There was a pendulum that was going back to the internal combustion engine and now it’s coming back because of high petrol prices and subsidies by governments [in Europe],” says Leiters.

“You have to be very careful . . . so we have all the tools we need to react to the markets.”

In addition to correctly predicting the pace of the electric transition, luxury car brands need to ensure that they do not leave their existing clients behind in the pursuit of new technology and design.

“We as a company have the responsibility to move forward the flag of innovation [while] respecting the values of the past,” says Ferrari’s Vigna.

Two months after unveiling the Luce, the company launched the 12Cilindri Manuale. With its massive V12 petrol engine and a transmission system that mimics the feel of a mechanical gearbox, the limited edition model is red meat for traditionalists. “A manual transmission is the ultimate emblem of the ability to reconnect to actually living,” says Blue, the car dealer.

Even the Luce’s design nods to tradition. Its interior features physical dials and buttons, in addition to a modern touchscreen panel. A vibrating sound from its motors and components inspired by an electric guitar compensate for the lack of traditional engine roar.

For the Torcal, Bentley’s engineers tried to create an emotional connection with a propulsion sound handcrafted by musicians and featuring a blend of percussion, crystal glass, birds and the tapping of leather.

“The consumer choice is very different in the acceptance of electric cars,” says Walliser, the Bentley chief executive, adding that this is why he and others will keep offering petrol and hybrid models as well as EVs.

Ed Kim, chief analyst at AutoPacific, an automotive market research group, does not expect combustion engines to leave the ultra-luxury segment in the foreseeable future.

“We should remember that there are still plenty of those traditionally minded old-money buyers left,” he says. “My hunch is that the ultra-luxury segments will be one of the last to let go of combustion.”

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

But while western carmakers deliberate over the pace of the electric transition and continue to develop models for petrol devotees, Chinese EV makers such as BYD, whose mass-market models are already making inroads in key European markets, are now setting their sights on the premium segment.

At the Goodwood Festival of Speed in July, BYD unveiled its new Denza Z electric supercar, which is capable of more than 320km/h and will have a starting price of £142,900 in the UK.

Asked why BYD was entering the premium segment, its top international executive Stella Li says: “It is natural, since we have the technology. Why not?

“Then, we need to make it super successful.”

rows.title: How the Supreme Court greenlit America’s gerrymandering battle
rows.content:
Kaye Wiggins in New York

Published October 2 2026

A clutch of southern Republican-led states have this year redrawn their election maps ahead of November’s midterm elections at the urging of President Donald Trump.

The gerrymandering rush was prompted by a US Supreme Court ruling that will make it harder for voters to challenge new maps in federal court. The case, Louisiana vs Callais, centres on the 1965 Voting Rights Act, a civil rights era law that sought to end race discrimination in the electoral system.

Maps are normally redrawn once a decade after a census and typically not too close to an election. But the president wants to change that in an attempt to tip the electoral balance in his Republican Party’s favour.

Trump started an arms race last year by pushing Texas Republicans to redraw that state’s maps mid-cycle, and the Democrats responded by redrawing maps in states that they controlled.

In the longer term, new maps could lower African American representation and reduce the election of Democrats in Republican states and vice versa.

The landmark civil rights era law is rooted in the Fifteenth Amendment to the US constitution, which in 1870 said citizens could not be denied the right to vote because of their race. It gave Congress the power to enforce the principle using legislation.

But Black votes were for decades suppressed through gerrymandering and onerous requirements such as literacy tests and property qualifications, culminating in the brutal 1965 attack by authorities in Selma, Alabama, on non-violent civil rights protesters marching to secure voting rights.

Later that year, Congress passed the Voting Rights Act, Section 2, which ruled states should not curtail voters’ rights on account of race.

The act was a way to challenge gerrymandering that diluted the impact of Black voters, often done by “packing” and “cracking”. Packing means cramming large numbers of Black voters, who tend to vote for Democrats, into a single district so that only one Democrat is elected rather than two or more; cracking is splitting a Black community across several districts so that their votes are drowned out by white Republican voters.

The Callais ruling has “essentially gutted” that part of the act, said Sarah Brannon, deputy director of the American Civil Liberties Union’s Voting Rights Project.

A 1982 amendment to Section 2 said the law would be violated if election processes based on the “totality of circumstances” meant Black voters had less opportunity to elect representatives of their choice than white voters. A 1986 Supreme Court ruling reinforced this, saying Section 2 might be violated if a district map meant that a large, geographically compact, politically cohesive group of Black voters could not elect a representative of their choice.

That led to a surge in the creation of “majority-minority” districts designed to ensure that Black voters in southern states could secure a level of political representation. Some of America’s best-known Black politicians, including the late civil rights activist John Lewis, have represented southern majority-Black districts.

But majority-minority districts were challenged in the courts, with some saying it was dangerous to organise voters by race because it risked entrenching stereotypes and deepening racial divisions. Such districts could also be geographically illogical.

The Supreme Court in 1993 ruled that classifying voters by race could be harmful and states would need a strong justification to do so when drawing districts.

The court in 2019 made it easier to gerrymander for purely political purposes. It ruled that such changes were not something federal courts could intervene in because the constitution did not give them the authority to decide what they said were political questions.

After the 2020 census, Louisiana redrew its congressional districts. In 2022 a judge said the new map likely violated section 2 of the VRA because it did not create a second majority Black district.

The state redrew its map, creating in 2024 a district that streaked diagonally across the state, connecting Black voters in Baton Rouge with those roughly 250 miles away in Shreveport. A roughly equivalent-looking UK map would put London and Liverpool in the same district. The unusual shape helped protect the seats of top Republicans including House Speaker Mike Johnson and House majority leader Steve Scalise.

That map was challenged almost immediately by a group of mostly white voters, led by Phillip “Bert” Callais, a man described in court filings as a “non-African American voter who resides in Brusly, Louisiana”. They said the map denied them the right to elect a representative of their choice. They won in lower courts, but the state appealed, leading the case to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court justices voted 6-3, largely along ideological lines, in favour of Callais. “No compelling interest justified the state’s use of race in creating [the new district], and that map is an unconstitutional racial gerrymander,” the majority ruled.

One impact of the ruling is that it will be far more difficult for voters to challenge new maps that dilute the impact of Black voters in southern states, including by dismantling existing majority-Black districts. To succeed, they will have to show the map was created with race rather than partisan interests in mind.

“We will not be able to bring successful section 2 cases,” said April England-Albright, national legal director of the campaign group Black Voters Matter. “Virtually unless you have them saying, we are doing this because they are Black, you cannot win this case.”

The ruling will end the creation of districts designed with race in mind, for example to enable Black or other minority voters to elect a candidate of their choice.

Clarence Thomas, one of the Supreme Court’s two Black justices, wrote in support of the ruling, saying such measures had divided the country along racial lines in ways he found unacceptable.

But his fellow justice Elena Kagan wrote in a dissent that the ruling has “laid the groundwork for the largest reduction in minority representation” since the years that followed the civil war.

The full impact of the map changes is uncertain, but the Callais ruling has at least “increased the chances that Republicans will hold on to the House”, said Benjamin Schneer, associate professor of public policy at Harvard Kennedy School.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

He added gerrymandering ahead of the November vote could create 10 more seats that the Republicans are likely to win even with the Democrats redrawing their own electoral maps mid-cycle.

But it could also result in so-called “dummymandering” where, for example, an attempted Republican gerrymander in the South could backfire by spreading Black voters among other districts in a way that, combined with a large swing, leads to more Democrats being elected.

Non-partisan election forecasters say Democrats are likely to retake the House given Trump’s declining approval ratings and the historical trend of the party out of power making gains in midterm elections.

But in the longer term, the Callais ruling, combined with the Supreme Court’s 2019 decision that keeps federal courts out of political gerrymandering issues, might unleash unrestrained gerrymandering by both parties.

Schneer said “maximising gerrymanders everywhere would roughly cancel each other out”, producing a House of Representatives whose total number looks similar to today.

But the breakdown would be very different, with more states having representatives only from one party, making the House election map look more like the electoral college where the dominant party takes all.

However, it would be harder for Democrats to gerrymander because many of their states have independent commissions or other measures limiting the practice, so Republicans would probably have “a bit of an edge in the longer run”, Schneer added.

There are some. State courts can intervene and could become a more significant forum for contesting claims of racial and partisan redistricting.

Some state legislatures have laws banning partisan gerrymandering and some state constitutions ban redistricting outside the post-census period.

There is also resistance to redrawing electoral maps even among Republicans: in Indiana, party representatives last year voted against redistricting and the state senate has declined to take up a new map in time for the midterms.

Campaign groups are actively trying to prevent redistricting: the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People is asking Black athletes and fans to withhold athletic and financial support from public universities in southern states that they say are “attacking Black voting rights”.

The Black Votes Matter group is campaigning to raise turnout in response to the gerrymandering. “Eighty-nine million people did not vote in the presidential election; that’s more people than voted for either side,” England-Albright said.

“So we’ve got to awaken folks . . . if everyone comes out, we could capture these seats even in districts that they are trying to take away from us.”

rows.title: EG Group delays IPO plans and draws takeover interest
rows.content:
Ivan Levingston , Ashley Armstrong and Alexandra Heal in London, and Oliver Barnes in New York

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Petrol station empire EG Group is delaying plans for an initial public offering until next year, opening up the possibility that the group will explore a sale.

The company, which is 50 per cent owned by private equity firm TDR Capital, has also received early takeover interest from groups including the infrastructure investment firm Stonepeak, people familiar with the matter said.

Deliberations remain in the early stages, the people warned, with no certainty of a transaction. EG is still focused on pursuing a listing, some of the people added, in part because its owners believe that it can achieve a higher valuation in a listing rather than a sale.

EG had filed for an IPO under its Cumberland Farms brand and was discussing listing as soon as this autumn in New York, with the aim of raising about $1bn at a $9bn valuation.

But the market for new listings has become increasingly difficult and some planned flotations, including that of smart ring maker Oura, have been postponed. EG was likely to struggle to achieve its target valuation with investors, some of the people said.

As a result, a stock market listing is unlikely to take place before 2027, one of the people familiar with the matter said. The company could still pull the trigger on a listing if market conditions dramatically improved, another added.

Alongside London-based buyout group TDR — which first invested in the business in 2014 — the brothers Mohsin and Zuber Issa each have stakes of 25 per cent.

The company, which started with a single petrol station in the Greater Manchester town of Bury 25 years ago, quickly expanded across Europe via a debt-fuelled acquisition spree during the era of low interest rates.

EG no longer has any petrol stations or convenience stores in the UK after selling the bulk of its portfolio to supermarket group Asda, a sister business also owned by TDR and Mohsin Issa.

The group has been selling assets in order to reduce its debt of $5.8bn. Rating agency Fitch said in January that the company had an elevated debt-to-earnings ratio that it expected to fall in the coming years.

EG said in its IPO filing that it had total revenues of nearly $4bn in the first quarter of this year, up about 7 per cent on the same period last year. First-quarter gross profits were $652mn, up 13 per cent. Stonepeak, a major infrastructure investor with $93bn of assets, has previously invested in similar assets such as the German and Austrian fuel retailer JET Tankstellen Deutschland. It also acquired a majority stake in the lubricants group Castrol from BP last year in a $10bn deal.

Stonepeak, TDR and EG Group declined to comment.

Additional reporting by George Steer and Euan Healy

rows.title: How to keep the lights on in an electrified world
rows.content:
Rachel Millard , Ian Bott , Aditi Bhandari , Clara Murray , Richard Topping

Published October 2 2026

Often described as the largest and most complex machines in the world, modern electricity systems involve dozens or hundreds of generators spinning in tandem to send power through thousands of miles of cables and into homes and businesses.

Across this sprawling and ever-changing network, electricity supply and demand must be constantly matched so that generators do not fall out of step and trigger widespread power cuts — a task that is becoming even more complicated in the era of lower-carbon electricity.

Countries trying to shift towards renewables face the dual challenge of incorporating intermittent wind and solar power and dealing with more demand from the likes of electric cars and heat pumps.

The scale of the challenge is illustrated by modelling from Britain’s electricity system operator, which suggests total electrical generation capacity could need to rise by between 206 and 245 per cent between 2024 and 2050 to manage both expected rising demand for electricity and the intermittency of wind and solar technologies.

While in the past engineers keeping the system in balance second-by-second would be working with a few large, lumbering coal and gas-fired power plants, they now have to cope with hundreds of wind turbines and solar panels scattered around the country, each prone to bursts or lulls in supply depending on the weather or time of day.

Supply and demand on the electricity grid need to be kept precisely matched to avoid blackouts.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Adding to this high-wire act is the proliferation of cheap rooftop solar panels, which are harder for electricity system operators to monitor and forecast, and means the flow of power is now a two-way street between customers and the grid.

Alongside this change in where electricity comes from, the grid is also set to be loaded with more and more demand, as governments encourage people to swap petrol cars and gas-fired boilers for electric vehicles and heat pumps.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The rationale for this “electrification” shift is twofold: not only avoiding carbon dioxide emissions that cause climate change, but also the huge amounts of energy wasted when fossil fuels are burned in a combustion engine.

Electric cars are around two to four times more efficient than their fossil fuel counterparts, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA), while heat pumps are around three to five times more efficient than gas-fired boilers.

But these shifts also means countries need to develop ways to get through periods of too much or too little sun or wind, either by storing electricity, trading it with other countries, or getting consumers to adapt when they use electricity according to when it is best for the grid.

“Substantial increases in the flexibility of power systems are required for secure and cost-effective integration of generation, load and storage technologies that characterise this new era,” the IEA says.

As well as being intermittent, wind and solar also differ in another important way from oil, gas and nuclear power plants.

The latter’s big, heavy and fast-spinning turbines are synchronised to the grid’s frequency and hold kinetic energy that can act as a natural buffer in times of disruption elsewhere in the grid.

Wind and solar farms instead rely on sophisticated equipment such as inverters to connect to the rest of the system, making them potentially more vulnerable to disruption.

So how might electricity grids deal with these challenges? They are exploring a range of tactics, from using people’s electric car batteries, to ways of storing energy in lakes or even compressed air.

Like many countries, Britain is looking to its growing fleet of electric cars as both an asset and a burden on the grid — a huge source of demand but one that can also help to balance the network by selling electricity back to the grid when needed or charging when it is plentiful.

Alex Scoch, director of flexibility and electrification at Octopus Energy, the UK’s largest household supplier, says that “smart charging” arrangements, under which the owner’s car is charged automatically at times when electricity is abundant and cheap, are rapidly becoming mainstream.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

“Electrification is great for consumers’ wallets,” he says. Meanwhile, 22 EV models in production this year are able to sell electricity back to the grid, according to IEA figures, including 13 in Europe.

There are reasons to be cautious about the prospects for “bi-directional charging”, ranging from cost and electricity network capacity to the challenges of agreeing technical standards.

But Schoch argues it is not unrealistic to think that 2mn UK cars could be selling electricity back to the grid by 2030. At an export rate of five kilowatts per car, in aggregate that would be equivalent to several nuclear power plants.

“What is consistently underestimated is the pace of consumer adoption and the pace of change,” Schoch says. “Unless you are really leaning forward and looking five steps ahead, you’re always going to be caught with your pants down.”

The smart charging of electric cars is part of a broader push on “demand-side flexibility” which Britain’s electricity system operator hopes will increase roughly fivefold by 2030, compared with 2024 levels. This is a tall order which requires far greater uptake of time-of-use tariffs and smart meters to encourage consumers to, for example, do the washing on a Sunday or turn a heat pump off just before getting home.

The targets could also be helped by major users such as data centres and factories bypassing frustratingly long waits to get a larger connection to the electricity grid by cutting how much electricity they draw from the network at times when national demand is highest.

“We do see them [industrial users] starting to look at flexibility as a way of solving that problem,” says Anna Moss, head of market flexibility at Cornwall Insight, the consultancy.

The push on consumers comes as the falling cost of lithium-ion batteries — due to huge manufacturing output in China — means they are being built at far greater scale and can discharge electricity for longer periods.

Globally, batteries are the fastest-growing electricity technology, according to the IEA, while in June this year, batteries formed the bulk of planned projects provisionally picked in a competition run by British regulator Ofgem for “long-duration” storage — capable of dispatching electricity at full output for eight hours or more.

Britain now has almost eight gigawatts of batteries available, most of which can discharge at full rate for two hours, but Aurora Energy Research expects installed battery capacity to more than double over the next five years and for the length of time they can discharge to increase. “Big listed portfolios are upgrading their duration,” says Victor Yip, senior associate at Aurora Energy Research.

But Britain is also betting on other ways of storing energy. This includes technologies that use changes in water flows or air pressure to drive an electrical turbine.

Ofgem, the UK regulator, has provisionally backed what would be the first new hydro-electric power projects to be built in a generation, including SSE Renewables’ proposed Coire Glas project next to Loch Lochy in Scotland, which would be able to supply 1.4GW of electricity for 32 hours straight.

The process is appealingly simple: when electricity is cheaper, SSE will pump water from a reservoir up to a higher reservoir, where it is ready to be let back down again when prices are higher.

Such “pumped storage” projects work well alongside intermittent renewables, and SSE has the option to upgrade its Sloy hydroelectric plant, next to Loch Lomond, to work in the same way.

Electrification visual explainer

Ofgem has also backed a relatively small plant planned by Storelectrics in Teesside, north-east England. This would store electricity by using it to compress air, storing the compressed air in a salt cavern and releasing it to drive a turbine when needed. On the other side of the country, in Greater Manchester, Highview Power is building a power station that will store air in compressed and chilled liquid form. Processes like this are less efficient than modern lithium-ion batteries, but their development reflects the huge interest in trying to store electricity for extended periods.

Ofgem has now launched a contest for “ultra long-duration” storage projects capable of supplying electricity for 100 hours straight or more. This is likely to consider the feasibility of storing hydrogen — made through electrolysis using excess electricity when it is windy or sunny — deep underground. However, doing this at scale is in doubt due to the high costs of making hydrogen and poor efficiency when using it for electricity storage.

As well as storing electricity, Britain relies heavily on a growing web of giant electricity cables, known as interconnectors, to the continent so it can sell other countries excess electricity when it is very sunny and windy in Britain and vice versa when it is not.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Since the weather and daylight hours are often not that different in neighbouring countries, there are limits to this approach. This started to show during the summer, when the National Electricity System Operator (NESO) had to abruptly cut off exports to the Netherlands during one night of low wind and high temperatures in June, and repeatedly told traders not to book trades on certain cables during similar conditions in July.

But the cables still provide crucial flexibility as Britain transitions to a new electricity system. In 2025, net imports amounted to 29.7 terawatt-hours, equivalent to just over 9 per cent of total electricity demand, while NESO has said the country should be a net exporter of electricity by 2030.

Of the huge rise in electricity generation that NESO modelling suggests will be needed, just under a third would need to be either storage or “dispatchable” — meaning that it can quickly increase or decrease output on demand to balance out wind and solar power when the weather changes.

The huge need for new infrastructure comes amid concern over high electricity bills and delays to major electricity cable projects. “Good progress is being made, but the scale of the challenge shouldn’t be underestimated,” says Sam Peacock, managing director of regulation and policy at SSE.

“Britain is rapidly increasing renewable generation, and investment in storage, networks and system flexibility needs to keep pace.”
