rows.title: KPMG general counsel retires after Australia whistleblower scandal
rows.content:
Stephen Foley in New York and Nic Fildes in Sydney

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 2 2026

KPMG on Thursday announced the departure of its global general counsel, who attracted scrutiny for her handling of whistleblower allegations that rocked the accounting firm in Australia.

Anne Collins, a Sydney-based lawyer who had been general counsel since 2016, left the role this week as part of a wider executive reshuffle, according to an update on the firm’s website. KPMG International’s new chief executive Gary Wingrove formally took the helm on Thursday.

A person familiar with internal communications said Wingrove told senior partners that Collins’s departure had been long planned to coincide with the retirement of outgoing chief executive Bill Thomas.

Wingrove and Collins had both been hauled before an Australian parliamentary committee investigating KPMG partners’ use of confidential client information to win audit business in the country.

KPMG ousted the CEO and other senior figures of its Australian business after the claims came to light. A whistleblower who first raised the claims in 2024 was not taken sufficiently seriously by the Australian leadership, the firm admitted.

The FT reported in June that the whistleblower had also contacted KPMG’s global leadership, including Collins and Thomas, and had been told they would not open a formal investigation.

Unlike traditional multinationals, KPMG operates as a network of locally owned partnerships, with the global leadership team controlling an umbrella organisation that manages the brand. The whistleblower was told KPMG International could not force the Australian firm to take action and that there was not enough evidence for it to launch a probe of its own, according to people familiar with the months-long correspondence.

Wingrove was chief executive of KPMG Australia until becoming chief operating officer of KPMG International in London in 2022.

Collins joined KPMG in 2010 after a two-decade-long career at the law firm Ashurst. She was general counsel of KPMG Australia before taking the global role. She has been replaced by London-based Susan Walsh, previously deputy global general counsel.

The Big Four firm has been in turmoil for months after allegations, first raised in the Australian parliament, that some of its most senior audit partners used confidential client documents to gain information they used to pitch for additional business. In the resulting political furore, some large clients dropped the firm and government work has shrunk, forcing the new Australian leadership to cut hundreds of jobs.

On Friday, Australian bank ANZ said it would stop using KPMG as its auditor, severing a 59-year relationship.

The decision represents another blow for KPMG, which has been the subject of a public sector contract freeze following Senate hearings over the whistleblower allegations.

Insurer IAG, property company Lendlease — whose confidential documents were accessed by KPMG’s audit partners — and Macquarie are among the other clients that have cut ties with the consultant in recent months.

rows.title: Foreign bid highlights Australia’s battle to forge a gold champion
rows.content:
Nic Fildes in Sydney

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Australia has created some of the world’s biggest mining groups — yet it has failed to produce a global gold champion.

Northern Star Resources, Australia’s largest gold miner and a stock market darling, was a candidate to rise to global significance as the booming gold price boosted its valuation to A$44bn ($31bn) earlier this year.

That was before a sharp downturn in its fortunes in recent months as production warnings eroded investor confidence and triggered an executive exodus.

The company is now in play after it two weeks ago rejected an A$39bn ($27bn) bid from South African rival Gold Fields. A deal would be the largest mining combination since the $38bn Xstrata-Glencore tie-up in 2012, according to Dealogic.

Activist hedge fund Elliott Management had called for a sale in June, leaving Northern Star Australia’s putative gold champion vulnerable to a takeover.

The rejection of the offer was made public just as executives from the gold industry arrived in Denver for the Mining Forum Americas 2026 conference this week. Some bankers landed after 15-hour flights from Australia to discover that the news had leaked when they turned their phones back on.

The conference provided Gold Fields with a chance to sell the combination to its investors in closed-door meetings and from the stage.

Mike Fraser, chief executive of Gold Fields, used a keynote speech in Denver to argue that the potential combination with Northern Star presented “a very compelling story”.

He picked through an estimated $5bn of potential synergies in the form of tax savings and cost cuts as maps of the Kalgoorlie region, where both companies own significant gold-mining and processing assets, were displayed.

“We continue to remain open for dialogue and believe this proposal warrants further consideration by the Northern Star board,” Fraser said, putting pressure on his target.

A Northern Star presentation in Denver by acting chief executive Ryan Gurner, its former finance chief, was less explosive.

The company’s new chief executive Suresh Vadnagra is walking into a bid situation when he joins the company from Glencore on Monday. Two board members proposed by Elliott, including former Anglo American chief executive Mark Cutifani, have also just joined.

One gold industry veteran said the timing of Gold Fields’ approach would put pressure on the Australian company to weigh its options.

A combined Gold Fields and Northern Star would create Australia’s largest gold producer, based on output, and the second largest globally to US miner Newmont .

Elliott has urged Northern Star to open talks with Gold Fields, which could move to sweeten its offer if talks resume, according to a person with direct knowledge of the situation.

Northern Star has said that the Gold Fields’ bid undervalues its growth potential. The offer means its shareholders would own a third of the Johannesburg-listed company, introducing more risk for cautious Australian investors.

Morningstar analyst Jon Mills said that there was a 50 per cent chance that Gold Fields would offer more: “We think Northern Star remains in play and a higher offer is likely.”

Mitch Ryan, a mining analyst with Jefferies, said there was “moderately low” risk of a counterbidder given the scale and premium required.

Australia’s mining industry has historical connections to South Africa but recent corporate activity has been tumultuous.

BHP took over Billiton in 2001 and acquired significant South African operations that were later spun out into South32. The “Big Australian” then tried to acquire Anglo American in 2024 but the deal was contingent on the demerger of two substantial businesses in South Africa — a plan that caused political uproar in the country.

Some in the industry remain puzzled that Australia lacks a gold producer in the same league as Newmont, Barrick Gold or Agnico Eagle given the country’s mining history, particularly in gold. Former domestic giants like Newcrest and Normandy have been scooped up by foreign buyers.

Australia’s largest miners historically mined gold but transitioned away from the precious metal in pursuit of high-value iron ore and copper production. BHP has remained a substantial gold producer in Australia but deems the yellow metal to be a byproduct of its copper mining rather than a core metal.

Company executives argue that Australian investors have been less comfortable with local gold companies pushing into high-risk overseas markets including Africa and the Pacific in pursuit of growth than international peers.

Jake Klein, founder and chair of A$27bn gold and copper miner Evolution Mining, said that Australia was adept at building great gold mining groups but not at turning them into global players.

“If Northern Star does fall to a foreign player, then it’s another missed opportunity for Australia’s gold mining industry,” he told the FT. “We grow companies very well, but we have not yet been able to take them to the next level and build a peer to the biggest global gold companies like Newmont, Barrick and Agnico.”

Australia’s original gold rush in the 1800s transformed Melbourne into the world’s richest city on a per capita basis. More recently, however, the focus of the industry has been around the rich “Goldfields” region of Kalgoorlie, 600km east of Perth, the Western Australian capital.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The region has been a hive of consolidation for decades as companies trade assets to build gold empires. That includes Gold Fields, which bought a small player in 2001 and now produces 1mn ounces a year from the region.

Northern Star is itself a consolidation story. Its main asset is the gigantic “Super Pit” in Kalgoorlie, whose ownership was previously split between Newmont and Barrick Gold before they sold it. The mine now produces almost half a million troy ounces of gold a year — a figure that is projected to almost double by the end of the decade as a new mill comes online.

Northern Star has been a remarkable success story for Australian investors since it raised A$5mn in a late 2003 listing. The company earned a reputation for creating substantial value from unloved assets such as the Super Pit.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

A stock that was trading for less than A$0.40 in 2011 peaked at almost A$32 in March. The Gold Fields offer was pitched at an implied value of A$27 per Northern Star share.

Northern Star is likely to shed smaller gold mines whether or not it is sold, creating a knock-on effect for smaller companies with about $4bn of assets up for grabs. But the hopes of a global gold giant emerging from Australia still look far-fetched, with cautious investors unwilling to back the level of cross-border M&A that has defined the growth of US, Canadian and South African gold companies.

“Australia has all the ingredients to be the global epicentre for mining: investors, bankers, engineers, lawyers and analysts who have a deep understanding of the industry and are widely respected as best in class,” Evolution’s Klein said. “But for whatever reason, to date we have fallen short and not been able to create that global gold champion.”

rows.title: South Korea brings powerful prosecution agency to heel
rows.content:
Daniel Tudor and Song Jung-a in Seoul

Published October 2 2026

For 78 years, South Korea’s prosecutors were feared and admired for their broad authority to investigate crimes as well as to bring cases to court.

But this Friday the prosecution service will be abolished and its functions divided between two new agencies — a victory for reformers, but one that some fear could leave an investigative vacuum in areas such as financial crime.

The new Serious Crime Investigation Agency, under the interior ministry, will shoulder major investigations, with police handling the rest. The Public Prosecution Office, under the justice ministry, will decide whether to bring charges and represent the state at trial.

President Lee Jae Myung’s Democratic Party has long argued that the outgoing system enabled politically motivated investigations and gave prosecutors near-unchecked authority.

At a meeting of senior aides on Thursday, Lee said: “We are bringing an end to an era of wrongdoing—a time when the prosecution monopolised both investigation and indictment, exercising unchecked power and, even worse, acting as a ‘political prosecution’ to suppress and eliminate political rivals.”

Former president Yoon Suk Yeol , now imprisoned over his botched December 2024 martial law declaration, was himself a former chief prosecutor. His ascent to power in 2022 and appointment of old colleagues to senior posts revived criticisms at the time of a “prosecutors’ republic”.

Under the reforms, the Seoul Southern District Prosecutors’ Office, known as the “grim reaper” of Yeouido, the banking district, for the rigour of its financial crime investigations, will see its specialist operations dismantled and rebuilt inside the SCIA.

“White-collar crimes may be difficult to handle,” said Park Ju-geun, head of corporate research group Leaders Index. He believes the SCIA and police would need more time to build up expertise.

A serving prosecutor who wished to be identified only by their surname, Son, said that SCIA officers, of whom they estimate 70 per cent have come from the old prosecution service, “have a building with desks in it, but no computers or even pens yet”. Yet at the same time, the agency feels pressure to “go after a big target, to prove itself”, they added.

Handing more investigative power to the police is also coming under scrutiny because of recent scandals . In July, a police team leader was arrested over alleged evidence tampering in the murder of a schoolgirl; the accused killer’s father, himself a serving officer, was suspected of destroying evidence. Then just over a month ago it emerged that a police officer had allegedly falsified the closure of two missing-person cases, with both people later found dead.

Lee referenced such concerns at the Thursday meeting, stating police reform would also be a “key task” for his administration.

A particular flashpoint of the reforms has been the loss of prosecutors’ power to conduct “supplementary” investigations when their review of a police file exposes gaps before an indictment decision. Under the new system, prosecutors may identify missing facts but must ask police to investigate them again.

The uncertainty surrounding the changeover is the latest chapter in a long and controversial history. The prosecution service was founded in September 1948 — less than a month after South Korea itself — and accumulated power under successive autocratic governments.

Pro-democracy activists reviled the service both as an instrument for pursuing dissidents and as a pipeline into the authoritarian political elite. A young prosecutor named Kim Ki-choon embodied both: in 1972, Kim helped draft military ruler Park Chung Hee’s authoritarian Yushin Constitution, before rising to become justice minister and, decades later, chief of staff to Park’s daughter, then president Park Geun-hye.

The organisation survived democratisation in 1987, and its clashes with progressive leaders made reform a cause of the left. Supporters of former president Roh Moo-hyun viewed the corruption investigation preceding his 2009 suicide as politically driven; Lee has likewise portrayed cases against him as selective justice.

“The death of Roh was a great shock, and a tragedy. Prosecution reform is maybe a sort of holy grail,” said Park Ye-rin, a rank-and-file member of Lee’s Democratic Party. “But speaking less emotionally, it can’t be right to have all that power with one place.”

Prosecutorial prestige was cultural as well as political. Son said joining the service “overjoyed” their parents and meant both acquiring “a job with power” and being recognised as a “state-certified elite”. Prosecutors were “objects of aspiration”, they added, due to their authority, the future opportunities available to them in law and politics, and media portrayals that enhanced their mystique.

For Son though, regardless of how the system is structured, “any holder of power seeks to utilise the prosecution once they take office”.

rows.title: Bangkok cements its place as gem-trading hub
rows.content:
Francesca Fearon

Published October 2 2026

Thailand’s ruby and sapphire mines may have been largely exhausted more than three decades ago, but the country remains one of the world’s most important centres for the coloured gemstone trade. Its dealers, cutters and treatment specialists handle stones sourced from across Africa and Asia, supplying jewellery manufacturers and international luxury houses.

Gem and jewellery exports excluding unwrought gold reached $13.6bn in 2025, up 41 per cent from the previous year, according to the Gem and Jewelry Institute of Thailand. The wider sector made up almost 8 per cent of the country’s exports and employs more than 800,000 people across the supply chain.

That position comes into focus each September, when gem and jewellery fairs in Bangkok and Hong Kong concentrate buyers, dealers and inventory in two of the industry’s most important Asian trading centres. Last month’s Bangkok Gems & Jewelry Fair generated more than $174mn in trade and attracted more than 50,000 buyers and visitors from 123 countries. Gem trading continues year round, but larger transactions often cluster around the shows as buyers inspect stones and parcels in person and make sourcing decisions face to face.

“Bangkok remains the place to see the finest ruby and sapphire, and those two stones have long sat at the centre of high-jewellery programmes, which is why many European houses return two or three times a year,” says Simon Dussart, founder of Asia Lounges, which trades rubies and sapphires alongside emeralds, garnets, spinels and tourmalines.

For GemMatrix, a trader in rubies, sapphires and emeralds, Bangkok and Hong Kong consistently produce the strongest commercial results, after the company also tested fairs in Las Vegas, Tucson and Vicenza. “Thailand is at the heart of our production and gemstone expertise, while Hong Kong strengthens our access to China and other international markets,” says chief executive Andrei Kornilov.

Thailand is ranked as the world’s third-largest exporter of coloured gemstones, according to the GIT. Its gemstone trade dates back to the 14th century and was once supported by ruby and sapphire mines around Chanthaburi and Trat in the south-east. Although those deposits were largely exhausted by the 1990s, Thailand had by then developed into an international centre for cutting, polishing, heat treatment and trading.

That shift was helped by expertise brought by Burmese émigrés following the 1962 military coup in what is now Myanmar, as well as access to stones from neighbouring countries, Sri Lanka and, increasingly, Africa. When Paraíba tourmaline deposits were discovered in Mozambique, for example, stones were sent to Thailand for heat treatment to enhance their distinctive blue-green colour.

“Thailand-based gem dealers have sharp business intuition,” says Sasha Golokoz, who is the owner of Bangkok-based dealer Vitalit Fine Gems. “They are always on the front line of new discoveries worldwide. They were the first to open buying offices in Madagascar and Mozambique, then Tanzania.”

That combination of trading and processing expertise allows Bangkok-based companies to serve different parts of the jewellery market. GemMatrix supplies calibrated gemstones to manufacturers in Russia, China, India and the US. “We purchase rough emerald, sapphire and ruby at auctions, and the material is then cut in Thailand into calibrated sizes according to exact millimetre dimensions,” says Kornilov.

Such orders require consistency in size, colour, cut and quality, as well as clear disclosure of treatments. A second part of GemMatrix’s business involves sourcing selected rough material or individual stones, which may be cut or recut and assembled into matched pairs, suites and layouts for major jewellery houses.

Those clients may be looking for individual rubies of three carats or more, which Kornilov says are becoming increasingly difficult to source, or suites of smaller stones where colour consistency is more important. For sapphires, he says demand remains concentrated on traditional shapes including ovals, cushions, emerald cuts and pears.

Thailand’s gemstone network also supplies smaller jewellery brands. Kavant & Sharart, a Bangkok-based jeweller for which the US is the largest market, sources most of its coloured stones through established local dealers.

“Having substantial gems physically in front of us is very important, particularly when we are developing collections,” says Shar-Linn Liew, who co-founded the company with Nuttapon “Kenny” Yongkiettakul in 2011. “Side by side we can see how they work with designs.”

Relationships with dealers remain particularly important in a market where stones vary considerably and purchasing cannot always be standardised. “We’ve worked with many of our dealers for years,” says Sophia Hirsh of London-based family jewellery house Hirsh. “For me, the best relationships in this industry are built over time — you develop trust, you learn each other’s tastes.”

The breadth of stones traded in Bangkok is also expanding beyond the rubies and sapphires on which the market was built. “Demand is not limited to ruby and sapphire; spinel, garnet and tourmaline are also on the rise,” says Dussart. “Ruby and sapphire set the tempo for the season; the rest of the palette is what we spend most of the year looking at.”

Dussart uses the fairs primarily to buy for clients rather than to sell. He says demand for colour has benefited garnets, while teal sapphires are again being requested by clients in Europe and Asia. His inventory includes Mandarin, Malay, tsavorite, grape and demantoid garnets.

For Golokoz, smaller independent jewellers can be particularly attractive customers because purchases can be agreed quickly. “They are their own decision makers and can make purchasing decisions on the spot,” she says. Major jewellery houses, by contrast, often work on consignment, with approval and purchasing processes that can take months.

Supply is another concern. Golokoz, who built her business around spinels, tourmalines and garnets, says high-quality spessartite and tsavorite garnets have become increasingly difficult to obtain. Mandarin garnet featured prominently in high jewellery this year, she says, just as supplies of suitable material were becoming scarce.

She has seen similar cycles with Mahenge spinels and lagoon tourmalines from Namibia, where jewellery demand followed earlier activity among gemstone traders. Golokoz is now increasing her focus on neon-pink rubellites, which she says are attracting greater interest and formed part of her offering at Jewellery & Gem World Hong Kong in September.

rows.title: Japanese watchmakers push for overseas growth
rows.content:
Rachael Taylor

Published October 2 2026

Japan’s watchmakers are expanding overseas at a time when growth in the global watch market has become harder to find. The value of Japanese watch exports rose 10 per cent to ¥207.9bn ($1.32bn) in 2025, according to the Japan Clock & Watch Association (JCWA), while Swiss watch exports fell 1.7 per cent to SFr25.6bn ($31.2bn).

The two industries remain vastly different in scale, but the figures point to a broader shift. Japanese manufacturers, long associated internationally with reliable and affordable timepieces, are pushing further into higher-priced mechanical watches and expanding distribution beyond their domestic market. At the same time, smaller Japanese brands are finding overseas buyers attracted by their craftsmanship, design and relatively accessible prices.

The shift is also evident at Japan’s three largest watch groups. Seiko, Citizen and Casio have all reported strong growth in their latest quarterly results. In the three months to June 30, Seiko Group’s watch business sales rose 34 per cent to ¥63bn, with operating profit up 77 per cent to ¥13.3bn. Citizen Group’s watch sales increased 32 per cent to ¥54.8bn, with operating profit up 62 per cent to ¥7.1bn, while Casio’s watch sales rose 29 per cent to ¥51bn.

The momentum extends beyond exports. Japan became the world’s second-largest market for Swiss watch exports in 2025, while domestic shipments by Japanese manufacturers also increased. Mechanical watch volumes rose 29 per cent and digital quartz volumes fell 31 per cent, according to the JCWA.

At Seiko, much of that growth is being driven by a strategy of building its brands internationally and moving further into higher-priced watches. Akio Naito, president of Seiko Watch Corporation, says the group’s recent performance “reflects the steady progress of the global brands strategy we have been pursuing over the past decade, rather than simply favourable market conditions”.

The clearest example is Grand Seiko, the group’s upmarket brand. Its watches had been sold in Japan since 1960, but were not exported until 2010. In 2017, Grand Seiko became a standalone brand, a move that accelerated its international expansion.

Grand Seiko Evolution 9 Spring Drive

Hypebeast x Citizen Zenshin

“One clear example is the US, where Grand Seiko sales increased approximately 10 times within five years of becoming an independent brand,” says Naito.

“The contribution of international markets has grown significantly compared with the period before the brand’s separation. Today, the sales to the non-Japanese consumers are as big as those to the Japanese consumers, if not bigger.” Seiko Group now plans to repeat this with its other fine watchmaking brand, Credor, which began exporting last year after just over 50 years of selling solely within Japan.

Naito says the US is “one of the most important growth markets” for Seiko Group, led by sales of Grand Seiko, Prospex, Presage and Seiko 5 Sports. This year, Seiko extended its relationship with Japanese baseball superstar Shohei Ohtani, who plays for the Los Angeles Dodgers. He is now an ambassador for Seiko and Grand Seiko, and Naito expects the partnership to raise the brands’ profiles not only among US consumers, but also in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, where the sport is also popular. Other global markets delivering “strong momentum” for Seiko include India and Australia.

Naito says Seiko’s international growth has also been accompanied by a shift in consumer perception. “I cannot speak for the entire industry but, in my view, historically Japanese watchmaking was generally valued in the context of functional and practical excellence,” he says. “However, in recent years at Grand Seiko we have seen a growing appreciation not only for functionality, but also for the craftsmanship and aesthetic sensibility behind our watchmaking.”

This is a trend that Sven Erik Henriksen has also been monitoring closely. A decade ago, the longtime Swiss watch executive discovered small-batch Japanese brand Minase, which specialises in the zaratsu mirror-polishing technique. It was launched in 2005 by Japanese toolmaker Kyowa and uses Swiss-made movements.

Henriksen began representing the brand as a sales agent in Europe and the Middle East in 2016, and his first move was to create branding that focused on its Japanese DNA. “We spent about a year preparing the material,” he recalls. “You can imagine that Japanese people selling Japanese watches to Japanese people do not need to show temples or Mount Fuji.

Minase Seven Windows

Orient Bambino

“They were following a different line of industrial manufacturing and precision, which are the strengths of the brand, but you couldn’t tell that it was Japanese. I sent photographers to Japan to get the feeling of the countryside, and impressions of the traditional dancing, cooking, sake brewing.”

Henriksen says overseas collectors have also become more receptive to Japanese brands. “Customers are more excited about Japanese brands than Swiss brands because they all own two or three Swiss watches and they are looking for something different,” he says. Henriksen exhibits the brand at collector shows in Europe, including Geneva Watch Days and a specialist show called Matsuri that took place in Lyon, France, at the end of September, organised by Japanese watch magazine Wadokei.

With annual production of 600 watches, Minase is one of several boutique Japanese watchmakers gaining international attention. Kurono Tokyo, led by watchmaker Hajime Asaoka , is another. It produces sought-after timepieces at accessible prices, and limits new releases to one per customer. Its latest watch, which opened for pre-order at the end of September, is the $2,380 Calendrier Small Batch Release with a blue dial bearing vertical guilloche stripes and “Japan Made”.

Independent watchmaker Masahiro Kikuno, who in 2013 became the first Japanese full member of the Académie Horlogère des Créateurs Indépendants — the world’s most prestigious assembly of skilled independent watchmakers — has temporarily suspended new orders until at least 2032.

Price is another factor in Japanese brands’ international positioning. Many remain relatively inexpensive compared with Swiss mechanical watches, an advantage that extends beyond small independent makers.

Wiebke Bird, head of Orient Europe at Epson Europe, has been charged with growing the Japanese-made Orient watch brand’s sales in her territory, and its pricing has helped win retail distribution. Seiko Epson — a separate, independently managed company from Seiko Watch Corporation — acquired a majority stake in Orient Watch in 2009, making it a wholly owned subsidiary before fully merging operations in 2017.

“Our offering for in-house mechanical movements is so unique at our price point that really that’s the thing that makes us the most interesting,” says Bird, who says the brand has “largely moved away” from quartz movements. Its entry-level AC0F mechanical model sells for less than £260, and Bird says the brand attracts particularly strong interest from consumers in their twenties and thirties.

The UK, which Orient entered in 2023, has become one of its faster-growing European markets, where it sells directly to consumers online while also partnering with retail chains including Ernest Jones and F Hinds. Last year, it achieved sales growth of 100 per cent in the UK, and expects it to be between 50 per cent and 75 per cent up in 2026. Much of the sales growth in Europe is being driven by watches priced at £500 or less, which Bird says is very different to Orient’s domestic market, where its premium line Orient Star is more dominant.

Despite its European strategy being led by affordability, Bird believes that outdated perceptions of Japanese watches as being “less than” Swiss watches is linked to its history with quartz movements. Seiko was the first brand to launch a commercial quartz wristwatch with the Seiko Astron in 1969, which led Swiss manufacturers to follow suit. This ushered in the so-called quartz crisis of the 1970s as inexpensive quartz watches flooded the market, decimating sales and production of mechanical timepieces.

“[In the decades since the quartz crisis] people have found that [the Japanese watch industry] wasn’t just about the performance of timekeeping at the expense of the craftsmanship or the desirability of a mechanical watch,” Bird says.

“Japanese brands like us are seen more and more to be continuing that mechanical watch tradition and craftsmanship. It’s recognised that we’re using efficiency, design and engineering to deliver an affordable mechanical watch, not just affordable quartz.”

rows.title: Andy Burnham searches for UK alternative to Palantir
rows.content:
Chris Smyth , Lucy Fisher and Laura Hughes in London

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

Andy Burnham’s government is searching for a UK alternative to Palantir, as the prime minister’s “Buy British” push triggers a hunt to find a homegrown replacement for the controversial US software group in the NHS and the Ministry of Defence.

Ministers have identified a handful of UK technology companies they hope might be candidates to take over the health service’s Federated Data Platform, as they consider applying a break clause in Palantir’s contract in March next year, people familiar with the matter told the FT.

Meanwhile, a defence minister has told parliament that the government is sounding out alternative suppliers for its MoD contract.

Some government figures are pushing to replace Palantir , which has come under fire over its links to the Trump administration and the US defence sector, to reduce the risk of a backlash by progressives against Burnham’s drive to foster the British AI industry.

Palantir won a £330mn contract from NHS England (NHSE) in 2023 to run the health service’s Federated Data Platform, a system designed to drive efficiencies and improve care in hospitals by joining up data better.

But the project has been beset by controversy, with NHSE claims about the success of the platform under growing scrutiny after the FT identified a litany of errors in a key underlying dataset.

This year, a minister was forced to apologise after the FT revealed some Palantir staff would have “unlimited access” to identifiable patient information while working on one part of the FDP, which NHSE had failed to disclose.

One option under consideration is to offer Palantir a temporary contract extension of about 12 months to give more time to develop a British alternative, according to people familiar with discussions. The current contract stipulates a minimum two-year extension from March.

Ministers are also considering whether the FDP programme could be divided between several companies, rather than run solely by Palantir.

Quantexa, which was in the running for the FDP contract in 2023, is among three or four British tech companies being considered, according to people familiar with discussions. The others are not known.

However, no decisions have yet been taken, and some Labour figures argue that Palantir’s UK-based business should be considered a British company under Burnham’s definition.

Tom Bartlett, former deputy director of data engineering and integration at NHS England, said it would be “hugely risky” to replace Palantir and “a leap into the unknown”.

“There isn’t a platform that can replace the functionality that Palantir can bring,” he said. “They [the NHS and government] can assemble a group of people who are confident they could do it, but they would be proving themselves for the first time and it would be a gamble.”

While the government began a review of Palantir’s contract when Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister, a specific search for a British alternative is under way after Burnham said he wanted more government spending to go to UK businesses.

“I don’t think we should allow the culture of sending everything outside of this country to continue — this will be a big change under this government,” he said in his first House of Commons appearance as prime minister.

At the Labour Party conference in Liverpool this week, first secretary of state Louise Haigh said the government wanted to build “sovereign capabilities” in AI and boost the UK tech sector. This would ensure the country would not “be in hock to foreign giants”, she added.

One Labour figure confirmed that Haigh’s intervention was “a shot across the bows” at Palantir, adding: “There’s a wider question here about building up sovereign capabilities and capacity — and we do have world-leading UK expertise in this area.” The person said there was a general sense among officials that the UK state was “overly reliant on Palantir and overseas capabilities more widely”.

The Cabinet Office, which runs the machinery of government, has recently reviewed its public procurement rules and rewritten the “social value” requirements to focus more narrowly on UK job creation and skills development.

However, officials have stressed that these criteria are legally “country agnostic”: while they favour companies supporting British jobs and training, that does not have to mean British-owned groups.

Another government figure said there was a particular focus on sovereign capabilities in health technologies, which ministers hoped could transform the NHS while fostering an industry based on its rich data sets.

AI minister Kanishka Narayan told a Politico event on the sidelines of Labour’s conference that polling consistently showed “the British public wants to make sure that their private data, particularly in healthcare, isn’t in the hands of foreign billionaires and foreign firms abroad”.

James Frith, the health innovation minister, told MPs last month that he was “concerned about mistrust of Palantir and the impact it could have on people’s willingness to share data with the NHS”.

Questions about Palantir’s involvement in the health service are seen as more acute than its work with the MoD, according to officials, but it is also being examined.

In November 2022, Palantir was awarded a three-year contract by the MoD worth £75.2mn after the tender was not advertised. In December 2025, the company was directly awarded another three-year contract, again without any competition, worth £240.6mn.

Speaking in June, in response to questions on the contract, defence minister Lord Vernon Coaker said: “We are seeking to look at options with small and medium-sized and other companies that could provide the same capability, so that we have a competitive process in future.”

The process would “keep Palantir on its toes in the marketplace as well”, he added.

Other European governments are seeking to cut their reliance on American technology providers amid growing concern over US President Donald Trump’s foreign policy.

France and Germany have excluded or cut contracts with Palantir from their armed forces and intelligence agencies in recent months, seeking more local alternatives.

Palantir said in a statement that its software was “helping to deliver better care” and that it was “deeply committed to the UK”.

“More than one in six of our global workforce is based here . . . And all UK government data is stored in the UK,” it added. The Department of Health did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

An MoD spokesperson said: “As set out in the Defence Investment Plan, we will bring forward a package of ‘backing British’ measures to ensure that defence spending is driving value back into local communities, while remaining consistent with our international obligations.

“We continue to work with a range of international suppliers based on operational requirements, including Palantir, which is a longstanding technology investor in the UK economy.”

rows.title: Nike to cut jobs as it forecasts revenue decline in the coming year
rows.content:
Gregory Meyer in New York

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

Nike set out plans to cut jobs and forecast a decline in revenue in the coming year as its shoes and sportswear sales stall in markets from the US to China.

Sales in the current fiscal year, which began in June, would probably fall by billions of dollars, the company said as it released its first-quarter results on Thursday.

The US company intends to reduce its 73,000-employee headcount as part of a new $2.5bn cost drive. Nike also plans to open a new campus in Bengaluru, India, and consolidate its geographic divisions to three from four.

“The future will belong to companies that can move faster, serve athletes and consumers more locally, and invest more aggressively in innovation. To do that, Nike must make changes to become a more agile, efficient and athlete-focused company,” chief executive Elliott Hill said in a note to employees.

Shares fell by 6.6 per cent to their lowest since 2013 in after-market trading, deepening a decline that has taken Nike down by more than half over the past year.

The results come as Hill is about to mark two years in the job pursuing a turnaround strategy after the company had suffered from an over-reliance on classic brands and lost shelf space in retail stores after emphasising direct sales.

It has been slow to catch fire. Revenue in the first quarter that ended in August totalled $11.2bn, down 4 per cent year on year and worse than consensus estimates compiled by Visible Alpha. Net income fell by 2 per cent to $712mn.

Sales plunged by 22 per cent in China , where competing local brands, with origins as manufacturers for western labels, have squeezed Nike’s market share.

Nike’s sportswear revenue also shrank by double digits, Hill told analysts. Another source of weakness was its Jordan basketball shoe and apparel brand, named after the former NBA star.

“With Jordan brand footwear, we’re going to get back to leading the scarcity model that we created. Simply put, we’ve been oversupplying our iconic retro product, asking them to do too much,” Hill told analysts.

Nike said the new cost-cutting programme, called Pace, is expected to save $2.5bn over the next five years. It did not disclose how many or where jobs will be cut. On the campus in Bengaluru, Hill described India as “an important growth market and manufacturing hub for Nike, with strong capabilities and access to talent”.

“As we change how and where we work, Nike will require fewer roles over time,” Hill said in his note. “These decisions are about redirecting investment toward the areas most critical to winning: product innovation, brand storytelling, consumer connection, sport and growth.”

rows.title: US sanctions Kremlin-backed fintech A7 for allegedly assisting Iran
rows.content:
Amy Mackinnon in Washington

Published October 1 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

The US Treasury has designated Kremlin-backed fintech company A7 a transnational criminal organisation, accusing it of enabling Iran and its proxy groups to evade western sanctions.

The measures announced on Thursday would freeze any assets held by the cross-border payments company in the US and prohibit Americans from doing business with A7 or any subagents acting on its behalf.

A7 was established by sanctioned Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor with support from Promsvyazbank, a state-owned Russian bank with close links to the Kremlin’s defence industry, which is also subject to US sanctions.

The Kremlin has touted A7 as an alternative to the western payments system as Russia’s economy has been isolated by western sanctions imposed in the wake of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

An FT investigation last month revealed how A7 relied on a vast document-forgery operation to move billions of dollars through the international finance system, using an extensive network of front companies.

Hundreds of thousands of internal files the FT obtained detailed how the company was able to funnel more than $6.9bn through the international banking system, including through lenders such as Standard Chartered and Citigroup.

The FT found evidence of 100 A7 front companies making payments between late 2024, when the fintech was established, and August 2025, while the documents mention at least a further 100 such groups. These include at least 61 in the United Arab Emirates, 87 in Hong Kong, 16 in Kyrgyzstan and 14 in Indonesia.

The Treasury said: “These subagents form a core layer of the A7 network’s operational architecture as a purpose-built sanctions evasion and money laundering mechanism connected to Russian illicit finance and exploited by other illicit finance threat actors, including Iran.”

At a September conference attended by Russian President Vladimir Putin, Shor said the platform processed 1,500 to 2,000 transactions daily. He claimed that in the preceding 10 months, it had processed some Rbs7.5tn ($91.5bn).

As part of the package of measures announced on Thursday, the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network has also proposed a rule that would bar the transmittal of funds involving A7’s vast network of subagents.

The EU and the UK imposed sanctions on A7 last year, while the US imposed sanctions on select entities from the group’s network involved in sanctions evasion.

Donald Trump’s administration, which has largely held off imposing financial sanctions on Russia over the war in Ukraine, framed the move as part of ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ which seeks to isolate Iran’s economy.

Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said: “Treasury is dismantling the financial infrastructure that allows Iran and other adversaries to evade sanctions, move illicit funds and undermine the integrity of the global financial system.”

rows.title: Investigative outlet deepens antisemitism claims against French far right’s Jordan Bardella
rows.content:
Leila Abboud and Sarah White in Paris

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

An investigative media outlet has published what it said was authenticated proof that Jordan Bardella, a top figure in the French far right, wrote antisemitic private messages as a teenage activist, despite his vehement denials.

The fresh revelations by Mediapart come three days after it reported that Marine Le Pen’s right-hand man — who she has billed as her future prime minister on a joint ticket as she bids to become French president — had expressed deeply anti-Jewish views to party colleagues from 2013 to 2015, starting when he was 17.

Bardella , leader of the Rassemblement National party, immediately hit back against the new report, saying the “so-called proof” consisted of “crude montages, obscure and easily manipulated screenshots, recycling vile statements that I obviously never made”.

Mediapart on Thursday published more extensive excerpts from the messages referenced in its original story and explained its verification process. Its reporters said they had received information from two separate anonymous sources, who were in Bardella’s entourage when he joined the RN. They then requested logs directly from Facebook to prove that the conversations on its messaging system were not falsified or doctored.

Mediapart said it then carried out other steps to establish that the account did belong to Bardella.

“This is terrible for Brand Bardella,” said Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group consulting firm. “It does raise the question of whether he remains the number two on the ticket, as it is a joint proposition.”

A lawyer for Bardella did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest revelations.

Appearing on France’s LCI news channel on Thursday evening, Bardella said: “Like many French people, I am appalled by how flimsy this investigation is . . . So we will explain ourselves before the courts, and I think Mediapart could rename itself ‘Mediaflop’.”

Bardella has filed a defamation case against Mediapart and accused the outlet of being run by radical leftists intent on “assassinating” him politically and bringing down the RN. On Tuesday, Le Pen expressed her “absolute confidence” in Bardella, vowing to prove that the Mediapart report was “a crazy manipulation”.

The scandal has badly damaged the Rassemblement National just as Le Pen is polling as the frontrunner to take the Élysée Palace in the two-round vote in April. It risks undercutting her 15-year campaign to “detoxify” the far-right movement founded by her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, who was convicted of hate speech for downplaying the Holocaust.

She and her closest allies have viewed shedding the movement’s antisemitic past as key to it becoming France’s most popular party, based on a platform of intense opposition to immigration combined with advocacy for the working class. In 2015, Le Pen kicked her father out of the party after he repeated his claim that the Nazi gas chambers were a “detail” of second world war history and made other controversial remarks.

According to the messages published by Mediapart, Bardella allegedly wrote: “All the banks are owned by Jews,” that “the Jew must dominate other people, squash them or steal from them” and warned against “a new world order dominated by Israel”.

Le Pen has sponsored Bardella’s rapid rise up the RN ranks, even naming him as her potential successor to run for president when there was a risk she would be banned over an embezzlement conviction. Le Pen was cleared to run by an appeals court in July.

Bardella, 31, is wildly popular among the RN voter base. He was seen by some as an even stronger candidate than his mentor because he did not carry the stigma of the Le Pen name. With a slick TikTok presence that has won over both young voters and retirees long wary of the RN, he was also supposed to represent the new face of the far-right movement.

“Jordan Bardella did not merely produce antisemitic writings at the start of his political career,” Mediapart wrote. “He also lied to the entire country by refusing to acknowledge that he had written the texts himself.”

rows.title: Europe braces for ‘severe hybrid attacks’ from Russia, says Friedrich Merz
rows.content:
Anne-Sylvaine Chassany and Katya Arenina in Berlin

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

Europe is preparing for “severe” Russian hybrid attacks, said German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as Vladimir Putin threatened that his conflict with the west could reach a “fatal point of no return”.

Russia’s escalating rhetoric underscores a tenser phase of the war in Ukraine, with Moscow intensifying its strikes on Kyiv and EU leaders sounding the alarm over what they describe as a Russian campaign of sabotage, cyber attacks and other destabilising operations.

Moscow’s escalation was a “sign of Russia’s desperation in the face of its unsuccessful war in Ukraine”, Merz said on Thursday.

“We are preparing for further hybrid attacks, including severe ones,” he said in a speech marking the award of the Westphalian Peace Prize to Nato. “Should they occur, we would respond quickly and very clearly.”

Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow on Thursday, Putin confirmed that Russia’s foreign ministry had sent warnings to several countries and said Moscow would consider using all weapons at its disposal in the event of a direct attack on Russian territory.

“If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation — in this case, [the Baltic Sea exclave of] Kaliningrad, although other territories could also be involved — the question of Russia using every weapon at its disposal will inevitably and immediately be put on the agenda.”

The German government has blamed Moscow for an explosives-laden drone attack in August at Leipzig airport, a crucial logistics hub for military aid sent to Ukraine.

Belgium’s defence minister Theo Francken on Wednesday warned of a “dark winter” ahead as a result of Russia’s continuing campaign of hybrid attacks on Europe, while Danish intelligence recently warned that Moscow could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months.

Putin said the world was living through a dangerous moment. Speaking about the possible use of nuclear weapons in the event of a direct attack on Russia, he said Russia might have to rely on what he called its military “competitive advantages” against a much larger European adversary.

He noted that France and the UK were also nuclear powers, but added: “No one else has the kind of strike capabilities that Russia has today. And that is our competitive advantage.”

He added: “The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return. At the heart of this escalation lie arrogance and overconfidence. This is a path to the brink of the abyss . . . Can we be certain that these weapons will never be used? Well, of course not. We must bear this in mind and avoid such an outcome.”

In a letter sent this week to Nato , Moscow said it could use nuclear weapons against Nato countries in response to what it described as the military alliance’s plans to hinder access to Kaliningrad.

Two officials familiar with the matter said that in the letter Moscow had accused Nato of taking a “dangerous and reckless course” towards Russia and its exclave. The letter included a warning about “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict”.

Nato responded by accusing Moscow of “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric” and said it posed no threat to Russia.

Moscow claimed Nato was preparing for potential military operations to blockade Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave bordering Poland and Lithuania, citing the defence alliance’s exercises in the region and the Baltic Sentry mission to protect undersea infrastructure.

Asked about the letter on Thursday, Putin insisted that Moscow was “not trying to frighten anyone”.

The warning was “not intimidation”, he said, but “a response to attempts to intimidate us”.

rows.title: US mortgage rates jump the most in four years in blow to housing market
rows.content:
Peter Wells and Zehra Munir in New York

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

US mortgage rates jumped the most in four years as an accelerating sell-off in government bonds deals a fresh blow to the housing market just weeks ahead of midterm elections.

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.28 per cent as of October 1, an increase of 0.25 percentage points from a week ago, Freddie Mac said on Thursday.

The quarter-point jump was the biggest since October 2022.

It brings US mortgage rates to their highest level since late 2023, in an increase fuelled by expectations that the Federal Reserve will need to raise borrowing costs again after a September increase as it seeks to stamp out a bout of inflation that has been exacerbated by President Donald Trump’s Iran war and a surge in AI-related spending.

The rise comes weeks before crucial midterm elections as polls show Americans are increasingly concerned about the spiralling cost of living.

The 30-year mortgage rate dipped below 6 per cent in late February for the first time since September 2022, days before the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran. It has climbed since then as disruptions to commodity exports from the Middle East have spurred inflation around the world.

Mortgage rates have jumped following a sell-off in US government debt, with Treasuries having posted their worst month in four years in September.

Rising mortgage costs have piled pressure on the housing sector , with prospective buyers deterred by elevated borrowing costs and record-high house prices, according to the Case-Shiller home price index. Homebuilder sentiment has also been depressed by a lack of buyer demand and the high cost of construction.

KB Home, one of the US’s biggest listed homebuilders, last week reported a 20 per cent year-on-year decrease in third-quarter revenue and a 19 per cent drop in homes delivered as it acknowledged that market conditions had weakened since June.

Jeffrey Mezger, executive chair at KB Home, said: “Higher mortgage interest rates have further pressured affordability and, together with geopolitical uncertainty and broader economic headwinds, have caused many prospective buyers to be more cautious on purchasing a home.”

Industry rival Lennar Corporation, the second-biggest home builder in the US by volume, last month pinned year-on-year declines in third-quarter revenue, new orders and adjusted earnings on deteriorating buyer affordability.

“Skyrocketing oil prices, a dismal job market and a war no one wanted are ingredients for a disaster,” said Jake Kennedy, a Nashville-based affiliate broker at Compass. “I think anyone who has been actively or passively looking now has yet another reason to press pause on their home search.”

Trump has emphasised housing affordability as a central mission of his presidency, introducing measures including a clampdown on investors buying up single-family housing.

The cost of living is a major concern for Republicans as they strive to maintain control of the Senate and the House of Representatives in the upcoming midterm elections.

rows.title: Ex-HSBC banker banned for dodging £5,900 in train fares
rows.content:
Martin Arnold

Published October 1 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

A former HSBC banker has been banned from working in financial services by the UK watchdog after being convicted of fraud over a “doughnutting” scam he devised to dodge almost £6,000 of train fares.

The Financial Conduct Authority said it banned Joseph Molloy from working in any regulated financial services activity because his conviction “shows he lacks honesty and integrity” and he was not fit and proper to carry out such roles.

Molloy, who was head of passive equity at HSBC Asset Management until he retired last year, pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation this year after being caught using fake names and addresses to buy smart cards, which he used to dodge fares at least 740 times.

The 53-year-old devised a “doughnutting” scheme to buy tickets for short trips at the start and end of the journey from his home in Orpington, south London, to HSBC’s office in Canary Wharf. The scam meant he avoided paying for a “hole” in the middle of his commute.

The former banker also obtained a Jobcentre Plus discount, for which only unemployed people or those seeking work are eligible, to get 50 per cent off ticket prices.

The FCA’s lifetime ban for Molloy, who evaded £5,911 of fares, underlines the watchdog’s determination to crack down on examples of unethical conduct or dishonesty in the City of London. Last month, it broadened its powers to tackle more types of non-financial misconduct such as harassment and bullying.

The move mirrors a similar ban the FCA gave in 2014 to Jonathan Burrows, a former managing director at BlackRock Asset Management, who paid £43,000 to settle allegations of fare dodging over a period of several years.

The FCA said on Thursday that Molloy had not exercised his right to challenge the ban and the former HSBC executive had “informed the authority that he accepts that he fell below the standards of behaviour expected by the authority”.

In February, Molloy, who previously worked at State Street and Legal & General, was sentenced at Inner London Crown Court to 10 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 18 months. He was prohibited from travelling on Southeastern rail for 12 months and ordered to carry out 80 hours of unpaid work and 10 rehabilitation activity days.

He was also ordered to pay £5,000 in compensation to Southeastern, costs of £150 and a victim surcharge of £187.

At the sentencing hearing, the judge said Molloy had devised “a sophisticated and determined fraud” that had been “sophisticated, with considerable planning, conducted over a period of almost 12 months”.

The judge said that although Molloy was “clearly in a financial position to pay the fares, you decided to evade them and that causes a loss to the whole of society”.

However, the judge also took into account a number of mitigating factors, including that Molloy was experiencing difficult personal circumstances after his mother’s death, that he ceased the activity of his own volition and had shown genuine remorse.

Will Hanson, a barrister at Garden Court Chambers who represented Molloy, did not respond to a request for comment. HSBC declined to comment.
